title: How heavily will Buffalo Bills lean into tight ends in Week 1, throughout 2026 season?
summary: Josh Allen is going to throw the football to receivers more frequently this season than he did in 2025, but we can’t forget about the tight ends — particularly Dalton Kincaid — in this Buffalo Bills offense. It’d be next to impossible for Allen to throw the ball to receivers less than the 270 targets […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - NOVEMBER 2: Dalton Kincaid #86 of the Buffalo Bills celebrates after winning the game against the Kansas City Chiefs at Highmark Stadium on November 2, 2025 in Orchard Park, New York. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images Josh Allen is going to throw the football to receivers more frequently this season than he did in 2025, but we can’t forget about the tight ends — particularly Dalton Kincaid — in this Buffalo Bills offense. It’d be next to impossible for Allen to throw the ball to receivers less than the 270 targets to wideouts last year, which was the seventh-lowest figure in the NFL. And for as much as we’re all aware of the receiver glitz and glam of Joe Brady’s national title winning season at LSU as the offensive coordinator in 2019 with Justin Jefferson and Ja’Marr Chase at his disposal, that magical year isn’t necessarily a glimpse into how the Bills head coach will deploy offensive personnel — anyone in their right mind would’ve been wideout-heavy with Jefferson and Chase as headliners. Remember, the Bills decided to keep just five receivers to four tight ends on their initial 53-man roster after the preseason, and Kincaid is playing on the final “cheap” portion of his rookie contract this season. Earlier this week, Joe Buscaglia of The Athletic wrote he believes Kincaid is in line for an “enhanced role” in the Bills, which won’t be difficult given former first-rounder only appeared on 26.8% of Buffalo’s offensive snaps in 2025. Kincaid didn’t play against the Texans last season, a game in which Allen and Co. certainly could’ve used the tight end who ultimately led at his position in yards per route run — the ultimate efficiency metric — at 2.79 yards. In his prolonged absences, Dawson Knox enjoyed his most productive season since his nine-touchdown 2021 and highest YPRR of his NFL career to date (1.35). Jackson Hawes, who played 43% of Buffalo’s offensive snaps, amassed a rather impressive YPRR of 1.89 and Allen had a 143.7 rating when targeting the rookie. Another byproduct of Kincaid’s prolonged absences… the Bills were in fact not near the top of the league in ‘12’ personnel — the most common personnel grouping with 2+ tight ends on the field. In fact, Buffalo’s 11.5% usage of 12 personnel was the third-lowest percentage in football in 2025. But what if we’ve been perceiving Kincaid wrong all along, or, at least differently from how the Bills have — and may continue — to view him? Check this tweet from Cover 1’s Anthony Prohaska on how Buffalo utilized their tight end: Note —it does feature a typo, it should read 2025 not 2026* Out of 106 TEs in 2026 with at least 100 snaps, here is where Dalton Kincaid ranked in positional alignment rate/usage: Inline: 32.6% (101st) Slot: 43.5% (9th) Wide: 23.4% (3rd) In general, the Bills ran the ball to Kincaid’s side at a rate of 30.2% which s 104th out of the 106 — Anthony Cover 1 (@Pro__Ant) May 8, 2026 Add those slot and wide percentages together for Kincaid to get 66.9% at one of the classic “receiver” pre-snap alignments. Pretty insane, right? And there’s more on this front: When lined up inline, the Bills ran toward Kincaid at a rate of 26.8%. Which is 91st out of 92 TEs with at least 100 inline snaps — Anthony Cover 1 (@Pro__Ant) May 8, 2026 From 2023-2025 Dalton Kincaid is 59th/60 qualifying TEs in rate of runs ran towards him at 37.5% When lined up inline, he’s 71st/71 qualifying TEs in rate of runs ran towards him at 38.3% When he’s on the field, the Bills are 9th in pass rate at 69.5% https://t.co/vy8eK5w6Ui — Anthony Cover 1 (@Pro__Ant) September 8, 2026 For all intents and purposes, Kincaid was more receiver than tight end in 2025, and the Bills have used him as such for the majority of his NFL career to date. Now, don’t get it twisted. I don’t look at Kincaid as a receiver, nor has he or should he be expected to provide the Bills with receiver-like volume and productivity. Being treated “like a wide receiver” is far different from actually being a wide receiver in the modern-day NFL. For example, among all receivers and tight ends who have run at least 750 routes since the start of 2023, Kincaid’s 5.1 targets per game would rank 51st among receivers. Of course, a quasi-argument of sorts can be made that the Bills could’ve / should’ve made sure they secured a receiver in the first round of the 2023 NFL Draft. Armed with the 27th overall pick and no receivers selected as the Seahawks went on the clock with pick No. 20, the Bills likely felt very good about their chances to pick a receiver in Round 1. Then, four receivers went consecutively, and Beane feverishly traded ahead of the Cowboys to secure Kincaid’s services. Afterward we heard Kincaid was Buffalo’s final prospect with a first-round grade, which is what prompted the trade up, and I believe that. He also could’ve been the consolation prize for an offensive-weapon hungry club that didn’t get the chance to draft a Round 1 receiver. Whether the latter is how the Bills were actually thinking, we’ll never know. But Kincaid has been deployed about as close to a receiver as a tight end can conceivably be through three NFL seasons. We’ve all heard about Kincaid bulking up this offseason — was that intention due to his knowledge of a more traditional tight end role for him in 2026? If so, it’d significantly decrease the run-pass telegraphing for Joe Brady’s attack this season, which, theoretically, could have a massively positive impact on Buffalo’s offensive efficiency that’s already established as one of the league’s best. On Sunday, with All-Pro Derek Stingley on the outside and Kamari Lassiter emerging as one of the better young No. 2 cornerbacks, in football, it feels like featuring Kincaid over the middle is the prudent decision for the Bills pass game. Yet, I don’t believe Knox and even Hawes will suddenly see their roles reduced. In 2025, the Bills were middle of the pack in 13 personnel usage — one running back, three tight ends — at 4.32% of their offensive snaps. The Rams were lightyears ahead of the rest of the NFL in 13 utilization, at a whopping 30.4%. Fascinatingly, Buffalo led the league in 22 personnel rate — two running backs and two tight ends — at 13.3% of their offensive snaps. With DJ Moore on the roster, it’d be easy now for the Bills to swap the extra running back for a receiver to ramp up multiple-tight end sets, right? Very easy. Given Kincaid’s receiver-like prowess at tight end along with his added strength, Knox’s reemergence in the offense a season ago, and Hawes in Year 2 after a successful rookie campaign, we shouldn’t be surprised if Brady leans into his luxurious depth at tight end and features the position, with positional hybrid Kincaid as the headliner against the Texans and throughout the 2026 season. And, heck, if internally the Bills don’t view him as a tight end, maybe simply a sizable jump in workload for Kincaid this season will actually make Buffalo believe it’s one of the more “receiver-heavy” offenses in the NFL.

title: Week 1 rooting interests for Buffalo Bills fans
summary: We made it, Bills Mafia.   The NFL season kicks off tonight. We have hours and hours of meaningful football ahead of us this weekend, and we definitely aren’t going to watch it without choosing sides. We’re the number one fan base in the league, after all.  There’s just one problem: We don’t really know who all of our enemies are yet. We […]
full_text: ORCHARD PARK, NEW YORK - JANUARY 04: A Buffalo Bills fan holds a sign reading "Bills Mafia" during the second quarter against the New York Jets at Highmark Stadium on January 04, 2026 in Orchard Park, New York. The Bills defeated the Jets 35-8. (Photo by Jason Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images We made it, Bills Mafia. The NFL season kicks off tonight. We have hours and hours of meaningful football ahead of us this weekend, and we definitely aren’t going to watch it without choosing sides. We’re the number one fan base in the league, after all. There’s just one problem: We don’t really know who all of our enemies are yet. We know we will almost never root for the AFC East, but beyond that, there are no playoff scenarios to calculate, no strength-of-victory tiebreakers to chase, and no late-season games where we suddenly find ourselves cheering for a team we’ve spent the previous four months making fun of. Rooting Interests is almost ridiculous in Week 1, but we’re Bills fans, so of course we’re doing it anyway. We don’t know which AFC teams will be standing between Buffalo and the Number 1 seed in January. We don’t know which teams will be fighting for the final wild-card spots, which supposedly good teams will fall apart, or which team nobody is thinking about right now will become a problem. But we still need somebody to root for; so, until the 2026 season gives us enough information to know exactly what Buffalo needs, we’re going to make our own rules. Think of this as the early-season Rooting Interests constitution: Always root for the Bills Build Buffalo’s tiebreakers for later. Knock last year’s AFC division winners down a peg. Push struggling AFC teams away from premium draft picks. Keep the best draft picks in the NFC. When two irrelevant NFC teams play, root for the better team to win and the worse team to lose. When the rules conflict, Buffalo’s 2026 interests come first. And, above all else, never forget that the Patriots, Dolphins and Jets can lose every single game they play, and we won’t feel even a little bit bad about it. One important reminder before we get started: These are rooting interests, not predictions. We aren’t picking who we think will win, who Vegas favors or even necessarily who we think is the better team. We’re simply deciding which outcome Bills Mafia should want based on what could help Buffalo — now, later or somewhere way down the road. AFC East Buffalo Bills over Houston Texans Seattle Seahawks over New England Patriots Tennessee Titans over New York Jets Las Vegas Raiders over Miami Dolphins Rest of the AFC Cincinnati Bengals over Tampa Bay Buccaneers Batlimore Ravens over Indianapolis Colts Cleveland Browns over Jacksonville Jaguars Atlanta Falcons over Pittsburgh Steelers Los Angeles Chargers over Arizona Cardinals Kansas City over Denver Broncos NFC vs NFC games LA Rams over San Francisco 49ers Chicago Bears over Carolina Panthers Detroit Lions over New Orleans Saints Green Bay Packers over Minnesota Vikings* Philadelphia Eagles over Washington Commanders Dallas Cowboys over New York Giants * This one doesn’t really matter. Buffalo plays them both. They had a half game separating them in last year’s final standings. But I’m petty, and the Vikings made me mad, so I’m going Green Bay. Are we going to look back at some of these picks in October and wonder what we were thinking? Almost certainly. There’s a decent chance one of the teams we’re rooting for this week becomes the team we need to lose games in December. But that’s a problem for future Bills Mafia. Right now, we have a full slate of football, a handful of rules, and absolutely no intention of sitting through any of these games without knowing who we want to win. Soon enough, we’ll be digging through strength of victory, conference records, and playoff scenarios looking for every tiny advantage Buffalo can get. The rules will change. The priorities will shift. And the standings will eventually tell us who the real enemies are. The math will come later. For now, we pick sides.

title: Panthers vs Bears: Matchups to watch
summary: The NFL season is off and running. We got our first ever Wednesday night opener and we’re going to get our first ever game in Australia of all places on Thursday. The league will get back to normal on Sunday, and the Carolina Panthers will play host to the Chicago Bears when that happens. These […]
full_text: Nov 30, 2025; Charlotte, North Carolina, USA; Carolina Panthers wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan (4) celebrates with Carolina Panthers wide receiver Jalen Coker (18) after a play during the fourth quarter against the Los Angeles Rams at Bank of America Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Scott Kinser-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The NFL season is off and running. We got our first ever Wednesday night opener and we’re going to get our first ever game in Australia of all places on Thursday. The league will get back to normal on Sunday, and the Carolina Panthers will play host to the Chicago Bears when that happens. These two teams share a link with one another that’s going to give meetings between them a little extra juice. The teams essentially swapped first overall picks in 2023 and 2024, resulting in Bryce Young landing in Carolina and Caleb Williams landing in Chicago. Both teams ascended to the playoffs last season but did so with lots of late winners and close game luck. Both are looking to prove that last season wasn’t a fluke and that they are going to be players when the postseason comes around in a few months. There are a fair few similarities in the roster constructions as well, and that makes for some interesting match-ups across both units. We’re going to look at one of those match-ups on each side of the ball. The Panthers defensive front vs the Bears offensive line The Bears had one of the best offensive lines in the NFL last season. According to ESPN’s pass block win rate statistic , the Bears were the best team in the league at protecting their quarterback, and they’re returning most of the key components from that unit. Darnell Wright, who the Bears picked with the first round pick they received in the Bryce Young draft, is one of the best right tackles in the league. Jonah Jackson and Joe Thuney are an elite guard duo, while Braxton Jones will retake his starting left tackle spot that he vacated due to injury last year. The one exception is at center. Last year, Drew Dalman earned a Pro Bowl spot for his elite play at that spot, but he surprisingly retired this past offseason at age 27. They’re replacing him with Garrett Bradbury, a Charlotte native who has just been a serviceable center to this point in his career. On the other side of the line is a Panthers front that has struggled to generate pressure for several seasons now. They ranked 24th in pass rush win rate last season, so they went out and spent big money on Jaelan Phillips to try to rectify that. He’ll have his hands full trying to make an impact against such a formidable tackle duo, so the real difference maker here might have to be Derrick Brown. He had a career high five sacks last season, and he’s the best interior presence the Panthers have. He’ll probably spend most of his time against the guards, but he should get some pass rush opportunities over Bradbury, who projects to be the weak point on this offensive line. He and rookie Lee Hunter on early downs will need to make some noise to mitigate the advantage the Bears offense has in the trenches. Tetairoa McMillan and Jalen Coker vs the Bears secondary The Bears overcame a brutal defense to make the playoffs last season, so they devoted their offseason to revamping that group. The biggest overhaul came in the secondary, but their big signing, cornerback Coby Bryant, is already out for the season with a knee injury. That leaves the Bears relying on Tyrique Stevenson (of Commanders Hail Mary fame) as their number two corner, which is exactly what they were trying to avoid by signing Bryant. Starting nickel Kyler Gordon is also out, leaving the Bears to rely on Cam Lewis to start in that spot. Their new starting safety duo is rookie Dillon Thieneman and veteran Xavier Woods, who Panthers fans should be familiar with. Jaylon Johnson is very good, so he’ll give problems to whoever is lined up across from him. Any other receiver on the field should be expected to have success. The unit has a reputation for catastrophic breakdowns in coverage, which should open up big play opportunities for McMillan and Coker. They need to capitalize on those opportunities and find the space provided to them, and quarterback Bryce Young needs to find those breakdowns in coverage and make some throws down the field. Bryce Young vs Week 1 This will be Young’s fourth Week 1. In his first three, he completed 49.5% of his passes for 4.4 yards per attempt (153.7 yards per game) with two touchdowns and six interceptions. It’s been nothing but bad. He’s entering a make or break year as it pertains to his future in Carolina. He can’t afford to start off so poorly once again.

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 3 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA--OCTOBER 27: Linebacker Sam Mills #51 of the Carolina Panthers follows the action against the Philadelphia Eagles in the game between the Carolina Panthers vs Philadelphia Eagles on October 27, 1996 at Veterans Stadium in Philadelphia Pennsylvania. (Photo by Al Pereira/Michael Ochs Archives) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #3. Sam Mills “When I found out I had cancer, there were two things I could do: quit or Keep Pounding. I’m a fighter. I kept pounding. You’re fighters, too. Keep Pounding! On offense. On defense. On special teams. On every. Single. Play. Keep pounding!” On January 2, 2004, Sam Mills unknowingly created the mantra for the Carolina Panthers franchise. He was a cancer riddled linebackers coach, uncharacteristically speaking to the whole team the day before a home playoff game against the Dallas Cowboys. But let’s back up first and get some perspective. Sam Mills was “the little guy who plays big” long before Steve Smith donned the black and blue. After going undrafted out of Montclair State following the 1981 NFL Draft, Mills signed on with the USFL’s Philadelphia Stars. Standing all of 5’9” and 230 pounds, played three years in the USFL before getting the chance at the NFL with the New Orleans Saints in 1986. He won one of the starting inside linebacker jobs in his first year with the team and wouldn’t relinquish that role for the next nine seasons, becoming a mainstay in the infamous Dome Patrol defense. During his Saints tenure, he earned four Pro Bowls and two Second Team All-Pro selections. In 1995, the expansion Carolina Panthers jumped at the chance to sign the Field Mouse after he was released by New Orleans. In Charlotte, Mills really shined. His first year with the Panthers, he made 110 tackles, five interceptions (one returned for a touchdown), 4.5 sacks, five forced fumbles, and four fumbles recovered. Mills was so good, he finished tied for third in the Defensive Player of the Year voting that year. He continued his dominance in 1996, earning another Pro Bowl nod, his first First Team All-Pro selection, and again finishing in the top five for DPOY. 1997 became his final NFL season, retiring after a solid but unremarkable statistical year that saw a huge drop in splash plays. His ties to Carolina, however, would stay strong as he joined the coaching staff as a defensive assistant for the 1998 season. He continued coaching the defense, particularly the linebackers, for the Panthers until a few months before his death in April of 2005. During the 2003 season, Mills was diagnosed with intestinal cancer. Regardless, he kept coaching, kept showing up every day. He didn’t miss a single game, scheduling his chemotherapy and radiation treatments around team activities. To make sure he could still be present for the team, Mills moved from the sideline to the coaches box on game days, still managing to attend one or two practices each week. The Panthers finished the season 11-5, drawing inspiration from Mills. From player accounts, Mills would still run sprints before practice despite the grueling treatment. He was never one to complain and never one to make grand speeches. So when he spoke up on that January day, the less than 100 people present listened intently. The Panthers went on to pummel the Cowboys 29-10. Then they beat the Rams on the road 29-23 in double overtime in a game they weren’t supposed to be competitive in. Then they beat the Eagles on the road 14-3 in a dominant performance by the defense. No matter the expectations, no matter the odds, no matter the opponent, Mills and his Panthers kept pounding. Mills lost his battle with cancer in 2005, earning a posthumous enshrinement in the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2022. While his time with the Panthers was brief, he achieved elite highs both personally and with the team. He starred in the franchise’s first NFC Championship Game and coached in the team’s first Super Bowl appearance. The undersized linebacker out of some no-name college in New Jersey changed the game for so many. So while the rival Saints can also lay claim to the beloved man, his dedication to the game of football and the Carolina Panthers specifically more than earned him this spot in our countdown.

We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - NOVEMBER 24: Luke Kuechly #59 of the Carolina Panthers reacts during a game against the New Orleans Saints at the Mercedes Benz Superdome on November 24, 2019 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Jonathan Bachman/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #4. Luke Kuechly Welcome to football season. Today is the first day of the NFL season, and there are just four days separating us from the start of Panthers football for the 2026 season. It seems fitting that the subject of today’s countdown piece is the Panther that was just enshrined in the Hall of Fame as part of the class of 2026, Luke Kuechly. Luke Kuechly is an all time example of a questionable process resulting in an incredible result. The Panthers drafted Kuechly ninth overall in 2012 despite having a three time Pro Bowler playing at his position (though he was coming off a significant injury, to be fair). They also had Thomas Davis trying to come back from his knee injuries and the evert reliable James Anderson at the other linebacker positions. Linebacker is typically not a premier position in general, so using a top 10 pick on one when you don’t really need one isn’t a great allocation of resources. But the move couldn’t have turned out better. Jon Beason, who never missed a start in his four years in the league, could never stay healthy after his achilles tear in 2011. His season ended after just four games due to a shoulder injury during Kuechly’s rookie season. Kuechly would step in as the starting middle linebacker to begin one of the greatest primes the league has ever seen at that position. Kuechly was on and off the field while Beason was healthy, which resulted in a slow start out of the gates. However, he played every snap from the time Beason was hurt through the end of the season and was able to amass a league high 164 tackles. That earned him Defensive Rookie of the Year Honors. That season would also be the only season of his career in which he wasn’t an All Pro. Luke Kuechly dominated the game from the linebacker spot in a way few players could. He was a maniacal film studier, which allowed him to key in on opposing offenses and diagnose plays even before the ball was snapped. In the run game, he would frequently beat running backs to the hole or shoot gaps right off the snap. He was elite in coverage as well, using his speed and anticipation to cover enormous amounts of ground and undercut routes in the middle of the field. His motor was relentless, and you’d be hard pressed to find many plays in which he wasn’t around the ball by the end of it. Kuechly’s career was cut short by repeated concussions, so he didn’t amass the counting stats that other all time greats have, but there is no denying the greatness of his peak. In his eight seasons, he was a first team All Pro five times and a second team All Pro twice. He led the league in tackles twice and intercepted at least one pass in every season. He finished his career with 21 interceptions (including postseason) and he ran three of those back for touchdowns. Two of those pick sixes came in the 2015 run to the Super Bowl. Kuechly returned to the Panthers a scout after his retirement but resigned from that job after just a year. He later joined the team as a color commentator on radio broadcasts along side Jake Delhomme. He’s now going to be the lead color commentator for NFL games on Netflix, so we’ll get to hear him in action on Thursday. Luke Kuechly was enshrined in the Pro Football Hall of Fame back in August, He’s the second player to spend the majority of their career with the Panthers to make the Hall of Fame, and he’s the first player to be drafted in the 2010s to make the Hall of Fame. It’s hard to earn that honor playing just eight seasons of NFL football, but that shows just how dominant Kuechly was during those eight seasons. There are very few players that played NFL football at a higher level, and for that, Luke Kuechly lands at number 4 on the list of top 100 Panthers of all time.

title: Bears vs. Panthers Injury Report: Odunze Listed As Limited
summary: As the Chicago Bears prepare for their first regular season game of the year against the Carolina Panthers on Sunday, the first official team injury reports for week 1 have been released. The Bears did not practice on Wednesday, so player participation listed on the injury report is an estimation. Just one player was listed […]
full_text: As the Chicago Bears prepare for their first regular season game of the year against the Carolina Panthers on Sunday, the first official team injury reports for week 1 have been released. The Bears did not practice on Wednesday, so player participation listed on the injury report is an estimation. Just one player was listed as DNP (did not practice): QB Tyson Bagent (back). Listed as limited were WR Rome Odunze (calf) and OL Ozzy Trapilo (knee). #Bears Injury Report The Chicago Bears did not practice on Wednesday, participation is an estimation. pic.twitter.com/B2LGzEsOXX — Bears Communications (@BearsPR) September 9, 2026 Of note, Odunze’s injury is not the same foot injury he was dealing with last year. There was some misinformation going around the internet concerning the nature of his injury in recent days. The calf injury is something new. Trapilo continues to work back from his season-ending torn patellar tendon injury, suffered in the playoffs against the Green Bay Packers. The fact that he already has just a “limited” designation in week one is quite remarkable given the seriousness of the injury he sustained in January. The Panthers also listed three players on their official injury report. OLB Patrick Jones II was listed as DNP, while both RB Jonathan Brooks and DT Bobby Brown III were listed as limited. The Bears take on the Panthers this Sunday at Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte, NC. The game takes place at 12:00 p.m. (Chicago time) and will be broadcast on FOX.

Caden Barnett, OG Kyle Hergel, iOL Christian Jones, OT Salvon Ahmed, RB Zavier Scott, RB Scotty Miller, WR Kaden Davis, WR J.P Richardson, WR Stephen Carlson, TE Qadir Ismail, TE Wayne Matthews III, LB Buddy Johnson, LB Marlen Sewell, S Deantre Prince, CB Marcus Davenport, DE Keidron Smith, S Here are the qualifications for practice squad eligibility and some rules to remember. A 17th player is permitted as long as he qualifies for the NFL’s International Pathway Program. Players with no accrued seasons (rookies) and those with fewer than nine regular-season games in their lone accrued season. A maximum of ten players are allowed who have earned no more than two accrued seasons. Up to six players with unlimited accrued seasons are permitted on the practice squad. However, the number of players in the last two categories cannot exceed 10 total players. Teams can elevate up to two practice squad players for each game, but they can still only have 48 players active on game day. After the game, the elevated player(s) will revert to the practice squad. A player can be elevated up to three times, but if he’s needed after that, the team would be required to sign him to the 53-man active roster. Players on practice squads are free agents who can be signed to another team’s active roster. A player’s current club can’t block him from leaving; they can only make a counteroffer to keep him. Ultimately, it’s the player’s decision. If a player is signed away, his new team must keep him on its 53-man roster for three weeks, but if he’s released, he’ll revert to his previous team. Players signed to another active roster are also guaranteed three weeks’ salary. A practice squad player can’t sign with his team’s upcoming opponent unless he does so six days before the upcoming game or ten days prior if his team is on its bye week.

title: Can the Bears stop Carolina’s Tetairoa McMillan when he’s lined up in the slot?
summary: The Chicago Bears kick off a highly anticipated 2026 season on Sunday, and they are matched up against a team that may have helped catapult them to that realm of anticipation. I am of course referring to the historic trade that netted the Bears Caleb Williams, DJ Moore, Darnell Wright, and others while giving the […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - JANUARY 10: Tetairoa McMillan #4 of the Carolina Panthers celebrates after a play during an NFL wild card playoff football game against the Los Angeles Rams at Bank of America Stadium on January 10, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Kevin Sabitus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Chicago Bears kick off a highly anticipated 2026 season on Sunday, and they are matched up against a team that may have helped catapult them to that realm of anticipation. I am of course referring to the historic trade that netted the Bears Caleb Williams, DJ Moore, Darnell Wright, and others while giving the Panthers the chance to select Bryce Young in 2023. This article isn’t meant to rehash the returns on this trade — though it is general consensus the Bears won by a wide margin — but it does underscore how these two teams are connected. Both have been on steady inclines back to relevance since the fateful trade, and both teams will be looking to return to the playoffs after both teams earned berths in 2025. A primary piece of the Carolina Panthers rebuild is wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan, or T-Mac for short. McMillan was a monster in his rookie campaign, notching just over 1,000 yards and 7 TDs, making him only one of 21 WRs since 2000 to surpass the 1k yard mark. Many view him as a boundary receiver exclusively, and why wouldn’t they? He is 6’5″ and has the athleticism to go up and snatch anything that comes his way. However, that discounts his versatility. T-Mac has already shown the propensity early in his career to play in the slot, as a sort of jumbo possession receiver. In fact, TMac ran 107 routes (20.7%) from the slot last year according to NFL Next Gen Stats. That’s not excessive, but also shows how the Panthers might exploit a clear weakness on the Bears. In fact, on 9/2, Panthers coach Dave Canales suggested that McMillan will work out of the slot more this season, per Sheena Quick of Fox Sports Radio 1340. Beyond that, T-Mac caught a whopping 69.7% of passes thrown to him when lining up in the slot. That amounted to 18 catches for 220 yards and 2 touchdowns. Again, not massive, but something worth emphasizing given the Bears’ hole at the slot corner position. While I still expect a heavy dose of McMillan lining up across from Jaylon Johnson or Tyrique Stevenson on the outside, their size could match up a little better with T-Mac on jump balls. Panthers QB Bryce Young ranked 22nd in the league with a 16.4% bad throw percentage, which could leave more room for hawking corners like JJ and Stevenson to come down with an INT. With the current uncertainty around Kyler Gordon and the presumed start for rookie Malik Muhammad II at nickelback, it’s entirely possible that Young turns to T-Mac in the slot early and often. And while Muhammad has decent size and length (6’-0″ tall with 32 3/8″ arms) he is still slight at 182 lbs, and prone to being bullied by the larger TMac. Or perhaps the Bears get Cam Lewis some reps at nickel, but Lewis (5’9″, 183) is shorter than Muhammad. I expect Chicago defensive coordinator Dennis Allen to mix up his coverages and bring in the likes of TJ Edwards, Devin Bush, and D’Marco Jackson to support Muhammad when TMac lines up inside. Keeping him contained will be crucial so that the Bears defense can stay on schedule and keep the Panthers behind the chains. What is the key one-on-one matchup you’ll have your eye on for Week 1?

title: 10 Thoughts on the NFL as the season starts tonight!
summary: Who said we had to wait until Week 1 was over to fire one of these up? We have Wednesday Night Football tonight (for some reason that escapes me)! So let’s talk about it, and what we can look forward to in the first week of the 2026 season. That way, if I’m wrong about […]
full_text: SANTA CLARA, CALIFORNIA - FEBRUARY 08: Christian Gonzalez #0 of the New England Patriots breaks up a pass intended for Jaxon Smith-Njigba #11 of the Seattle Seahawks during the second quarter in Super Bowl LX at Levi's Stadium on February 08, 2026 in Santa Clara, California. (Photo by Thearon W. Henderson/Getty Images) | Getty Images Who said we had to wait until Week 1 was over to fire one of these up? We have Wednesday Night Football tonight (for some reason that escapes me)! So let’s talk about it, and what we can look forward to in the first week of the 2026 season. That way, if I’m wrong about everything, you can laugh at me next Tuesday. 1. Call me a sucker, but I do like a good Super Bowl rematch to kick off the next season. This time around, I do expect the Patriots to put forth a way better showing than that ass-kicking they took in the championship game against the Seahawks. Having a bona fide WR1 like AJ Brown is eventually going to pay some dividends for MVP runner-up Drake Maye, and their defense is going to be motivated to put the clamps on Sam Darnold and Seattle’s offense. I’m remembering how the Chicago Bears handled the Indianapolis Colts back in the 2008 season opener—albeit two years after they faced off in the Super Bowl—and I’m getting some similar vibes about tonight. 2. Speaking of the Pats: I didn’t think there was ever a world in which the Patriots didn’t pay Christian Gonzalez before the season to make sure Week 1 featured the two highest-paid cornerbacks of all time (him and Seattle’s Devon Witherspoon). But man, Bob Kraft just had to push it to the 11th hour, didn’t he? You can talk about injury risk and a lack of interceptions if you want, but there aren’t many reasons I’ll accept for making Gonzalez, an All-Pro and Pro Bowler the last two years, respectively, wait for his bread. Any man who can put clamps on Jaxon Smith-Njigba can take my money. All I know is the Patriots better not pull this with Maye this offseason, or stuff’s gonna get weird in Foxborough. 3. The Chicago Bears look like a prime regression candidate in 2026, with a tougher strength of schedule, early injury issues, a bad defense (on paper, anyway) and a league that is now gunning for them, their head coach Ben Johnson, and their star quarterback Caleb Williams. And you know what? I don’t care. Some things about last year, like the insane takeaway production, are too variable to count on this season. But Johnson’s maniacal attention to detail and dedication to pounding the rock, along with Williams’ cold-blooded killer mentality, aren’t going anywhere. Whatever step back the Bears take in the luck department can be more than mitigated by Williams taking a step toward superstardom in his third season, and that doesn’t even account for the likes of Colston Loveland and Luther Burden III potentially taking bigger leaps in their second seasons. I’ll gladly take anyone’s cast-off Bears stock, thank you. 4. DJ Metcalf and Aaron Rodgers are made for each other. A hidden civilization under the ice of Antarctica? Okay, pal. As a man of science, my take on conspiracy theories is pretty simple: when you don’t know anything, it’s easy to believe anything. Which is why Rodgers seems able to keep convincing people to take him on even though he hasn’t been good since the Biden administration. 5. One person I’m very eager to watch this coming week? Patrick Mahomes. Given how the Chiefs offense has looked the last few years and Mahomes still working his back from an ACL tear, I’m not expecting him to look perfect in Week 1. I also don’t envision him running around or scrambling much, which could hinder some of his upside. But that’s actually part of the intrigue for me. We know Mahomes can dominate from the pocket, even without an elite supporting cast around him. (Don’t look now, but did Travis Kelce just gain a step back after looking slow and old last year?) With his legs still getting back under him, let’s see if Week 1 marks an evolution in the future Hall-of-Famer’s game. 6. Call me crazy, but I think this just might be Lamar Jackson’s year. The Ravens have fumbled away opportunity after opportunity, flamed out with title hopes on the line over and over. But something about this Jesse Minter addition and the growing urgency Jackson’s feeling to win before his prime years are out makes me think interestingly of the Seahawks last year. The Ravens under John Harbaugh were a mainstay that were carried largely by talent and simply not being as bad/unlucky as the rest of the division. This squad feels like it’s going to have some edge to it. I, for one, am ready to see Lamar finally get his. 7. I’m not entirely sure what to make of the Rams and the superteam they’re forming. But I did find myself asking a question that I’d love for you all to chime in on below: will Myles Garrett and Aaron Donald be the two best defensive players to line up next to each other? At this rate, Garrett will go down as one of the five best pass rushers ever to play the game, as long as he reaches 15 relatively healthy seasons. (If he averages no more than 10 sacks a year for the next six seasons, he’ll be top three in sacks all-time.) And Donald had an argument for being the most dominant interior defender of all time before he decided to come back and potentially add to his trophy case. Now, there will be times when the Rams put those two fiends next to one another on passing downs…Seriously, give me your best dynamic defensive duos ever in the comments below. 8. My personal over-under for Deshaun Watson starts before he’s finally benched for Shedeur Sanders is 5.5—and that’s only because they seem deadset on playing him purely for financial reasons. (Once again, give me your predictions below.) Personally, I’m here for all the Watson slander and can’t wait for him to fail. But honestly, why not just fail with Shedeur, bench Watson for the year, and get this over with? All that dead money you’re going to owe Watson next year will hurt a lot less when you get your pick of cheap first-round rookie quarterbacks. Either way, everyone knows that man’s future in football is cooked. Why delay it any longer? 9. My upset of the week: I have the Giants getting a rare win over Dak Prescott and the Cowboys on Sunday Night Football. It’s at home for New York. They have a new coach. They’ve revamped their lineup, especially the skill group around Jaxson Dart. And the Cowboys are the Cowboys, man. Dak is 14-3 against the Giants in his career, so history suggests this isn’t the smart bet. But this Giants team feels young, stupid, and arrogant enough—especially Dart—to think they’re going to come in and beat Dallas on national television. Count me in for that. 10. Bold prediction: the New York Jets get that first interception of the 2026 season in their first game, likely off some Cam Ward off-platform lob into double-coverage. Please. Let’s get that out of the way early. Because a whole year of no interceptions? That’s just sad, especially when your head coach specializes in defense!

title: 2026 Chicago Bears Season Preview: The Hunter is now the Hunted
summary: For every professional sports team, the end goal is always the same: Win a championship. Although that didn’t happen for the Chicago Bears in 2025, last season was easy to call a dream come true in many ways. Time flies, and sometimes it’s easy to forget the past. For most fans, 2024 was a season […]
full_text: For every professional sports team, the end goal is always the same: Win a championship. Although that didn’t happen for the Chicago Bears in 2025, last season was easy to call a dream come true in many ways. Time flies, and sometimes it’s easy to forget the past. For most fans, 2024 was a season they’d like to purge from their memories forever. While living through former head coach Matt Eberflus’s last season in Chicago wasn’t pleasant, it also reminded everyone to enjoy the good times while they last. That’s exactly what Ben Johnson provided this team last season: Hope. Eberflus became the first head coach in franchise history to be fired midseason. While that alone isn’t uncommon, his failures came at the cost of Caleb Williams’ development as a rookie. Johnson not only righted those wrongs, but he also instilled a new culture in the team and the city that should leave a lasting impression for years to come. Now comes the hard part: Maintaining that success. It’s been 20 years since the Bears experienced back-to-back playoff seasons. Johnson and his team broke multiple “curses” last year. Will this be the next? Despite a lack of “flash” this offseason, the organization is optimistic its core is in place and that last year’s experiences (both good and bad) will give the team more tools to complete the road to Super Bowl 60. With the season set to kick off this week, let’s dive into our yearly Chicago Bears season preview. Offseason Additions Pre-Draft: LB Devin Bush S Coby Bryant C Garrett Bradbury DT Neville Gallimore Others: WR Kalif Raymond, DB Cam Lewis, DT Kentavius Street, DT James Lynch, LB Jack Sanborn, and Xavier Woods. For the first time since the start of the rebuild, general manager Ryan Poles and the team took a more conservative approach to the start of the acquisition period. Losing Drew Dalman to retirement forced a trade for Bradbury, but the primary focus was adding speed. Both Bush and Bryant provide that in the second and third levels of the defense, while Raymond gives Johnson a familiar face to rely on at receiver. Gallimore, Woods, and Lewis should provide quality depth at their respective positions. Oh, and Jack Sanborn is back for a Round 2 with his hometown team. There’s no doubt that this free agency period lacked flash. Now, fans must hope that the core they established last season is enough to take them to the next level in 2026. They’ll be starting the season without Bryant at safety, which is a tough pill to swallow for a team that was hoping he’d set the tone for the entire defense. Draft: Trades: No. 460 to Tennessee Titans for No. 69 and No. 144 No. 129 & No. 144 to Carolina Panthers for No. 124 and No. #166 No. 239 and No. 241 to Buffalo Bills for No. 213 1st Round (#25) S Dillon Thieneman (Oregon) 2nd Round (#57) C Logan Jones (Iowa) 3rd Round (#69) TE Sam Rousch (Stanford) 3rd Round (#89) WR Zavion Thomas (LSU) 4th Round (#124) CB Malik Muhammad (Texas) 5th Round (#166) LB Keyshaun Elliott (Arizona State) 6th Round (#213) DT Jordan van den Berg (Georgia Tech) Following a lackluster free agency period, the Bears set their sights on yet another impactful draft class. Thanks to the DJ Moore trade, they came into the draft with four picks over their first three rounds. Round 1 started with a pleasant surprise in Thieneman. It was clear that safety was a top need for them, and having a player projected to go 10 picks early still on the board at 25 was about as good as it gets. They followed up the Thieneman pick with a trio of names on Day 2 that included Jones and two surprises in Roush and Thomas. Not many could have expected them to go all offense on Day 2, especially with the value of some of those picks in question. Luckily, they followed up on Day 3 with a trio of defensive players that, at worst, should provide quality depth over the next few seasons. All in all, this wasn’t the same impactful class as we’ve seen (on paper) over the last few years, but that was expected considering how much lower in each round they picked. All in all, they added what should be multiple Year 1 contributors with the idea of developing them into bigger contributors down the line. Fans shouldn’t expect the same early impact from this class, but as the season goes on, most should settle into roles that have them contributing weekly. Retained Free Agents: LB DeMarco Jackson LT Braxton Jones OL Theo Benedet S Elijah Hicks Others: QB Case Keenum, DE Daniel Hardy, and iOL Jordan McFadden. The ongoing trend of Poles and his front office not retaining many of their impending free agents continued this offseason. Despite having multiple starters hit the market, the team retained just two projected starters, along with some key depth pieces. Jackson was a must-re-sign after a breakout season, and picking up Benedet’s ERFA tag was a no-brainer. Retaining Jones for another year was a mild surprise, but much needed with Ozzy Trapilo’s status for the season still up in the air. The team also decided to keep their quarterback room together for another season, which seems smart after how well things went in 2025. All in all, each move made sense, even if fans expected to see more players back from last year’s roster. Contract Extensions: RT Darnell Wright 4 years, $116 million ($93 million guaranteed) Barring any last-minute surprises, Wright enters the regular season as the only player to receive a long-term extension this offseason. Given the money and resources needed for Caleb Williams and his offensive weapons in the near future, it makes sense. Wright was well-deserving of his new contract, and now holds the highest guarantee of any offensive lineman in NFL history. Offseason Subtractions S Kevin Byard WR DJ Moore (Traded) C Drew Dalman (Retirement) LB Tremaine Edmunds (Released) S Jaquan Brisker DT Gervon Dexter Sr. (Traded) Others: CB Nahshon Wright, WR Olamide Zaccheaus, DB C.J. Gardner-Johnson, DT Andrew Billings, LS Scott Daly, DE Dominique Robinson, LB Amen Ogbongbemiga, iOL Ryan Bates, DE Joe Tryon-Shoyinka, S Jonathan Owens, DT Chris Williams, TE Durham Smythe, CB Nick McCloud, WR Devin Duvernay, RB Travis Homer, and iOL Ricky Stromberg. Heading into the start of the new league year, many expected Byard to be retained on an affordable deal. Despite productive talks heading into the legal negotiation period, the Bears chose a different direction at both safety positions. Moore’s trade surprised some, but for those who watched his usage before Rome Odunze’s injury, it was clear Johnson never valued him as a top option in his offense. Edmunds was a no-brainer to release, considering his play and money owed. Wright and Gardner-Johnson were two unsung heroes of last season’s secondary, but both got bigger deals elsewhere. The rest of the names on this list were simply depth pieces or role players. While it would have been nice to retain more of last year’s “core,” this type of roster churn is expected for every team in the league each offseason. Reasons for Optimism 1. Year 2 of Ben Johnson and Caleb Williams should produce even more fireworks. As expected, last year’s offense looked worlds better than anything we saw under Eberflus. In some ways, it was reminiscent of Nagy’s first year as the team’s head coach, but if the early returns continue to trend in the right direction, Johnson’s reputation as one of the best offensive minds in football will be cemented. The work the first-year head coach was able to do in 2025 shouldn’t be overlooked, especially following a slow start to the season. Getting the most out of a young quarterback was his most important task, but the way he rebuilt the offensive line and drastically reshaped the running game might have been equally impressive. Chicago went from having one of the worst offensive lines in football to one of the best. Although two of their projected starters won’t be in the lineup for 2026, there’s reason to believe that Johnson and offensive line coach Dan Roushar will find a way…

title: Cost and complexity of how to watch the Bengals in the 2026 NFL season
summary: The ease of being able to watch your favorite NFL team each week has gotten to a breaking point for most fans. As the NFL has been able to sell off streaming rights for packages of games rather than as a whole to one company, you likely will need several subscriptions if you have cut […]
full_text: Bengals fans cheer on a home win after the fourth quarter of the NFL Week 12 game between the Cincinnati Bengals and the Pittsburgh Steelers at Paul Brown Stadium in downtown Cincinnati on Sunday, Nov. 28, 2021. The Bengals beat the Steelers 41-10. Pittsburgh Steelers At Cincinnati Bengals | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co The ease of being able to watch your favorite NFL team each week has gotten to a breaking point for most fans. As the NFL has been able to sell off streaming rights for packages of games rather than as a whole to one company, you likely will need several subscriptions if you have cut the cord. We are about to look at the real cost of being able to watch all 17 regular season games, and the reality of what watching the NFL in 2026 has become. Luckily, the Bengals aren’t as bad off as some teams that have to have Netflix. Below is The Athletic’s schedule along with what network will be airing the game. Cable or Satellite We are getting to the point that cord-cutting is getting as — if not more — expensive than the alternative of traditional cable or satellite TV. You could also potentially find an indoor antenna to potentially get games that way, but it also requires you to be in-market. NFL Sunday Ticket and NFL RedZone For out-of-market fans looking for a legitimate way to watch games, NFL Sunday Ticket on YouTube TV, or bought through your YouTube profile, will cover games outside prime-time slots. NFL RedZone tries to follow the most exciting action. Typically following games that are close to scoring or have a drastic turn. You do not have control over what you watch, so it isn’t ideal for watching specifically Cincinnati. This can also be found on NFL+ Premium (that can be bundled with ESPN Unlimited). Online Stream options for the TV games We are talking CBS (Paramount+), Fox (Fox One), ABC/ESPN (ESPN Unlimited), and NBC (Peacock). It may also be worth adding NFL Network here since they fall under the Disney umbrella now. With ESPN, you can get the Madrid game in Week 9 on ESPN Unlimited, NFL+ Premium, or regular NFL+ (both are mobile only). Depending on your cable package, all of these games should be available with the exception of maybe NFL Network. It is very important to note that all of these apps that stream afternoon games are in-market games ONLY. Prime Video Surprisingly, one of the easiest and most accessible streaming options. You just need Amazon Prime, which will give you access to Prime Video. You could also watch free on Twitch with a registered account. Unfortunately, this only covers the New Year’s Eve game against the Ravens in Week 17. Grand Total In-market fans: Basic Cable ~$30 (CBS, FOX, and NBC), Prime Video ~$15, NFL+ (mobile only) ~$7, and ESPN Unlimited (because the Bengals Week 11 Monday Night Football game is exclusive to ESPN and not simulcast on ABC) ~$30 Total a month: ~$82 or ~$67 (if you are willing to watch the Prime Video game on Twitch). You could also cut out cable costs entirely for an antenna, but you are risking quality and video dropping. You aren’t saving by streaming with Paramount+ ~$9, Peacock ~$13 (their base plan does not include live sports) and FOX One ~$20 totaling to ~$42 a month. Peacock and Paramount+ at least also let you have shows and movies for the ~$12 more Out-of-market fans: For new users, NFL Sunday Ticket is $30 a month ($60 a month for existing), Prime Video is ~$15 a month, NFL+ (mobile only) ~$7 a month, and ESPN Unlimited ~$30 a month Total a month: $82 for new Sunday Ticket users or $112 for existing (because you get punished for loyalty) As a reminder, you wouldn’t even have the choice of streaming the big three channels as out-of-market fans. That ~$42 a month would easily clear and be a much better deal than the ~$60 for returning customers. This is trying to map out the cheapest way for fans to enjoy all the Bengals’ games from at least the comfort of their own home. You can also account for maybe only getting subscriptions like NFL+ or ESPN Unlimited for just the month Cincinnati plays their game, but you have to remember to cancel those subscriptions. That also means you won’t be watching most Monday Night Football or international games, though. We are all just going to have to start finding people nearby to watch Bengals games with just to split the cost of watching the games. I at least hope this helps some of you plan out how you will be watching some of these games.

title: NFL analyst predicts Cashius Howell will win NFL Defensive Rookie of the Year Award
summary: The Cincinnati Bengals front office made an unprecedented move this offseason in trading their first round pick to the New York Giants in exchange for Dexter Lawrence. The Bengals were without a first round selection in this year’s draft, but Duke Tobin and his staff were able to snag a first-round talent in the second […]
full_text: PHILADELPHIA, PENNSYLVANIA - AUGUST 28: Cashius Howell #55 of the Cincinnati Bengals warms up prior to an NFL preseason game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field on August 28, 2026 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Cincinnati Bengals front office made an unprecedented move this offseason in trading their first round pick to the New York Giants in exchange for Dexter Lawrence. The Bengals were without a first round selection in this year’s draft, but Duke Tobin and his staff were able to snag a first-round talent in the second round. Cincinnati drafted Texas A&M edge Cashius Howell, the former SEC Defensive Player of the Year, in round number two to help boost a revamped defense. Howell recorded 32 total tackles (21 solo), an SEC-leading 11.0 sacks, and 1 forced fumble in 2025 for the Texas A&M Aggies and earned himself unanimous All-American honors. CBS Sports recently posted some predictions for the 2026 season, and John Breech has Howell bringing home some hardware this upcoming season. Breech believes Howell will be named the 2026 Defensive Rookie of the Year and also predicts the Bengals will go 11-6 and earn a wild card playoff berth . “The easiest way for a defensive player to win this award is to rack up sacks, and Howell is in the perfect position to do it,” Breech wrote. “With Dexter Lawrence now on the team, you can pretty much bet that every offense the Bengals play this year will be worried about slowing down Lawrence. That likely means Lawrence will regularly see double teams, which should open the door for someone on the defensive line to shine, and I think that someone will be Howell, who was taken with the 41st overall pick back in April.” It will be exciting to see this revamped defense in action next week against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, and it will also be fun to see how second-year defensive coordinator Al Golden will use his new weapons.

title: More buzz that the Bengals won’t get any big contract extensions done with 2027 free agents
summary: Throughout training camp and the preseason, much of the attention surrounding the Cincinnati Bengals was focused on Dexter Lawrence’s immediate impact on the defense and the growing pains of the offense implementing an under-center element to their playbook. But you know what didn’t get a lot of attention? Players eligible for contract extensions. That’s refreshing, […]
full_text: Oct 16, 2025; Cincinnati, Ohio, USA; Cincinnati Bengals cornerback DJ Turner II (20) gestures toward his bench as he walks off the field with an apparent injury against the Pittsburgh Steelers during the third quarter at Paycor Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Joseph Maiorana-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect Throughout training camp and the preseason, much of the attention surrounding the Cincinnati Bengals was focused on Dexter Lawrence’s immediate impact on the defense and the growing pains of the offense implementing an under-center element to their playbook. But you know what didn’t get a lot of attention? Players eligible for contract extensions. That’s refreshing, after how the last, really, five offseasons have been. Cornerbacks DJ Turner and Dax Hill, and running back Chase Brown, are all eligible for contract extensions going into this season. With only four days until kickoff in Week 1 against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, the question now is: Will any of these three players get paid before the Bengals open their 2026 campaign? ESPN’s Jeremy Fowler joined First Word with James Rapien on the Crown Network on Wednesday morning to discuss the situation surrounding Turner and Hill as well as Brown, Here is what Fowler said about the Bengals’ two cornerbacks. “I don’t sense much hope here. DJ Turner was the one where I pretty much earmarked as a no-green-light here,” Fowler said on the show , later adding, “I don’t expect a deal for him, so he’ll play it out, and then you’re looking at doing really well in free agency, or he could get the franchise tag, which Cincinnati has done in the past.” The running back position is a little different, as it relates to the Bengals. Chase Brown isn’t quite at the level that fellow 2023 NFL Draft class running backs Jahmy Gibbs and Bijan Robinson are, with both of those guys signing extensions this offseason. Robinson’s contract is $25 million per year. Brown’s contract extension would likely not reach that average annual value, but he could still sign an extension with the Bengals. Here is what Fowler says about the contract situation involving Chase Brown. “I haven’t heard of anything hard and fast about an extension for some of those players, but they’re certainly workable if Cincinnati wants to get aggressive here,” Fowler concluded. “Chase Brown, who I think will have a big year, and the running back money is a little more reasonable than some of these other positions. So yeah, he’s certainly a player that I had on my list, at least as somebody who could get an extension at some point.” Sounds like a deal with Brown could be reached if the Bengals were agressive with it, but for now, it doesn’t appear they are. The clock is ticking on these extensions, even if they’re not a major headline. It’s good that they’re not a distraction, but it is a simmering question as we head into Week 1.

title: The Ringer somehow has the Bengals QB room ranked 10th in the NFL
summary: Joe Burrow is arguably the most talented QB in the league. Joe Flacco is a former Super Bowl MVP who still has a lot of life left in his arm. Yet somehow, The Ringer’s Diante Lee thinks those two are only the 10th-best QB room in the NFL, behind even that of the Chicago Bears. […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Flacco (16) and quarterback Joe Burrow (9) chat during practice at the Paycor Stadium practice facility in downtown Cincinnati on Tuesday, Aug. 4, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Joe Burrow is arguably the most talented QB in the league. Joe Flacco is a former Super Bowl MVP who still has a lot of life left in his arm. Yet somehow, The Ringer ’s Diante Lee thinks those two are only the 10th-best QB room in the NFL, behind even that of the Chicago Bears. Here’s what he had to say about the Bengals’ quarterback situation : Burrow is an established postseason force, but he hasn’t ever seriously factored into the MVP or All-Pro conversation. And after three consecutive seasons of missing the playoffs (including two in which Burrow suffered injuries), it’s fair to wonder whether he’ll deliver a return on his current $275 million deal. Cincinnati’s backup plan is confusing. The Bengals have wisely put veteran pocket passers behind Burrow, himself a pocket passer, for the sake of scheme continuity, but the 41-year-old Flacco no longer provides much upside. He was a sack and turnover machine at times last season. And Cincinnati’s third quarterback, 40-year-old Josh Johnson, puts the “journey” in journeyman. Flacco’s $6 million salary is a huge overpay relative to his performance on the field, and the $1.5 million for Johnson’s veteran minimum deal could’ve been spent on a younger, more interesting developmental option that the Bengals could keep behind Burrow long term. You can read his entire piece here . Burrow, of course, doesn’t have time to worry about arbitrary rankings. He’s completely focused on a Week 1 matchup with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers. title: Pair of NFL experts do not have Bengals making the playoffs
summary: Kyle Brandt revealed his selections to make the AFC playoffs on Good Morning Football Tuesday morning. The Cincinnati Bengals were not among the teams he chose to make it to the playoffs. After missing the playoffs for three straight seasons, it seems the Bengals still have a lot to prove when it comes to the […]
full_text: CINCINNATI, OH - AUGUST 22: Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow (9) walks onto the field before the preseason game between the Chicago Bears and the Cincinnati Bengals at Paycor Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Cincinnati, OH. (Photo by Ian Johnson/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Kyle Brandt revealed his selections to make the AFC playoffs on Good Morning Football Tuesday morning. The Cincinnati Bengals were not among the teams he chose to make it to the playoffs. After missing the playoffs for three straight seasons, it seems the Bengals still have a lot to prove when it comes to the media. Brandt selected the Baltimore Ravens to win the AFC North this season. A pick that, going into this season, is at least understandable. The Ravens have won the AFC North two out of the last three seasons. The rushing attack returns Derrick Henry and Lamar Jackson. For a preseason prediction, there is at least nothing egregious about this one, even if it isn’t the selection I would have personally made. The more interesting selection came with his final wild card team. Brandt chose the Tennessee Titans to nab the final wild card spot for the AFC. Robert Saleh takes over as the head coach for the Titans, with Cam Ward entering his second season as the starting quarterback. While I do expect that defense to keep them competitive in a lot of games, I just don’t think they have the offensive firepower to be a playoff team this year. If we see the Titans make the playoffs over the Bengals, something has gone seriously wrong. The Bengals added Dexter Lawrence, Jonathan Allen, Boye Mafe, Cashius Howell, and Bryan Cook as key contributors to a revamped defense. The entire starting offensive line returns for the first time in the Joe Burrow era. Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins are the best receiver tandem in the entire NFL. Elsewhere, ESPN’s Bill Barnwell’s 2026 season predictions also do not have the Bengals making it back to the postseason. Barnwell has the Chiefs, Patriots, Ravens, and Texans winning their respective AFC divisions, while the Bills, Broncos, and Steelers of all teams get the Wild Card spots. He also has the Chiefs beating the Eagles to win the Super Bowl. There are a lot of reasons to be optimistic as Bengals fans heading into the first game of the season on Sunday. It appears they will have to convince a lot of the media as the season goes. Personally, I don’t mind them being underdogs in the eyes of the talking heads around the league. The time is now; go out and show the world exactly who you are. It is time to make a run at winning the whole thing this season. @KyleBrandt reveals his AFC & NFC playoff picture 🚨 pic.twitter.com/zx2LPBn8wz — Good Morning Football (@gmfb) September 8, 2026

full_text: Cincinnati Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow (9) shares words with center Ted Karras (64) Ofer being sacked in the third quarter of the NFL Week 7 game between the Cincinnati Bengals and the Atlanta Falcons at Paycor Stadium in downtown Cincinnati on Sunday, Oct. 23, 2022. Mandatory Credit: Sam Greene-The Enquirer Atlanta Falcons At Cincinnati Bengals Nfl Week 7 | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co There are the things NFL players say during training camp, and then there are the things that actually make you stop and listen. Ted Karras may have provided a little bit of the latter. Karras was once again named one of the Cincinnati Bengals ‘ team captains for 2026, marking the fifth consecutive season that the veteran center has held the honor. And considering how much football Karras has seen during his time in Cincinnati, his assessment of this year’s training camp is worth paying attention to. “This has probably been the toughest camp Coach Taylor has run in my five years here,” Karras said. That’s quite a statement. Five years is a long enough sample size to know what a Zac Taylor training camp typically looks like. Karras has experienced the good camps, the frustrating camps, the camps that produced legitimate optimism and the camps that ultimately didn’t translate into the kind of season the Bengals wanted. So when he says this was the toughest one, Bengals fans should probably take notice. But the most important part of Karras’ comments wasn’t necessarily the first sentence. It was what came next. “And I think we have a team that can handle that. We’re doing all the right things.” The Bengals Are Supposed to Be Tested There’s a natural temptation during training camp to focus on whether a team looks good. Who’s making plays? Which position group is winning? Who is standing out? Which rookie is generating buzz? Those things matter, but there’s another question that becomes increasingly important as the season approaches: Can this team handle adversity? That’s particularly relevant for the Bengals. Cincinnati doesn’t need another team that looks good when everything is going right. The Bengals need a team capable of surviving the grind of a 17-game season, handling injuries, responding to losses, and remaining focused when expectations get high. That’s where Karras’ comments become particularly interesting. He didn’t say the Bengals survived the toughest camp Taylor has put them through. He said they can handle it. There’s a difference. Karras Has Seen This Movie Before Karras isn’t some newcomer trying to establish himself in Cincinnati. He’s been through five training camps under Taylor. He’s been in the locker room for multiple playoff pushes. He’s been one of the team’s most consistent voices and has been selected as a captain every season he’s been with the Bengals. That continuity gives his comments more context. When Karras says the team has been “grinding,” he’s speaking from experience. And there’s another reason his perspective matters: the center position essentially gives him a front-row seat to the personality of the football team. He’s involved in every offensive snap. He’s communicating with Joe Burrow. He’s working with the offensive line. He’s dealing with the physicality of the defensive front. If the team isn’t practicing with the right level of intensity, a veteran center is going to know it. Apparently, that’s not an issue this year. This Is What Leadership Is Supposed to Look Like It’s also fitting that these comments came as Karras was once again named a captain. Cincinnati’s 2026 captaincy group contains a mixture of established leaders and new voices. Burrow and Ja’Marr Chase remain offensive pillars, while Karras provides the veteran presence in the middle. DJ Turner II, Bryan Cook and Dexter Lawrence II bring new leadership to the defensive side, while Evan McPherson represents special teams. Karras is the connective tissue. And perhaps that’s why his comments are more encouraging than a generic “we’re ready” quote. He’s not selling the idea that the Bengals are talented. Everyone knows they’re talented. He’s talking about work. “We’ve been grinding.” That’s the message you want coming from a veteran captain heading into a season in which the Bengals have made it abundantly clear that their expectations are much higher than simply making the playoffs. The Hard Part Is About to Begin Of course, none of this guarantees anything. Training camp isn’t the regular season. Being prepared to handle adversity doesn’t mean adversity won’t expose weaknesses. And ultimately, the Bengals will have to prove Karras right when the games actually count. But that’s precisely why his comments are encouraging. The Bengals aren’t talking about avoiding difficult circumstances. They’re talking about being prepared for them. That’s a subtle distinction, but an important one. The Bengals have the quarterback. They have elite offensive weapons. They have invested heavily in the defensive side of the football. They have added veteran leadership and young talent. Now they’re trying to build the kind of team that can survive everything that comes with being a legitimate contender. And according to one of the most experienced voices in the locker room, they’ve spent the offseason doing exactly that. Five years into his Cincinnati tenure, Ted Karras knows what a Bengals training camp looks like. He says this one was the toughest. And he says this team can handle it. Now comes the part where the Bengals have to prove him right.

title: Erick All isn’t thinking about his injury history ahead of his regular-season return
summary: Erick All has the potential to be a talented pass-catching tight end in the NFL. That’s why the Bengals selected him in the 2024 NFL Draft. Unfortunately, he hasn’t been able to really show it because he’s been injured throughout much of his young career in the league and in college football as well, which […]
full_text: Cincinnati Bengals tight end Erick All Jr. (83) stretches for a pass during practice at the Paycor Stadium practice facility in downtown Cincinnati on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Erick All has the potential to be a talented pass-catching tight end in the NFL. That’s why the Bengals selected him in the 2024 NFL Draft. Unfortunately, he hasn’t been able to really show it because he’s been injured throughout much of his young career in the league and in college football as well, which is why he fell to them in the fourth round. All dealt with a back injury in 2022, and then tore his ACL in his right knee in 2023, missing the second half of the season. Then, in his rookie season, he tore the same knee again, which cost him the rest of 2024 and the entire 2025 season thanks to complications that required a second surgery. Now, he’s back and cleared to play in his third season. He’s not dwelling on the past, though. “Not really thinking about it. Like now, it kind of gets you, but when you’re out there, you kind of forget about that part of it, and you just play,” All said in an interview with Fox 19’s Gabi Sorrentino . Erick All Jr. hasn't played a regular season game in almost two years after tearing his ACL his rookie season…after a long recovery, the Bengals Tight End is ready to take the field with no limitations next Sunday. #Bengals @FOX19 pic.twitter.com/Dv4y0JrDCb — Gabi Sorrentino (@GSorrentinoTV) September 6, 2026 All’s spot on the 53-man roster, as long as he came into the season healthy, was really never in doubt. However, with so many mouths to feed in this offense, including Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins, it’ll be interesting to see what kind of role he plays in the offense, and how that role evolves. All hopes to make it through an entire season for the first time since his 2021 season with Michigan, when he led the Wolverines in receptions with 38 catches for 437 yards and two touchdowns. He played in 13 games with eight starts that season. “Individually, just making it out of the season healthy, and really, that’s all I care about, to be honest,” said All. “I don’t care about anything else. I mean, as long as I’m doing good and we win games, then that’s all I really care about.” With Mike Gesicki, Drew Sample, and rookie Jack Endries on the roster to go with the talent at wide receiver, All will have his work cut out for him. Hopefully, he achieves his goal and helps the Bengals get back into the playoffs.

title: Browns Week 1: Wednesday injury report is promising
summary: The Cleveland Browns open up the 2026 NFL season on Sunday when they take on the Jacksonville Jaguars at EverBank Stadium. Life on the road against the Jaguars has generally been good to the Browns over the past 20-plus years, as Cleveland has won five of their last seven road games against Jacksonville, including two […]
full_text: BEREA, OHIO - JUNE 10: Carson Schwesinger #49 of the Cleveland Browns runs a drill during the Cleveland Browns Mandatory Minicamp at CrossCountry Mortgage Campus on June 10, 2026 in Berea, Ohio. (Photo by Nick Cammett/Diamond Images via Getty Images) | Diamond Images/Getty Images The Cleveland Browns open up the 2026 NFL season on Sunday when they take on the Jacksonville Jaguars at EverBank Stadium. Life on the road against the Jaguars has generally been good to the Browns over the past 20-plus years, as Cleveland has won five of their last seven road games against Jacksonville, including two in a row. Throw in that Cleveland starting quarterback Deshaun Watson is a perfect 7-0 in his career against the Jaguars, and the Browns could be in for a good day on Sunday. Everyone will have to wait a few days to find out how the game goes, of course, but one thing that is known now is that the Browns have opened the practice week in good health. The club released its first injury report of the new season on Wednesday, and overall it looks promising: Listed as limited were center Parker Brailsford, who is still working his way back from a thumb injury, defensive tackle Maliek Collins, with the quad injury that kept him out of training camp and the preseason until recently, and offensive guard Teven Jenkins, who is dealing with a back injury. Listed as a full participant is linebacker Carson Schwesinger (shoulder), which is great news for the defense. our first practice participation report of the season pic.twitter.com/fKyx1eDwaO — Cleveland Browns (@Browns) September 9, 2026 When asked about the health of the team on Wednesday, head coach Todd Monken was feeling good about the situation : “I feel like we’re in a good place. Outside of losing (defensive end) Alex (Wright) a few weeks ago (to a season-ending ruptured Achilles), we’ve been relatively healthy. Some nicks and bruises here and there, but we feel good about where we’re at.” Unlike in previous seasons, the Browns have not been dealing with an onslaught of soft-tissue injuries, which Monken credits to the work of the training staff : “I think our training staff does an outstanding job in terms of getting our players ready. Our assistant coaches have done a great job with the rotations we’ve had during practice. I’d also say it’s been a relatively cool training camp. Last week, luckily, we got a little bit of weather, a little bit of heat, but I think it’s a combination. The guys have done a great job taking care of their bodies, and people within the building have done a great job.” Speaking of heat, the high in Jacksonville for Sunday’s game is forecast to be 91 degrees, with a 39 percent chance of thunderstorms, so hopefully everyone plans accordingly.

summary: Never in my wildest dreams did I think we would ever have the kind of whirlwind story about a practice-squad-level, developmental tight end as we have with Dae’Quan Wright.
