title: Start ‘Em, Sit ‘Em: Fantasy Advice for Your Broncos Players in Week 1
summary: The 2026 NFL season kicks off later tonight with a Super Bowl rematch (it should have included the Broncos) between the Seattle Seahawks and the New England Patriots. That also means the 2026 fantasy football season is underway, and I am here to tell you which Denver Broncos players you should start confidently, cautiously, or […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - AUGUST 21: Denver Broncos wide receiver Jaylen Waddle (17) runs after a catch in the first quarter during a preseason game between the Green Bay Packers and the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High on August 21, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Dustin Bradford/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The 2026 NFL season kicks off later tonight with a Super Bowl rematch (it should have included the Broncos) between the Seattle Seahawks and the New England Patriots. That also means the 2026 fantasy football season is underway, and I am here to tell you which Denver Broncos players you should start confidently, cautiously, or keep on the bench. The Broncos cap off the start of Week 1 with a key AFC West divisional showdown against the returning quarterback Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs. The Broncos will also have their quarterback, Bo Nix, returning from offseason ankle surgery and will be debuting explosive wide receiver and big offseason addition, Jaylen Waddle. So, with all that said, here are the Denver Broncos players I believe you should start or sit during Week 1 of the 2026 fantasy football season. Quarterback Bo Nix – Start Nix has had success vs. the Chiefs throughout his career. He has a 3-1 record vs. them and would be undefeated if it were not for a blocked game-winning field goal. Nix also has a passer rating of 108.8 with 1,013 yards, 7 touchdowns, and 1 interception in 4 games against the Chiefs in his career. Now, add Jaylen Waddle, an improved Pat Bryant, a strong running game, and Davis Webb calling the offense. This will be the strongest supporting cast Nix has ever had with the Broncos, and this offense is ready to take that next step. If Bo Nix is your quarterback, I would feel confident starting him this week. Running Backs: JK Dobbins, RJ Harvey, and Jonah Coleman JK Dobbins – Start: The Broncos are ready to unleash Dobbins after sitting him out the entire preseason. However, how many carries he gets is TBD. Second-year back RJ Harvey will get third down/passing game work, and rookie Jonah Coleman is expected to factor in as well. I have Dobbins as a cautious RB2/FLEX this week due to the uncertainty surrounding the backfield. It’s great for real football but muddy for fantasy. RJ Harvey – Start (PPR only): Harvey will be a risky flex start in deeper PPR leagues. His rushing output isn’t going to be consistent or good enough to warrant a spot on your team. However, he’s expected to be a big player in the Broncos’ passing offense and did have 12 total touchdowns last season. If you’re in a deeper league and have a FLEX option, I would consider starting him. Jonah Coleman – Sit/Stash: Obviously, Jonah Coleman isn’t fantasy relevant right now, but he’s worth a stash on your bench. He’s a JK Dobbins injury away from being a surefire RB2 and potentially a league-winning RB1. I have him stashed on my bench, and if he’s available in your league, I would do the same. Wide Receivers: Jaylen Waddle, Courtland Sutton, and Pat Bryant Jaylen Waddle – Start: Waddle is a popular breakout candidate in fantasy and is expected to get a heavy workload vs. the Chiefs. Sean Payton and Davis Webb likely have been drawing up plays for him all offseason and are prepared to showcase their new weapon on the primetime stage vs. their rivals on Monday Night Football. I would confidently start him as my WR1, and I believe he’s going to have a big game. Courtland Sutton – Start: Sutton’s overall production may take a hit, but he’s still Bo Nix’s trusted third-down and red-zone target. You’re chasing touchdowns here, and I believe Sutton could see plenty of touchdown opportunities with defenses focusing on Waddle. He’s a solid WR2 and a strong WR3/FLEX play for me. Pat Bryant – Sit but roster: Second-year wide receiver Pat Bryant was the star of training camp and is the Broncos’ WR3. However, I would keep him on my bench for now. We have to see how he’s utilized, how they split snaps with Mims, Franklin, and/or Lil’Jordan Humphrey, but there’s plenty of upside there. There’s a reality where he’s the Broncos’ WR2 by the end of the season. Roster and stash for now, and wait and see if it pays off down the road. Tight End Evan Engram – Only start in deeper leagues If you’re in a deeper league and do not have one of the top and more consistent fantasy tight end options, I would roll the dice on Evan Engram. He is expected to see a larger role in Davis Webb’s offense, which could lead to some red zone/touchdown opportunities. With that said, he will be competing for targets in a suddenly crowded Denver Broncos passing offense. For me, he’s borderline roster-worthy at this point, but hey, tight end is a roll of the dice most weeks, and if you’re desperate, Engram could pay off for you. Kicker Wil Lutz – Start During his career with the Broncos, Lutz has made 89% of his field goal attempts and 98.3% of his extra points. He’s a reliable kicker and will be paired with what is expected to be a high-scoring offense this season. There aren’t many better options out there than Wil Lutz, so I would feel confident starting him if he was the kicker on my team this week. Broncos Defense/Special Teams – Start Vance Joseph’s defenses have always fared well vs. Mahomes and the Chiefs during the time with the Broncos (even when they were bad), and I don’t see that changing this week. Mahomes will be playing his first game since suffering a major knee injury last season. Also, they will reportedly be down their starting left tackle and will be starting an undrafted rookie vs. the Broncos’ league-leading pass rush. I can see them get 3+ sacks and possibly multiple turnovers. If you drafted the Broncos defense, you should probably start them most weeks. As for their special teams, All-Pro returner Marvin Mims Jr. is always a threat to take one back for a touchdown. Combine that with their defense, and you have a high-upside pairing that I would start confidently this week.
author: Scotty Payne

title: Broncos at Chiefs preview: Denver aims for fast start
summary: The wait is over. This is true on multiple levels. The Denver Broncos will open the season. And quarterback Bo Nix is set to return to the field after an ankle injury ended his and the Broncos’ season. But there is something different about this season opener. Denver is coming off its best season in […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - DECEMBER 25: Bo Nix #10 of the Denver Broncos runs the ball for a touchdown against the Kansas City Chiefs during the third quarter at Arrowhead Stadium on December 25, 2025 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Jamie Squire/Getty Images) | Getty Images The wait is over. This is true on multiple levels. The Denver Broncos will open the season. And quarterback Bo Nix is set to return to the field after an ankle injury ended his and the Broncos’ season. But there is something different about this season opener. Denver is coming off its best season in a decade, having hosted and played in the AFC Championship Game, claimed the No. 1 seed in the AFC, won the AFC West, and beaten Josh Allen and the Buffalo Bills in one of the best wins in franchise history. Now, can Nix and the Broncos build off that incredible season and take the next step to the Super Bowl? The first test comes on Monday Night Football against Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs. FanDuel Sportsbook currently has Denver as the slight road underdog to its division rivals. The Broncos are +2.5-point underdogs to host Kansas City. The total sits at 43.5 points, with a lean toward the under at -112. Offensive Rankings (2025) Denver : Tenth in total offense (342.6 yards per game), 16th in rushing offense (118.7 YPG), 11th in passing offense (223.9 YPG), 14th in scoring offense (23.6 points per game). Kansas City : Twentieth in total offense (320.6 yards per game), 25th in rushing offense (106.6 YPG), 16th in passing offense (214.1 YPG), 21st in scoring offense (21.3 points per game). Defensive Rankings (2025) Denver : Second in total defense (278.2 yards per game), second in rushing defense (91.1 YPG), seventh in passing defense (187.2 YPG), third in scoring defense (18.3 points per game). Kansas City : Tenth in total defense (301.5 yards per game), ninth in rushing defense (105.7 YPG), 12th in passing defense (195.8 YPG), sixth in scoring defense (19.3 points per game). Here are the MHR staff’s keys to Monday night’s game. Start fast This applies to Monday’s game and the season. One of the reasons Nix and the Broncos had so many comeback wins last season is that the offense started slow. The best way to ensure you don’t have so many come-from-behind, one-score wins in 2026 is to have the offense consistently start games faster. There’s no better time for that than Monday Night Football in Kansas City to open the season. And why not do so in Davis Webb’s first game as the offensive playcaller? Send a message to the rest of the NFL. On the first play from scrimmage, dial up a deep shot to Jaylen Waddle and test that Chiefs secondary. Coming away with an opening-drive touchdown on offense puts Denver in a great position to start the season with a big road win. — Ian St. Clair Stop the run Make the Chiefs one-dimensional. Force Patrick Mahomes to prove he can carry his team with a surgically repaired knee. — Adam Malnati Close the deal on third downs Whether on offense or defense, the Broncos will win if they beat the Chiefs on third down. — Tim Lynch Score more points than KC This will be a tough opening week matchup, but the key to the game remains the same. Score more points than the other team. According to advanced metrics, the Broncos are undefeated when they score more points than their opponents. So, if they do that on Monday Night, they will defeat their division rivals and start the year 1-0. — Scotty Payne Win the turnover battle Creating more turnovers has been a focal point of the team’s defense all season long. In order to win on the road at Arrowhead, the Broncos have to be on the right side with respect to turnover margin. Whether it’s a key interception, a strip sack, or a force fumble elsewhere, the Broncos’ defense has to make a few big plays to come out of Kansas City with a victory in Week 1. — Christopher Hart Test Chiefs secondary Push matchups hard against the Chiefs’ reconstructed secondary. That unit is debuting three new starters and trying to replace a whopping 2,415 defensive snaps vacated by McDuffie, Watson, & Cook. With 29-year-old L’Jarius Sneed bracketed by two young CBs, that secondary should present some big-play opportunities with the talent matchups the Broncos’ WR group and receiving RBs bring to the table. Let’s see Waddle & Sutton debut a Thomas & Sanders style lightning & thunder WR duo in strong fashion. — Taylor Kothe Force second- & third-&-long The Broncos defense allowed a league-best 4.0 yards per play on first down in 2025 and only 15% of first downs on first down — also league-best. They need to continue that against the Chiefs on Monday night. Get them off schedule and force them into second, third, and long counts. The Broncos need to take advantage of the weak KC offensive tackles and bring pressure with four, which will force Mahomes to make throws into tight windows, leading to incompletions and turnovers. — Joe Mahoney What are your keys to Monday’s game?
author: Ian St. Clair

title: NFL picks and predictions: Broncos vs. Chiefs and the rest of Week 1
summary: Finally, the 2026 NFL season is upon us. With that, it’s the return of my weekly straight-up picks for every game. My 2024 NFL regular season picks record was 190-72. Last season, I regressed and finished with a 178-94 record. Let’s see if I can start this year off on a high note with my […]
full_text: (Photo by Tyler Schank/Clarkson Creative/Getty Images) | Getty Images Finally, the 2026 NFL season is upon us. With that, it’s the return of my weekly straight-up picks for every game. My 2024 NFL regular season picks record was 190-72. Last season, I regressed and finished with a 178-94 record. Let’s see if I can start this year off on a high note with my slate of Week 1 picks. New England Patriots at Seattle Seahawks — Wednesday Night Football What a game to start the season. A rematch of last year’s Super Bowl. Can Drake Maye elevate his play in Year 3 against top defenses? Can the Seahawks running game, now led by rookie Jadarian Price, be consistent enough to replace the lost production of Kenneth Walker III? Only time will tell. But for this game, I’m taking the defending champs at home. Winner: Seahawks San Francisco 49ers at Los Angeles Rams — Thursday Night Football Thursday Night Football kicks off this year with a bang in an NFC West matchup. I’m interested in seeing how the revamped wide receiver corps of the 49ers performs. For the Rams, I’m intrigued with the various upgrades they made to bolster their defense. I expect this to be a close division rivalry game, but am giving the nod to the Rams. Winner: Rams Tampa Bay Buccaneers at Cincinnati Bengals — Sunday (Early Game) I think this will be one of the more fun early games to watch on Sunday. I anticipate this game is going to be a high scoring affair. I’m giving the edge to the Bengals here. The Buccaneers have five new starters on defense, three of them being rookies, and it may be a while before they are firing on all cylinders. Winner: Bengals New Orleans Saints at Detroit Lions — Sunday (Early Game) The Lions are coming off a disappointing 9-win season despite having a Top 5 offense in the NFL in ’25. In my opinion, they have a good shot at reclaiming their spot as kings of the NFC North. I believe the Lions will earn a decisive victory over the Saints for the first game of the season. Winner: Lions Baltimore Ravens at Indianapolis Colts — Sunday (Early Game) This is an intriguing matchup. Both of these teams faltered last year and missed out in a tough AFC race for the playoffs. In my opinion, this game will come down to who wins in the trenches. Baltimore’s revamped offensive line or the Colts’ rising defensive front seven? I’ll push my chips in for the Ravens—making them my first road team victor of Week 1. Winner: Ravens Atlanta Falcons at Pittsburgh Steelers — Sunday (Early Game) I don’t have much to say about this game. Long story short, I think the Falcons won’t be good this year and will be in the running for a Top 5 pick in the 2027 NFL Draft. I’ll take the Steelers at home. Winner: Steelers Chicago Bears at Carolina Panthers — Sunday (Early Game) This NFC matchup features two division winners from last season. I don’t think the Panthers are poised to repeat as NFC South champions. However, the Bears certainly have the talent to challenge for a second consecutive NFC North title. I’ll be taking Chicago on the road in this one. Winner: Chicago Cleveland Browns at Jacksonville Jaguars — Sunday (Early Game) I really like what the Browns were able to cook up in the draft this past April. I’m just not confident an offense with seven new starters led by Deshaun Watson will be that competitive this season. I think the Jaguars will win this one quite handily. Winner: Jaguars Buffalo Bills at Houston Texans — Sunday (Early Game) This is one of my favorite matchups of the weekend. Two AFC playoffs teams last year trying to start off the season with a big victory. The Texans have one of the best defenses in the NFL, but Josh Allen is arguably the best offensive player in NFL. I think this will be a close one but have Allen and the Bills finding a way to win on the road. Winner: Bills New York Jets at Tennessee Titans — Sunday (Early Game) I honestly have a hard time getting a read on this one. Both teams had some drastic offseason changes and will be starting at least eight new players on their rosters for the upcoming season. I’ll just go with my gut and say Cam Ward will have a big day against a Jets defense that was one of the worst in the NFL a season ago. I’m taking the home team here. Winner: Titans Miami Dolphins at Las Vegas Raiders — Sunday (Afternoon Game) Easily one of the most boring games all weekend long. Two bad teams going head-to-head isn’t much fun to write about. Truth be told, the Dolphins could very well wind up being the worst team in football this year. I’ll be going with the Raiders at home. Winners: Raiders Green Bay Packers at Minnesota Vikings — Sunday (Afternoon Game) A classic NFC North rivalry matchup is a great way for Packers and Vikings fans to begin their ‘26 gridiron campaigns. Quite frankly, I’m worry about both team’s running games. I think that could be an issue for both of them this season. For this matchup, I’m banking on Kyler Murray having a big debut for the Vikings in front of a sellout crowd in Minneapolis to earn them the ‘W’. Winner: Vikings Washington Commanders at Philadelphia Eagles — Sunday (Afternoon Game) The Commanders reversed their record last season (5-12) compared to an impressive 12-5 outing in 2025. I expect them to be more competitive this season, but going up against the Eagles in an NFC East rivalry matchup to start the season is a tough draw. I think the Eagles come up with a big divisional win on Sunday. Winner: Eagles Arizona Cardinals at Los Angeles Chargers — Sunday (Afternoon Game) I’m not sure that the Cardinals have what it takes on offense to take down the Chargers on the road. I think their rushing attack with Jeremiyah Love and Tyler Allgeier will be formidable. But will Jacoby Brissett be able to dial up the heat against a quality Chargers defense? I’m not so sure about that. I’m taking Los Angeles in this one. Winner: Chargers Dallas Cowboys at New York Giants — Sunday Night Football Sunday Night Football is a classic NFC East rivalry matchup. I think the Giants will be a lot better than last year with their additions and John Harbaugh coaching them, but I think Dak Prescott and the Cowboys offense will come out hot and put up some points in primetime against the Giants defense. Winner: Cowboys Denver Broncos at Kansas City Chiefs — Monday Night Football This is a tremendous matchup to end the Week 1 slate of games. Can Bo Nix make a big jump in Year 3? Will Patrick Mahomes be able to revert to pre-ACL injury form? Those are two big questions that loom large for me for both teams this year. My gut tells me this is going to be a nailbiter, but I’m confident Denver can do enough to come out of Arrowhead with a big win against their AFC West nemesis. Winner: Broncos
author: Christopher Hart

full_text: Shoutout to Detroit Lions wide receiver Tom Kennedy, but we finally made it. Finally, we have regular season football this week as your Lions will be hosting the visiting New Orleans Saints this Sunday at Ford Field. And with that, myself and my good friend Meko Scott, host of the PODcast, are back with a new episode of, “Before the Roar,” where we preview the Week 1 matchup against the Saints. There has been a lot of turnover in New Orleans since the days when Lions coach Dan Campbell was both assistant head coach and tight ends coach. Save for longtime defensive end Cameron Jordan, the old guard is largely no longer with the Saints. This has given way for a new iteration of the proud franchise to step up, and after a rough start in 2025, they began to find ways to win down the stretch, winning four of their last five games of the year. Now that they have second-year quarterback Tyler Shough as the unquestioned starter, they will be looking to build on what they accomplished in 2025. We discuss the outlook for Shough in year two, as well as the rest of the Saints’ offense, which features some exciting skill players like wide receiver Chris Olave, tight end Juwan Johnson, and a pair of promising tackles in Kelvin Banks Jr. and Taliese Fuaga. From there, we dive into New Orleans’ defensive scheme and tendencies, including a quick breakdown of one of defensive end Chase Young’s 10 sacks from last year. Lastly, we highlight a few key matchups that are worth keeping an eye on, and offer up our predictions for the game. If you haven’t already, please be sure to like and subscribe to the Pride of Detroit YouTube Channel. Your support helps us reach other Lions fans around the world.

title: Lions, Saints injury report: Only 3 players limited on Wednesday
summary: The Detroit Lions will kick off the new year inside the comfy confines of Ford Field, taking on the New Orleans Saints in Week 1 of the 2026 season. Both teams are dealing with some early-season injuries, and that’s reflected in their initial injury reports. As is the case with most beginning-of-the-year schedules, the Lions […]
full_text: DETROIT, MICHIGAN - AUGUST 22: Derrick Moore #9 of the Detroit Lions plays against the Washington Commanders at Ford Field on August 22, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. (Photo by Gregory Shamus/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions will kick off the new year inside the comfy confines of Ford Field, taking on the New Orleans Saints in Week 1 of the 2026 season. Both teams are dealing with some early-season injuries, and that’s reflected in their initial injury reports. As is the case with most beginning-of-the-year schedules, the Lions have taken a slightly different approach to Week 1. They practiced earlier in the week than they traditionally do, and as a result, Wednesday is a day off for the players. This means participation levels for this initial practice are only estimates based on what the coaching staff projects each player could have produced in a full practice. With that in mind, let’s take a look at Wednesday’s injury report and get you up to date with what we know. Injured list updates RB Isiah Pacheco (MCL/Back) — injured reserve C Cade Mays (Wrist) — injured reserve OL Giovanni Manu (Undisclosed) — NFI S Brian Branch (Achilles) — PUP S Kerny Joseph (Knee) — PUP All five players listed here are required to sit out the first four weeks of the NFL season, but due to a new NFL rule, Branch and Joseph are eligible to begin practicing in Week 3, while Pacheco, Mays, and Manu can begin practicing in Week 5, if healthy. Once activated, they would begin a 21-day evaluation period and could be added to the 53-man roster at any point. Estimated no practice on Wednesday None As Jeremy Reisman noted, all 52 players on the Lions’ active roster were accounted for at practice on Tuesday . Estimated limited practice EDGE Derrick Moore (hamstring) DL Mekhi Wingo (groin) DB Christian Izien (groin) Moore got banged up near the end of camp, but expectations were that he would return to practices ahead of Week 1, so he appears right on track to return to play soon. Wingo wasn’t known to have an injury, so we’ll have to wait to hear what coach Dan Campbell says on Friday and/or see where he falls on the injury report to better understand where he is at. Izien suffered an undisclosed leg injury late in camp, and Campbell suggested that he may not be recovered in time for the opener against the Saints . His practicing this week is a great sign, but the Lions could elect to take things slow with him. Estimated full practice LB Jimmy Rolder (hamstring) LB Trevor Nowaske (knee) CB Ennis Rakestraw (ankle) CB Keith Abney (hand) S Thomas Harper (ankle) Rolder injured his hamstring just over two weeks into training camp, and while he suggested he’d be back in August , coach Dan Campbell noted it could take a bit longer . Some speculated that Rolder could be a candidate for injured reserve, but he remained on the active roster and practiced in front of the media on Tuesday. The Lions won’t want to rush Rolder back to play too quickly, and with six linebackers currently on the roster, they can certainly take their time, despite the full practice. Nowaske injured his leg near the end of camp, and while we never got a firm answer on when he would return to practice, it was a positive sign that he was back on the field on Tuesday, suggesting he’ll play soon. Rakestraw and Abney did not have known injuries when training camp concluded, so like Wingo, we’ll have to wait on updates from Campbell for more information. That being said, a full practice is encouraging news. Harper injured his ankle during the final week of training camp, but was back on the practice field this week. The Lions plan to take things practice by practice with him, but they expect him to be able to play against the Saints. “Harper’s going to be running around out there today, and then hopefully everything goes well today,” Campbell said on Monday. “We see him taking more reps tomorrow, and so we’re anticipating he’ll be ready to go. So, we feel good about that room right now.” No longer on the injury report TE Sam LaPorta (hip) S Avonte Maddox (undisclosed) LaPorta took an awkward hit that caused his hip to flare up, forcing him to miss a little over a week before returning to practice in the final days before cutdowns , and he has been practicing since. Getting let off the injury report this week is a great sign that he’ll play in Week 1. Maddox suffered an apparent injury on the final play of training camp practices, and while he didn’t play in the final game, that was likely by design, as most of the starters rested. Not being on the injury report is a great sign that he didn’t suffer anything significant and should be available against the Saints. Saint s’ initial injury report TE Oscar Delp (hamstring) — No practice RB Audric Estime (thigh) – No practice EDGE Cameron Jordan (hamstring) – No practice — Ruled out by Kellen Moore RB Alvin Kamara (knee) – Limited practice

title: Dan Campbell’s 2026 message to Detroit Lions fans: ‘We will be ready’
summary: This offseason, the Detroit Lions have been preaching their focus on getting back to their true identity. Though they’ve been a little vague on exactly what that means, the message has been clear: 2025 was both not good enough and not who they are as a franchise. So they’ve changed up their offseason program, they […]
full_text: Detroit Lions head coach Dan Campbell answers questions before practice during training camp at the Detroit Lions Headquarters and Training Facility in Allen Park on Sunday, July 23, 2023. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co This offseason, the Detroit Lions have been preaching their focus on getting back to their true identity. Though they’ve been a little vague on exactly what that means, the message has been clear: 2025 was both not good enough and not who they are as a franchise. So they’ve changed up their offseason program, they altered their emphasis on roster construction, and they’ve fine tuned their strategies on both offense and defense—with a new coordinator and fresh mind for the former and some slight alterations in Year 2 of this defense. So as the Lions begin the 2026 season, hope is on the rise. Lions fans are beginning to believe again, and with that optimism brings high expectations. Coach Dan Campbell isn’t one to hide from expectations. Rather, he leans into it. Therefore, it’s no surprise that during the conclusion of Campbell’s appearance on the St. Brown Podcast— which you can, and should, watch in its entirety here —he really leaned into his belief that 2026 will be a great year. Amon-Ra St. Brown asked him straight up what message he had for Lions fans going into the season. I will leave the rest of the article to Dan to hype you up: “We will be ready. We will be ready, and we will be a formidable foe for any opponent that gets ready to face us. It’s been an outstanding training camp. We’ve got weapons, and we’ve got an army on the o-line and d-line. So, we will be ready starting Week 1.”

title: 2026 NFL predictions: Detroit Lions breakout player of the year
summary: Because the Detroit Lions didn’t make a ton of offseason adds, in order to improve in 2026, they’ll need several players to take the next step. The good news is there are plenty of candidates to have a breakout season this year. Our 2026 Detroit Lions season predictions series continues today with our staff picks […]
full_text: Detroit Lions defensive tackle Tyleik Williams (91) practices during mini camp at Meijer Performance Center in Allen Park on Wednesday, June 17, 2026. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co Because the Detroit Lions didn’t make a ton of offseason adds, in order to improve in 2026, they’ll need several players to take the next step. The good news is there are plenty of candidates to have a breakout season this year. Our 2026 Detroit Lions season predictions series continues today with our staff picks for 2026 Detroit Lions Breakout Player of the Year. And don’t forget you have the opportunity to cast your own vote at the bottom of the story. Previously: Offensive MVP predictions Defensive MVP predictions Who will be the Lions’ breakout player of the 2026 season? Al Karsten: Tate Ratledge, Tyleik Williams I’m going to keep it in the trenches, where the Lions’ first two draft choices of 2025, Tate Ratledge and Tyleik Williams, will transform their games by becoming more consistent overall while emerging as difference-makers on the interior of their respective sides of the ball. In the process, they’ll prove to be the next wave of young, homegrown pillars on this roster. With both players approaching the idealized versions of themselves already in Year 2, they’ll also be complemented by a trio of breakout rookies turning heads in the trenches: Blake Miller, Derrick Moore, and Skyler Gill-Howard. All three should provide dynamic flashes alongside an above-average level of play throughout the season as they steamroll past minimal early-season rookie bumps in the road. Together, that young group will help restore the identity of Dan Campbell’s gritty, tough, physical sons of guns—the type of team opponents don’t want to play because of the physical toll they’ll feel long after the final whistle. Erik Schlitt: Tyleik Williams The Lions’ defensive line showed a lot of improvement in training camp, and the play of second-year defensive lineman Tyleik Williams was a big part of that. Williams showed steady growth throughout his rookie season, but he looks like he’s capable of a huge sophomore jump in production this season. John Whiticar: Tate Ratledge There are a few returning players (Isaac Teslaa, Tyleik Williams) and a few rookies (Miller, Moore, Abney) that could stand out this year. However, I give the nod to Ratledge. I think this year, he could jump into the top-10 guards in the league and prove that he was not merely benefitting from playing next to Penei Sewell last season. Ryan Mathews: DJ Wonnum DJ Wonnum will be the Lions’ breakout player of 2026. Even though he just arrived in Detroit, Wonnum finds himself in one of the most coveted spots on a defensive line in the NFL, playing alongside Tyleik Williams, Alim McNeill, and Aidan Hutchinson. Anthony Balaj: Sione Vaki Vaki, the best pick of the 2024 draft class, earns a Pro Bowl nod as a special teamer, but also scores multiple offensive touchdowns. Brandon Knapp: Isaac TeSlaa, Nick Whiteside TeSlaa gets bumped up to the WR3 spot and with a rocky preseason, I think he can overcome those struggles and grow as a player. With LaPorta back, there should be less pressure from TeSlaa to excel, and less eyes focused on him. Defenses will overlook him still and I think he could have a solid contribution to the offense in 2026. Whiteside starts the year on the practice squad, but I don’t think that stay is long-term. He had an excellent preseason and deserves to be on the 53-man roster, arguably as the team’s CB3. I believe Whiteside will be given chances to play and excel with the chances he’s given. Morgan Cannon: Tyleik Williams I am going with defensive tackle Tyleik Williams. In terms of statistical production, the rookie out of Ohio State didn’t make massive waves during his 2025 rookie year. Still, there were plenty of flashes for Williams. Especially when you turn on the all-22 and watch how he takes on double teams and is able to help the interior defensive line collapse the pocket around opposing quarterbacks. If fellow defensive tackle Alim McNeill can return to pre-injury form and Williams takes the next step or two in his development, the Lions’ defensive front could be fun to watch. Jeremy Reisman: DJ Reed I feel we were robbed of seeing what DJ Reed is truly capable of due to his early hamstring injury in 2025. Thus far in camp, it looks like he has his explosiveness back. Plus, with—hopefully—an improved pass rush, it can take some pressure off of Reed and force some errant throws. I wouldn’t be surprised if he tallied a few interceptions this year while remaining a strong presence in the run game.

title: Detroit Lions scouting report: Are the Saints a sleeper in 2026?
summary: In what was the longest offseason since the end of the 2022 season, your Detroit Lions are back to playing meaningful football! Training camp and preseason are over, the rosters are finalized (for the most part), and the regular season has arrived. The Lions kick off at home in Ford Field to play the New […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TEXAS - AUGUST 28: Tyler Shough #6 of the New Orleans Saints participates in warmups prior to an NFL Preseason 2026 game against the Dallas Cowboys at AT&T Stadium on August 28, 2026 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Stacy Revere/Getty Images) | Getty Images In what was the longest offseason since the end of the 2022 season, your Detroit Lions are back to playing meaningful football! Training camp and preseason are over, the rosters are finalized (for the most part), and the regular season has arrived. The Lions kick off at home in Ford Field to play the New Orleans Saints on Sunday in Week 1. The Saints are aiming to snag the NFC South divisional crown for the first time since 2020 and have higher expectations than last season. While most don’t believe this team can win it all, some think they can compete in what is known as the NFL’s easiest division. They have a young roster, but also veterans who can help them improve on last year. An up-and-coming team like the Saints could make a statement with a win on the road against the Lions. Detroit, on the other hand, could use a win to start the season after how 2025 went for them. Let’s dive in on the Saints and how much they’ve improved ahead of Week 1. New Orleans Saints 2025 Season 6-11 record (4th in NFC South) 28th in points for, 16th in point allowed Overall DVOA: 28 (27th on offense, 13th on defense) 2025 was a slight improvement for the Saints over their 2024 campaign, with one more win. Expectations were low heading into last year, with question marks at quarterback and a new head coach in Kellen Moore. With a young roster, it was going to be a difficult season, but in the end, they came away with clearer answers and a vision for the future. At quarterback, former starter Derrick Carr retired in May 2025 for health reasons, leaving the Saints with 2024 fifth-round pick Spencer Rattler and 2025 second-round pick Tyler Shough to battle for the starting job. Rattler won the job, but not for the entire season. After going 1-7, he was benched and replaced by Shough, who finished the year with 2,384 yards, 10 touchdowns, and six interceptions—and a 5-4 record. Shough also found the end zone three times on the ground for 186 yards. The biggest issue for the Saints offensively, despite the early quarterback play, was the rushing attack. Starting running back Alvin Kamara finished last year with 471 yards and one touchdown (career lows), missing six games due to an MCL sprain, and the depth behind him was nowhere to be found. Devin Neal had 206 yards and two touchdowns, with other running backs like Audric Estime and Kendre Miller getting a combined 391 yards and two touchdowns. The leading scorer on the ground was Shough, which says a lot about the running back room. When it came to passing the ball, the Saints found a lot more success, especially with wide receiver Chris Olave, who had the best season of his career. Olave finished with 100 catches for 1,163 yards and nine touchdowns. Another contributor was Rashid Shaheed, who had 499 yards and two touchdowns, but he was traded to the Seattle Seahawks midseason. Tight end Juwan Johnson had a career season as well, finishing with 889 yards and three touchdowns on 77 catches. On defense, the defensive line shone brightest. EDGE Cameron Jordan led the team in sacks with 10.5 and forced two fumbles, but right behind him was EDGE Chase Young, who had 10 sacks and also forced two fumbles. The secondary was led by second-year cornerback Kool-Aid McKinstry, who paced the team with three interceptions and 17 pass deflections. The Saints’ run defense is what held them in a few games, allowing just 4.0 yards per carry, which ranked seventh in the NFL. 2026 offseason Key additions: G David Edwards, RB Travis Etienne, RB Ty Chandler, LB Kaden Elliss, TE Noah Fant, EDGE Tyree Wilson (trade), K Daniel Carlson Key losses: CB Alontae Taylor, LB Demario Davis, TE Foster Moreau 2026 NFL Draft picks Round 1: WR Jordyn Tyson Round 2: DT Christen Miller Round 3: TE Oscar Delp Round 4: G Jeremiah Wright Round 4: WR Bryce Lance Round 5: S Lorenzo Styles Jr. Round 6: WR Barion Brown Round 7: CB TJ Hall Overall, the Saints have more talent coming in than leaving, a good sign that this team is headed in the right direction. Their biggest free-agent move was keeping Jordan around after he tested free agency for his final season. When it comes to new incoming talent, though, the biggest add was guard David Edwards. This should help both the pass and the run, with a veteran guard strengthening the front. The team also made a trade for Las Vegas Raiders EDGE Tyree Wilson, giving up a 2026 fifth-round pick to acquire him and a 2026 seventh-round pick, giving them a potential suitor to replace Jordan after he retires. Running back Travis Etienne should see ample playing time with Kamara currently dealing with an MCL sprain. Linebacker Kaden Elliss gives them a younger linebacker core as Demario Davis left. Another replacement is tight end Noah Fant, who takes the spot of Foster Moreau and gives the Saints another viable threat in the passing game. The addition of kicker Daniel Carlson gives the Saints a big upgrade at the position, as their previous kickers, Blake Grupe and Charlie Smith, combined for a 71 percent field goal percentage. The biggest loss, though, was cornerback Alonte Taylor, and the secondary could be tested early, with few moves to bolster it. The rookie class did add some much-needed depth. Getting three wide receivers, led by first-round pick Jordyn Tyson out of Arizona State. Tyson will miss at least the first four games of the season after being placed on IR with a hamstring injury. The Saints also got help on the interior defensive line with defensive tackle Christen Miller, and more depth at tight end with Oscar Delp. The offensive line has a potential future starter in guard Jeremiah Wright, and the secondary got a few late-round picks in safety Lorenzo Styles Jr. and cornerback TJ Hall. 2026 season outlook New Orleans has a bit higher expectations in 2026. They are still an underdog to win the NFC South (second in odds behind the Buccaneers), but this could be a year for them to finally be on top again. They have their quarterback in Shough, and he’s been given some upgraded weapons—though his biggest one is on the sidelines for the moment in Tyson. The team must improve its running game, and it made moves to address that, but with Kamara already dealing with an injury, the depth might be tested sooner than expected. On defense, it should be a slight improvement as the team got younger on that side of the ball, but lost key starters in Taylor and Davis. If the young guys can show out and fill the roles of the vets who came before them, there should be ample improvement. Moore will now be in his second year as a head coach, and that should give him a leg up on the year before, when everything was new and different. The NFC South is anybody’s game this season. The Carolina Panthers won the title last year at 8-9, and they aren’t the favorites to win the division again. The Tampa Bay Buccaneers are currently the favorites, but they still have questions at wide receiver and on defense. The Atlanta Falcons could be uncertain at quarterback and just signed their star running back, Bijan Robinson, to a new contract. No team in the division is standing out as a clear-cut favorite, which could be the perfect time for the Saints to swoop in and get back in the playoffs. Injury notes Key players ruled out : DT Bryan Bresee (IR), RB Ty Chandler (IR), WR Jordyn Tyson (IR) Key players to monitor : RB Alvin Kamara (MCL), EDGE Cameron Jordan (hamstring), LB Pete Werner (groin), CB Quincy Riley (groin) Injuries have struck the Saints early this season at key spots. First, losing defensive tackle Bryan Bresee to a torn ACL back in July hurt the interior defensive line. Then losing Tyson for at least four games hurts the offense’s ability to move the ball through…

title: NFL Week 1 power rankings: National media mixed on Detroit Lions returning to form
summary: The Detroit Lions open the 2026 season with high expectations and feel good about how they’ve prepared for the regular season, but it appears most of the National media is going to need some convincing, as we can clearly see in our NFL Week 1 Power Rankings roundup. Let’s take a look at where the […]
full_text: ALLEN PARK, MICHIGAN - JULY 29: Head coach Dan Campbell of the Detroit Lions speaks during a press conference during Detroit Lions Training Camp at Detroit Lions Meijer Performance Center on July 29, 2026 in Allen Park, Michigan. (Photo by Nic Antaya/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Detroit Lions open the 2026 season with high expectations and feel good about how they’ve prepared for the regular season, but it appears most of the National media is going to need some convincing, as we can clearly see in our NFL Week 1 Power Rankings roundup. Let’s take a look at where the national media believe the Lions stand entering the 2026 season in this week’s power rankings. ESPN: 8 (Previous rank: 15) From ESPN Staff, excerpt from Eric Woodyard : This season is a success if … the Lions return to the postseason. Detroit missed the playoffs for the first time since 2022 last season. The organization has committed over $1 billion in contracts and extensions over the past two years and is seeking a return on its investment. Sports Illustrated: 8 ( Previous rank: 18) From Connor Orr : Easy schedule + upgraded play-caller + a little bit more health and stability across the front seven = a nine win team from 2025 winning double-digit games in 2026. Certainly the secondary is a concern, but the way Detroit can deploy itself schematically, I’m less worried about the team getting gouged in the passing game. At the very least, the Lions can score enough to keep pace. The Athletic: 9 (Previous rank: 17) From Chad Graff and Josh Kendall : Mock’s projected win total: 10.3 After missing the playoffs last season, the Lions will benefit from one of this year’s easiest schedules. The division will be tough, but they have a new offensive coordinator in Drew Petzing and more depth on the defensive line. Still, the secondary could have some struggles early due to injuries to Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph, each of whom begins the season on the PUP list. Yahoo Sports: 9 (Previous rank: 17) From Frank Schwab : The Lions traded David Montgomery and might regret it. Isiah Pacheco is on injured reserve with general manager Brad Holmes saying he is “hopeful” Pacheco returns this season. The current backups are Jacob Saylors and Sione Vaki. They have a combined nine carries for 29 yards in the NFL. The Lions desperately need Jahmyr Gibbs to stay healthy. They are also very thin in the secondary to start the season. USA Today: 11 (Previous rank: 18) From Nate Davis : If you subscribe to the theory that good teams are strong up the middle … then this one could be in trouble with C Cade Mays and starting safeties Brian Branch and Kerby Joseph all at least a month away from playing. At least the Lions can lean on RB Jahmyr Gibbs, though there’s zero safety net behind a bona fide star who’s played fewer than 60% of this offense’s snaps through the first three seasons of his career. NFL.com: 15 (Previous rank: 14) From Nick Shook : The sidelining of center Cade Mays (wrist) has me feeling uneasy about this offense as Detroit embarks on a new campaign. Tight end Sam LaPorta followed up back surgery with a hip injury in August, which isn’t great, but I think the Lions still have the edge over the Saints in Week 1. Sporting News: 15 (Previous rank: 16) From Vinnie Iyer : The Lions are facing their first real adversity in the Dan Campbell revival era, having missed the playoffs at 9-8 last season. The defense remains a work in progress behind Aidan Hutchinson. The offense is headed toward being more pass-reliant with Jared Goff. The Ringer: 16 (Previous rank: 16) From Diante Lee : This might be the most banged-up team in football entering Week 1. Safeties Brian Branch (torn Achilles) and Kerby Joseph (bone bruise) still haven’t returned to practice after season-ending injuries last year. Cornerback Terrion Arnold was waived earlier in the offseason as a result of his arrest on eight felony charges, including armed robbery and kidnapping, in Florida. Backup running back Isiah Pacheco is dealing with a back injury that landed him on IR, and the Lions don’t have enough quality running back depth behind Jahmyr Gibbs for me to feel good. The Lions have been marred by injury issues like these the past few seasons, but I refuse to rank them lower than 16th because their championship potential is still evident. They could have the best offense in football. Receiver Jameson Williams is the Detroit offensive player I’m most excited to watch this season. If he lights up defenses deep downfield to start the season, the attention opponents will have to devote to him will open up the offense for everyone else. CBS Sports: 19 (Previous rank: 18) From Pete Prisco : They will again score a lot of points on offense, but there are issues on defense. The secondary is a mess.

In the past, general manager Brian Gutekunst stated that he wanted a Kraft deal done going into the regular season, but […]
full_text: (Photo by Joe Sargent/Getty Images) | Getty Images Jeremy Fowler dropped a long Week 1 buzz article for ESPN on Thursday morning, and it included some nuggets on where the Green Bay Packers and tight end Tucker Kraft stand on an extension. In the past, general manager Brian Gutekunst stated that he wanted a Kraft deal done going into the regular season, but there is no deal in place yet. Here’s what Fowler had to say about the situation: This summer has featured complete market resets at cornerback and defensive tackle, and tight end could be next. It’s the only offensive or defensive position without a player making $20 million or more per season, but the Packers’ Tucker Kraft is hoping to change that. He remains in discussions about a new contract, but it has been a bit of a standoff so far. Green Bay hopes to get something done by the end of Week 1, so perhaps urgency prevails here. If Kraft can get a deal above that $20 million threshold, that sets the stage for Detroit’s Sam LaPorta. The Lions have interest in extending him, but his situation might carry into the season. $20 million per year might sound like a lot for a tight end, but it’s really not that big of a jump from where the position is at right now. As we wrote after the Kyle Pitts extension , here are the four highest-paid tight ends in the league from an average-per-year perspective: George Kittle: $19.1 million per Trey McBride: $19 million per Kyle Pitts: $18 million per Isaiah Likely: $13.3 million per Once Pitts signed for $18 million per year, it was assumed that Kraft would receive more than him. The only question was whether he was going to get paid in line with George Kittle and Trey McBride or truly become the highest-paid tight end in the league, despite him coming off an ACL tear. At least according to Fowler, Kraft’s camp is eyeing to “reset” the tight end market, even if the ceiling at the position rises by only about a million dollars per year. Fowler is also correct in that Sam LaPorta is the other tight end situation to pay attention to, as he’s the only other significant tight end going into a contract year in 2026. With Pitts off the table, it’s the Kraft and LaPorta show, as far as tight end extensions go. A big question is who will be first to sign, and whether or not the second player’s number will rise to try to beat the first’s benchmark.

title: Chris Brooks could decide the Packers’ Week 1 matchup against Minnesota
summary: One of the more underrated matchups going into the Green Bay Packers’ regular-season opener against the Minnesota Vikings, at least to me, is how running back Chris Brooks will do against defensive coordinator Brian Flores’ blitz-heavy front. The Packers have said that they will be trying out a running back-by-committee approach early on in the […]
full_text: (Photo by Timothy Hurst/MediaNews Group/The Denver Post via Getty Images) | Denver Post via Getty Images One of the more underrated matchups going into the Green Bay Packers’ regular-season opener against the Minnesota Vikings, at least to me, is how running back Chris Brooks will do against defensive coordinator Brian Flores’ blitz-heavy front. The Packers have said that they will be trying out a running back-by-committee approach early on in the season, but I want to talk about blocking, not ball-carrying, when it comes to what Brooks can bring to the table. Everyone and their mother knows that Flores wants to blitz. It’s in his DNA. It’s who he has been, who he is and who he will want to be in the future. Arguably, Packers head coach Matt LaFleur’s best trait as a coach has been his team’s pass-rushing plans, as there have been few players up front who have been allowed to take over games, even when the team has matched up against the Aaron Donalds, Myles Garretts and Aidan Hutchinsons of the world. His line gets a lot of chip help from tight ends, funky spacing that puts rushers in bad positions pre-snap and running backs who add on to the protection. That’s where Brooks had thrived in the past. Below is a clip from Week 1 last year, where Brooks, against a mugged-up Detroit Lions front, passes off a linebacker and takes on a defensive tackle on a stunt to allow Jordan Love to make a big throw in the middle of the field. Yes, a defensive tackle. Packers RB Chris Brooks picking up a blitzing linebacker, passing him off and then taking on a defensive tackle pic.twitter.com/CD5olFPx84 — Justis Mosqueda (@JuMosq) September 8, 2025 Last year, PFF graded Brooks as the fourth-best running back league-wide in pass protection . To make this short and simple: He’s a really good blocking back. I’d expect that the Packers will want to lean into Brooks’ blocking ability, especially on obvious passing downs, against Flores’ aggressive scheme. Especially when three of Green Bay’s starting offensive linemen are currently on the injury report and were limited during Wednesday’s practice . So don’t discount Brooks being a difference-maker in the Week 1 matchup, even if he’s not going to receive the bulk of the carries out of the backfield. It also probably helps the Packers that they just signed safety Kahlef Hailassie, who was with the Vikings for all of training camp and was just released two days ago, to their practice squad. Teams usually spend two weeks of game planning for their Week 1 opponent, rather than one, because they receive that extra week between cutdowns and the start of the regular season. Maybe Hailassie knows a little about the pass-rush plan that Flores has for the Packers and had installed over the last week, and he’ll want to share that with Brooks. You’ve got to love a little gamesmanship.

title: The Packers’ defense was the opposite of the Seahawks last season
summary: Here’s an interesting stat that I saw last night during the NFL regular-season opener, when the Seattle Seahawks were able to take down the New England Patriots in the Super Bowl rematch. According to Sümer Sports, the 2025 Seahawks played five defensive backs 81 percent of the time when opposing offenses played two or fewer […]
full_text: (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here’s an interesting stat that I saw last night during the NFL regular-season opener, when the Seattle Seahawks were able to take down the New England Patriots in the Super Bowl rematch. According to Sümer Sports, the 2025 Seahawks played five defensive backs 81 percent of the time when opposing offenses played two or fewer receivers, which led the NFL, while the Green Bay Packers did so on just 14 percent of snaps, the second-lowest rate in the league, only behind the Detroit Lions. 2025 teams that refused to match heavy sets pic.twitter.com/RBCwI9tuMA — Sam Bruchhaus (@sambruchhaus) September 10, 2026 That might be a little wordy, so I want to break this down piece by piece. Generally, NFL defenses tend to match the number of outside cornerbacks and slot defenders on the field to the number of receivers the opposing offense throws out there. Why? So they can have bigger bodies on the grass against heavier personnel sets (like multi-tight end or multi-back looks) when teams are running the ball more frequently, and so they don’t have to play a linebacker in coverage against a slot receiver in three-receiver sets, when opposing offenses pass the ball more. Under defensive coordinator Jeff Hafley, the Packers stuck to their “matching” personnel rules pretty strictly, outside of the red zone and short-yardage plays. To me, it’s not a surprise that they only broke “matching” personnel 14 percent of the time. In fact, I was a little surprised it was that high. If you only measured plays between the 20s, that number probably drops. Meanwhile, the Seahawks, who play a quarters-based scheme that new defensive coordinator Jonathan Gannon is expected to run in Green Bay, played their nickel or dime subpackages on more than four-fifths of their plays when they got heavy personnel looks from the offensive side of the ball. For perspective, only five teams in the entire NFL didn’t match heavy personnel with primarily a “base” defense last year, and two of those — the San Francisco 49ers and Buffalo Bills — barely crossed the threshold with a 51 percent rate. The reason that Seattle can do this is that Nick Emmanwori, the Seahawks’ slot defender, essentially can play both as a slot defender and as a Sam linebacker. For the most part, a slot defender in a 4-2 nickel look is basically playing the 4-3 Sam linebacker role anyway, just split out from the formation when the slot receiver is detached from the formation. When that slot receiver motions into the formation, potentially as an insert player to help run block, the slot defender usually travels with him, putting the slot defender in a more traditional Sam linebacker role pre-snap. The Seahawks seem perfectly fine allowing Emmanwori to play both of those spots, no matter what opposing offenses throw out on the field. Meanwhile, the Packers haven’t been as confident in their slot defender, Javon Bullard, right or wrong. Gannon’s Cardinals didn’t match heavy personnel on 23 percent of snaps last year, a good jump up from the Packers’ 14 percent mark in 2025, but still nowhere near the Seahawks’ 81 percent rate. In the NFL of old, a slot defender and a slot receiver were both of the mold of players who were too small to play on the outside. Now, with how run games want to manipulate both positions, those players are much bigger, as slot defenders are also asked to be Sam linebackers and slot receivers are being asked to play some tight end-like roles. It should be no surprise that defenses with Emmanwori (6’2”, 220 pounds) and Kyle Hamilton (6’4”, 218 pounds) are the most comfortable in just letting their nickel personnel stay on the field and having their slot defenders add on as a strong-side linebacker. For what it’s worth, and it’s only the preseason, Gannon’s defense in the preseason typically matched personnel with the opposing offense. Maybe we’ll see his unit play more six-defensive-back looks against multi-tight-end sets in the regular season, though, as the team has shown a three-safety Penny defense , built to stop the run with extra defensive backs on the field, during the summer.

title: Packers Injury Report: Updates on the offensive line
summary: There were only two non-participants for the Green Bay Packers during their Wednesday practice: defensive lineman Warren Brinson (calf) and linebacker Ty’Ron Hopper (Achilles). Brinson’s injury stems from a pre-game issue he had going into Week 2 of the preseason, while Hopper’s injury appears to be a new issue. Even if Brinson and Hopper both […]
full_text: (Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images) | Getty Images There were only two non-participants for the Green Bay Packers during their Wednesday practice : defensive lineman Warren Brinson (calf) and linebacker Ty’Ron Hopper (Achilles). Brinson’s injury stems from a pre-game issue he had going into Week 2 of the preseason, while Hopper’s injury appears to be a new issue. Even if Brinson and Hopper both can’t go this week against the Minnesota Vikings, the Packers’ inactive decisions (the team has to scratch five players on its 53-man roster for gamedays) would be pretty easy. Brinson, Hopper, two offensive linemen and whoever the fourth tight end is will get Green Bay down to a 48-man gameday unit. That seems like the most logical choice at the moment. The limited participants in practice today were: LT Jordan Morgan (knee) LG Aaron Banks (knee) RT Zach Bako-Bewele (knee) DL Devonte Wyatt (ankle) DL Javon Hargrave (knee) ED Barryn Sorrell (foot) The only new injuries in this group appear to be the Morgan and Sorrell injuries. Otherwise, players were already dealing with their current injuries (or recovery from injuries) during training camp. After practice today, Bak0-Bewele told The Athletic’s Matt Schneidman that he “definitely” plans to play against the Vikings. Had Bako-Bewele not been able to go, Anthony Belton would likely have been his injury replacement. Before practice, head coach Matt LaFleur stated that both Banks and Bako-Bewele were going to be limited participants, so their status seems to be part of the plan this week. He also stated that if Banks is healthy, he will be the starting left guard. In camp, rookie fifth-round pick Jager Burton was rotating in and out of the lineup with Banks, even when Banks was cleared for practice. If Banks can’t dress for the game, assume that Burton will be starting in his place. The Packers also made a transaction today, as safety Murvion Kenion III was dropped to make room for safety Kahlef Hailassie. Kenion was signed by Green Bay as an undrafted free agent immediately following the draft and had been part of the team throughout the spring and summer. Hailassie spent a little more than a year at Oregon before transferring to community college and then landing back in the FBS with Western Kentucky. Hailassie has previously been a member of the Kansas City Chiefs, Cleveland Browns, Minnesota Vikings (twice) and Jacksonville Jaguars. Hailassie was just released from the Vikings’ practice squad yesterday, so there’s a chance the Packers might pick his brain about the team’s Week 1 opponent. You’ve got to love gamesmanship. Hailassie has played a total of 10 NFL games (2023 to 2024), all with the Browns. He played 105 defensive snaps and 110 special teams snaps during the regular season. In other practice squad news, running back Pierre Strong Jr. was seen working with the rehab group in practice, according to ESPN’s Rob Demovsky . This might help explain why the Packers used a practice squad spot to add a second running back, Damon Bankston , who was previously a pre-draft visitor with Green Bay before signing on as a UDFA with the New York Giants.

title: Packers Salary Cap: Jonnu Smith contract details released
summary: The contract for new Green Bay Packers tight end Jonnu Smith has finally been released, more than a week after he signed with the team. We previously knew it was a one-year deal, but that’s all the information we had. According to ESPN’s Rob Demovsky, Smith received a signing bonus of $350,000 to sign with […]
full_text: PITTSBURGH, PENNSYLVANIA - JANUARY 12: Jonnu Smith #81 of the Pittsburgh Steelers runs across the field during an NFL wild card playoff football game against the Houston Texans at Acrisure Stadium on January 12, 2026 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania. (Photo by Perry Knotts/Getty Images) | Getty Images The contract for new Green Bay Packers tight end Jonnu Smith has finally been released, more than a week after he signed with the team. We previously knew it was a one-year deal, but that’s all the information we had. According to ESPN’s Rob Demovsky , Smith received a signing bonus of $350,000 to sign with the team. Smith’s game checks (which will fully guarantee this week, as he’s a vested veteran) are worth $1.3 million. On top of that, he can also earn $350,000 in per-game roster bonuses. In total, it’s a $2 million deal, if Smith can be on the field for every game this season. Smith’s cap charge will also be $2 million, as his roster bonuses are considered “likely to be earned” by the NFL, since he played all 17 games with the Pittsburgh Steelers last year. For perspective, here are the cash earnings that Smith signed up for after his rookie contract: 2021: $16.9 million (Patriots) 2022: $9.8 million (Patriots) 2023: $8.5 million (Falcons) 2024: $4.3 million (Dolphins) 2025: $9 million (Steelers) He’s making significantly less than he ever has as a veteran in the NFL. Head coach Matt LaFleur believes that Smith can hit the ground running in the regular season, not only because Smith previously played for LaFleur with the Tennessee Titans but also because Smith played for Arthur Smith, a former LaFleur assistant in Tennessee, in 2023 (Falcons) and 2025 (Steelers). Smith was listed as the second-string tight end, ahead of both Josh Whyle and Mark Redman, on their first depth chart of the regular season .

title: New stats from Pro Football Reference highlight legendary Packers players
summary: Pro Football Reference has just rolled out some stats from the earliest years of the National Football League. In a blog post, PFR announced that courtesy of a donation from legendary sports researcher David Neft, they’re now able to offer fairly reliable stats from the 1920-1931 seasons (and 1932, in some cases). That means we’re […]
full_text: The Curly Lambeau statue is seen outside Lambeau Field in Green Bay, Wisconsin, on August 6, 2025. (Photo by Ross Harried/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images Pro Football Reference has just rolled out some stats from the earliest years of the National Football League. In a blog post, PFR announced that courtesy of a donation from legendary sports researcher David Neft, they’re now able to offer fairly reliable stats from the 1920-1931 seasons (and 1932, in some cases). That means we’re looking at numbers that predate the Packers’ presence in the NFL. For that matter, these numbers predate the NFL itself, since the league wasn’t officially born until 1922, having operated as the American Pro Football Association prior to that. The full writeup is worth your time , but let me draw out a few highlights that might pique your interest. The Packers were one of the most successful teams in the NFL during the era these numbers come from (though they didn’t win their first title until 1929), and the stats show why. Two of the most prolific passers from this era did most or all of their damage with the Packers: Red Dunn and Curly Lambeau. You’ll find a similar story among the most productive receivers; the first (Johnny Blood), second (Lavvie Dilweg), and third place (Charlie Mathys) pass catchers all spent the bulk of their productive years in Green Bay. The Packers don’t have a huge number of productive rushers on the list, but the one who does make an appearance deserves special attention. According to these numbers, Verne Lewellen ran for at least 2,278 yards during his NFL career, and that’s barely scratching the surface on his impact. The article from PFR describes Lewellen as a “glaring omission” from the Pro Football Hall of Fame ( I agree ), and these stats help show why. Not only was Lewellen a great rusher, he produced the most yards from scrimmage of any player during this era (beating out teammate Johnny Blood) and was a dominant punter. A dominant punter? It’s true. Punting was a much different part of the game in the early days of pro football. With no hash marks on the field and inconsistent offensive power, punting well could swing a game; you really could pin a team in their own territory if you managed to stick the ball deep in a corner. And when it came to punting, Lewellen was the very best. His 25,895 punting yards more than double the output of the next most productive punter in PFR’s numbers. He might have a claim as the best punter of all time, at least relative to his peers. Now, there are some disclaimers here. Pro Football Reference readily and openly admits that these stats are “pre-official” and come from a variety of sources of varying degrees of reliability. You shouldn’t necessarily take these stats to the bank, and I’m sure Packers historian Cliff Christl will be along in the relatively near future picking some of these numbers apart. And he should! Part of the process of “doing history” is having open and robust discussions about the provenance of historical data, and PFR just did us a great favor on that front. And some of their sources are truly remarkable, like this compilation of very early stats from the Packers themselves . (What I wouldn’t give to get my hands on that!) But even with those disclaimers, this is a huge win for understanding the historical context of a whole bunch of great players. Even if the stats aren’t official, anything that showcases the achievements of some of the best to ever do it is a blessing for football fans.

And that includes the Packers, who are currently without the services of Josh Jacobs (and likely will remain so for the foreseeable […]

(Photo by AAron Ontiveroz/The Denver Post) | Denver Post via Getty Images The Packers’ season will probably not hinge on the strength of their running backs, which is a good thing, because I’m not sure anybody really knows what the Packers have at running back. And that includes the Packers, who are currently without the services of Josh Jacobs (and likely will remain so for the foreseeable future). Beyond Jacobs, the backfield consists of MarShawn Lloyd, who has injured just about every body part known to man (and several previously unknown to science), Chris Brooks (more of a fullback, to be honest), and Kaleb Johnson, a second-year third round pick so disappointing the team that drafted him traded him for just a sixth round pick. They’ve also got Damon Bankston kicking around , but he’s merely an intriguing prospect at this point, and he’s barely been in town long enough to know where the bathrooms at Lambeau Field are. Maybe he could be a help at some point, but he’s got to get his feet wet first. None of this should be a season-long threat. Josh Jacobs will return at some point, though the Packers might be better off without him. If Lloyd can stay healthy, he and Brooks should be able to put together a more-or-less competent backfield. title: Packers vs. Vikings Week 1 TV broadcast map shows wide coverage
summary: When the Green Bay Packers open up the 2026 season against the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday, they will do so with the eyes of most of the pro football world upon them. Sunday’s kickoff will take place at 3:25 PM Central time, and the vast majority of the United States will get to see the […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - DECEMBER 29: Carrington Valentine #24 of the Green Bay Packers intercepts a pass intended for T.J. Hockenson #87 of the Minnesota Vikings during the third quarter at U.S. Bank Stadium on December 29, 2024 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Brace Hemmelgarn/Getty Images) | Getty Images When the Green Bay Packers open up the 2026 season against the Minnesota Vikings on Sunday, they will do so with the eyes of most of the pro football world upon them. Sunday’s kickoff will take place at 3:25 PM Central time, and the vast majority of the United States will get to see the game on local CBS affiliates. Week one is a doubleheader week for both FOX and CBS, one of the few weeks when each network gets to show a game in both the early and late Sunday afternoon time slots. CBS stations will carry one of Packers-Vikings or Cardinals-Chargers in the late game, while FOX stations get their pick of Commanders-Eagles or Dolphins-Raiders. Here’s a look at the initial broadcast map from 506sports.com, with Packers-Vikings in red: The blue areas will instead see Cardinals-Chargers, which will go out to those two teams’ home markets plus those of the other AFC West teams (the Raiders, Broncos, and Chiefs). On the call for the Packers’ opening game is CBS’ top commentating team. This year, Jim Nantz will be joined by color commentator J.J. Watt, who is stepping up from the network’s #2 squad to take the place that fellow Wisconsin native Tony had Romo previously occupied. Romo was suspended from CBS programming this summer after being arrested in Milwaukee for OWI, a charge to which he later pleaded no contest, and the network is reportedly negotiating a buyout of Romo’s remaining contract . This is the first of four games that the Packers are currently scheduled to play in the late afternoon “Game of the Week” time slot this season, though all four of those come in the first nine weeks of the season. Most of the country should expect to see all of those games, except for areas on the west coast that have home teams or divisional opponents also playing in that late time slot.

title: Green Bay Packers drop Week 1 depth chart: 6 takeaways
summary: The Green Bay Packers updated their depth chart on Tuesday, the first time that they’ve done so going into the 2026 regular season. For the most part, it looks accurate, based on our charting of preseason and training camp rotations, but there were a few things that stood out to me — so I want […]
full_text: DETROIT,MICHIGAN-December21: tight end Jonnu Smith (81) of the Pittsburgh Steelers stands on the field ahead of an NFL football game between the Pittsburgh Steelers and the Detroit Lions in Detroit, Michigan USA, on Sunday, December 21, 2025. (Photo by Amy Lemus/NurPhoto via Getty Images) | NurPhoto via Getty Images The Green Bay Packers updated their depth chart on Tuesday , the first time that they’ve done so going into the 2026 regular season. For the most part, it looks accurate, based on our charting of preseason and training camp rotations , but there were a few things that stood out to me — so I want to talk about them today. Disclaimer: I’m aware that the Packers probably put little to no mental energy into posting a public “unofficial” depth chart. A few things turned my gears, though. Running Back First of all, Kaleb Johnson was listed as the Packers’ third-string running back, which may not be a surprise to some — because he just got here a week ago . Personally, I still believe that Johnson will be the number two ball-carrier in Green Bay while Josh Jacobs is out , as Chris Brooks, who was listed as a second-stringer, is more of a blocking back than a true ball-carrier. Jonnu Smith While Johnson just got to Green Bay and seems too low on the depth chart, tight end Jonnu Smith, who was signed by the Packers the same day that the team traded for Johnson, is listed as the team’s second-string tight end behind Tucker Kraft. Smith has played for head coach Matt LaFleur when they were together with the Tennessee Titans, but I thought Smith’s standing going into Week 1 would be more of a question mark, considering he wasn’t signed with anyone this offseason — unlike Johnson, who at least went through training camp with the Pittsburgh Steelers. It’s going to be tough for the Packers to keep four tight ends active on gamedays (they have to scratch a minimum of five players from their 53-man roster), and Smith and Josh Whyle both overlap as off-ball move tight ends who are primarily pass-catchers. If Smith is already ahead of Whyle, who has been in the program for two years now, then Whyle’s time on the 53-man roster might be long. Mark Redman, who is sharing the third-string role with Whyle on the Packers’ depth chart, is a blocking tight end, a role that is much more valuable than Whyle filling in as Smith’s potential backup. If I’m guessing today, Whyle is probably going to be inactive against the Minnesota Vikings. Offensive Line The Packers’ starting offensive line was listed as Jordan Morgan, Aaron Banks, Sean Rhyan, Jacob Monk and Zach Bako-Bewele (left to right). That’s not really the question right now. It’s whether or not Banks (tendinitis in his knee) and/or Bako-Bewele (coming off a partially torn Patellar tendon) will be able to play a full 60 minutes this week. Rookie fifth-round pick Jager Burton was listed as the backup center on the depth chart, but don’t make too much of that. If Banks can’t go, it’ll be Burton at left guard (and it’ll be Anthony Belton at right tackle if Bako-Bewele isn’t playing). Even if Banks can play, I wouldn’t be surprised if Burton rotates at left guard. Defensive Line We never got the opportunity to see the entire defensive line healthy and active this summer, either on the Family Night broadcast or for preseason games. Because of that, we’re not really sure how the pieces of this puzzle are supposed to fit together. Devonte Wyatt has been a three-technique (a 3-4 defensive end role in Green Bay’s new scheme) his entire career, so we can plug him in as a starter there. To the surprise of many, the Packers bubble-wrapped Karl Brooks in the preseason and treated him as a true starter, and he’s another 3-4 defensive end type, not a nose tackle body. On Green Bay’s depth chart, the team listed both Wyatt and Brooks as the starting ends, with free agent signing Javon Hargrave as the starting nose tackle, one slot ahead of Jonathan Ford. It will be interesting to see just how many snaps Hargrave actually plays at the nose this year, as he looked a little out of place filling in that role with the Vikings last season. For what it’s worth, Ford got the “starts” as a true head-up nose tackle this preseason. The lone third-stringer on the line is camp sensation Anthony Campbell, who will probably be inactive in Week 1, unless Warren Brinson can’t suit up for action due to his calf injury. Brandon Cisse Two days ago we reminded everyone that rookie Brandon Cisse hasn’t been named a starting cornerback by the team , but I guess the depth chart release means that that’s no longer true. Yes, Cisse was listed as the starter opposite Keisean Nixon. Nixon has been handling the bulk of the left cornerback snaps with the first-team offense this summer, while Cisse and Carrington Valentine rotated at right corner. Going into Week 1, I’m assuming that Nixon will play left cornerback full-time while Cisse will get the “start” on the right, even if Valentine rotates in some at the position. For what it’s worth, Cisse is the only rookie starter listed on the depth chart for either the offense or defense. Returner Options One of the most inaccurate parts of the depth chart every year is who they list as the team’s returners, but I think the choices they listed as the second-string options behind receiver Skyy Moore actually make sense this time around. On punts, slot receiver Jayden Reed was listed as the number two returner. On kicks, the second-stringer is receiver Bo Melton. Melton, who does a lot on special teams without needing the ball in his hands, is generally the “off-returner” for the team, a role where he’s deep in the backfield on kicks but really fills in more as a lead blocker than a true returner. My question is whether the Packers would keep Melton as the “off-returner” if Moore ever went down (or was scratched), or if they would have someone else (like a J. Michael Sturdivant) fill in as the off-returner. I’m also unsure if Moore will keep the kick return job when receiver Savion Williams is activated off the injured reserve, but we have a few weeks to figure that one out.
