title: Las Vegas Raiders Week 1: Scouting the Miami Dolphins offense
summary: Just because the Miami Dolphins have made some major changes on offense this offseason doesn’t mean they are pushovers for the Las Vegas Raiders in the Week 1 matchup. Sure, they have a quarterback starting his first NFL season as “the guy.” There may be no more Tyreek Hill, Jaylen Waddle, or Darren Waller and […]
full_text: (Photo by Brandon Sloter/Getty Images) | Getty Images Just because the Miami Dolphins have made some major changes on offense this offseason doesn’t mean they are pushovers for the Las Vegas Raiders in the Week 1 matchup. Sure, they have a quarterback starting his first NFL season as “the guy.” There may be no more Tyreek Hill, Jaylen Waddle, or Darren Waller and an offensive line with question marks. But, what challenges does the Dolphins offense present? The Workhorse De’Von Achane is the Dolphins running back and primary offensive threat on paper. Last season, he made the now-defunct Pro Bowl, running for 1,350 yards on 238 carries a 5.7 yards per carry, scoring eight touchdowns on the ground. As a pass catcher out of the backfield he caught 67 passes for 488 yards and four more touchdowns. Achane is a one-cut runner with a whole lot of speed and enough wiggle to squeeze in between the smallest of creases. In truth, he should scare Raiders defensive coordinator Rob Leonard to death. Leonard has shown a multi-faceted approach to his defensive alignments, but if the Dolphins can counter certain looks with a well-timed audible, holes in the defense will be exploitable. The trenches With only three preseason games to go off of and a vanilla offensive scheme, it’s hard to predict what the offensive line will be. From the limited sample size provided by the first-team offensive line, a few things are apparent. It is a group with a healthy amount of size and athleticism. When the elephants go on parade, they keep it tight and don’t allow defenders past them. They are well coached, employing primarily a zone blocking scheme in the run game; there is a lot of organized chaos. Meaning, the blocking scheme is less about driving opponents off the ball and backwards and more about creating creases and walling off defenders with timing—lots of pulling offensive linemen and less hat-on-hat blocking. It is a scheme that will pose many challenges to the Raiders’ light defensive front. In pass protection, the line appears to be solid. A West Coast passing attack doesn’t ask linemen to protect for a long time, but rather to make an initial punch and keep lanes open for the quarterback to scramble. So far, they have been solid in their attempts. Defenses that employ a lot of twists and stunts will have success in bypassing the protection packages but then they will need to deal with the legs of Malik Willis. The quarterback Willis is a dual-threat quarterback drafted from Liberty University. He may not have set any NCAA records, but he was plenty effective for the Flames. In his final college season, he passed for 2,857 yards, 27 touchdowns and 12 interceptions while running for 878 yards and 13 touchdowns to boot. Willis isn’t particularly big, nor is he the fastest quarterback in the NFL, but he has a complete game. He can spin the pill, throw with touch, make solid decisions and his ball placement is impeccable. If his receivers are covered and the opportunity presents itself, he isn’t scared to pull it down, tuck it and run. Going back to the Raiders defensive interior, this set of skills will prove to be the most challenging for them to overcome. An accurate quarterback versed in working with less, who can scramble and assess where to go with the football and get it there, will be tough to deal with. Pass Catchers The wildcards of the offense are all the pass catchers the Dolphins will be using to attack defenses. Dolphins’ offensive coordinator, Bobby Slowik, has brought a style of offense geared towards spreading out defenses and attacking space. It’s a great way to operate when you don’t have a lot of known commodities on offense and guys have yet to establish themselves. The Raiders young secondary displayed a weakness against larger receivers running possession-type routes, as seen against the Arizona Cardinals in week 1 of the preseason. Malik Washington, Jalen Tolbert and Greg Dulcich aren’t going to scare many people individually. However, tight end Dulcich is a chain mover who started producing down the stretch last season. Washington, Caleb Douglas and Chris Bell, in my opinion, are the three most viable options to account for, as they have the greatest ability to make a difference with the ball in their hands. Washington is more of a return man/gadget player who, if provided with space, can make magic happen. Douglas and Bell are both tall rookie wide receivers with speed and good hands. Bell has shown promise as an all-purpose receiver and is worth keeping an eye on, yet hasn’t played an NFL regular-season game. Douglas was more of a deep guy last season for the Texas Tech Red Raiders. Having an NFL quarterback with more polish than Behren Morton should allow him to have even more success. Fair warning The 2026 Raiders schedule is daunting; while the Dolphins may be in transition, they can’t be taken lightly. Styles make fights and sometimes matchups overrule the consensus. On paper, the Dolphins are nothing special, but the Raiders last 20+ years of futility indicate that may be a greater cause for concern. This game can be simple if the Raiders are able to neutralize Achane, disrupt pass protection and contain Willis. If they can’t than the season will feel a whole lot longer than 17 games.

summary: The Las Vegas Raiders’ optimism that starting running back Ashton Jeanty will be ready to play Sunday in the Week 1 season opener against Miami Dolphins took a big step forward Wednesday when head coach Klint Kubiak said the No. 6 overall pick in the 2025 draft will practice. It’s Jeanty first practice since he […]
full_text: (Photo by Kenneth Richmond/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders’ optimism that starting running back Ashton Jeanty will be ready to play Sunday in the Week 1 season opener against Miami Dolphins took a big step forward Wednesday when head coach Klint Kubiak said the No. 6 overall pick in the 2025 draft will practice. It’s Jeanty first practice since he injured his ankle August 23 in practice. This is continued good news after the team was initially worried Jeanty suffered a serious injury. Jeanty was a full participant in practice Wednesday, which is a sign he will play Sunday barring a setback. Last week, both Kubiak and Raiders’ general manager John Spytek expressed optimism that Jeanty will be available in Week 1. On Wednesday, Kubiak went as far to say he expects all of the team’s 53 players to be ready to play Sunday. That is significant for a team that has been mostly healthy since the start of training camp. So, barring any changes, all of the Raiders’ inactive players Sunday will be coach’s decisions and not injury based. If he continues to go in the right direction, both Jeanty and rookie Mike Washington should get their share of carries Sunday.

title: Raiders-Dolphins: 5 things to watch
summary: The Las Vegas Raiders open the 2026 regular season Sunday at home when they host the Miami Dolphins. Kickoff is set for 1:25 p.m. PT. Here are five keys to watch: Offensive rhythm: The Raiders need to improve dramatically on offense. That’s why new head coach Klint Kubiak was hired. Getting the offense humming in […]
full_text: (Photo by Ethan Miller/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Las Vegas Raiders open the 2026 regular season Sunday at home when they host the Miami Dolphins. Kickoff is set for 1:25 p.m. PT. Here are five keys to watch: Offensive rhythm: The Raiders need to improve dramatically on offense. That’s why new head coach Klint Kubiak was hired. Getting the offense humming in this game is important to establish a positive trend forward both in the running and passing games. Get to Malik Willis: The Raiders need to establish a pass-rush beyond star Maxx Crosby and they need to do it quickly. Willis, the Dolphins’ new starting quarterback, can move and he can hurt defenses with his legs. But he can also get rattled. So, putting constant heat on him is vital. Wide receiver play: There has been a lot of questions about this unit all offseason and now into the regular season. Can Tre Tucker, Jalen Nailor and Jack Bech produce enough help for star tight end Brock Bowers? Offensive line: This is a major key for this game and every game. The Raiders’ offensive line was brutal last season and was a major reason why the offense stunk so badly. Kolton Miller is healthy at left tackle and big-money free-agent signing, center Tyler Liinderbaum is a great anchor to the unit. Still, there is some youth on this line and it has to show it’s ready to be a positive part of the team. Run defense: This has been a problem and it was shaky in the preseason. Miami’s De”Von Achane can be a game-breaking player, so the Raiders really have to play tight against the run Sunday.

full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FL - AUGUST 22: A Miami Dolphins flag is waved on the field before the preseason NFL game between the New York Giants and the Miami Dolphins on Saturday, August 22, 2026 at Hard Rock Stadium in Miami, FL (Photo by Peter Joneleit/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Miami Dolphins open the 2026 season on the road as they visit the Las Vegas Raiders on Sunday. title: De’Von Achane aiming for NFL rushing title, ready for Week 1
summary: The Miami Dolphins are set to begin their 2026 NFL regular season on Sunday, kicking off a 17-game-over-18-week schedule. The analysts expect the Dolphins to struggle this season, with many predicting Miami to own the first-overall pick in the 2027 Draft by the time the season ends. The Dolphins, themselves, are not buying into those […]
full_text: MIAMI GARDENS, FLORIDA - DECEMBER 28: De'Von Achane #28 of the Miami Dolphins runs with the ball against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers during the second quarter at Hard Rock Stadium on December 28, 2025 in Miami Gardens, Florida. (Photo by Julio Aguilar/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Miami Dolphins are set to begin their 2026 NFL regular season on Sunday, kicking off a 17-game-over-18-week schedule. The analysts expect the Dolphins to struggle this season, with many predicting Miami to own the first-overall pick in the 2027 Draft by the time the season ends. The Dolphins, themselves, are not buying into those prognostications and are still setting lofty goals – especially running back De’Von Achane. Miami’s 2023 third-round pick explained the importance of setting goals, saying, “I feel like you don’t got goals, I feel like what are you playing the game for? And you know, I kind of add more goals as we go through the season, but we always start with some.” When asked to share one of his personal goals, Achane set a lofty objective. “I always try to go for the rushing title so that’s just something I do,“ he stated. Achane, coming off his first career Pro Bowl selection, is expected to be the focal point of the offense this season. Head coach Jeff Hafley joked earlier in the summer that he would be looking to give Achane 45 touches per game this season. While 45 touches is not realistic, Achane was asked how many touches he thinks he will get in Sunday’s game against the Las Vegas Raiders. “I have no idea,” he replied. “I feel like, don’t nobody really know how many times you’re going to touch the ball. I feel like it’s just kind of a however the game is going type thing.” With all the focus on Achane, opposing defenses will likely keep defenders close to the line of scrimmage to slow him down. Asked about what they would do to the offense, the running back recognized how that would open up the passing game, saying, “It just gives opportunities for our young receivers, or whoever’s out there, to make plays. Like you said, this is a team game. I can’t just go out there and win by myself. So when teams do stack the box, we can still try to run the ball, but if we have to adjust, it just gives opportunities for receivers to make plays.” He continued, “It takes all of us. Just like they need me to run, I need them in the pass game. It goes both ways.” The Dolphins underwent a coaching staff change this offseason, with former head coach and offensive play caller Mike McDaniel fired after the year ended and former Green Bay Packers defensive coordinator Jeff Hafley hired as the 12th full-time head coach in team history. Bobby Slowik, working as the passing game coordinator under McDaniel, was hired as the offensive coordinator for Hafley, keeping some stability in the offense while bringing a new perspective to the attack. How will Slowick’s promotion impact Achane’s utilization? The fourth-year rusher said of the offense, “Of course it’s new…because it’s a new coach. So it’s kind of still the same, you add new stuff, but Slo was here last year with Mike, so some stuff is the same, some things are different. But at the same time, I feel like Slo uses me in the pass game, run game, so it’s good for me.” Achane has lofty goals for himself this season and is probably going to have a great opportunity to reach them. But, in the near term, he is excited just to get the season started this weekend, saying, “I mean, it feels good, man. Like you said, it’s been a long time since we actually played four quarters, and I’ll been excited to be out there and just to go out there, just watch our team, to see how we come and basically just see how we hold up against somebody else for a full game.”
author: Kevin Nogle

title: No snap count restrictions for Chris Bell in Dolphins opener
summary: The Miami Dolphins may have struck gold when they nabbed wide receiver Chris Bell from Louisville in the third round of the 2026 NFL Draft. After all, the player was projected to be a late first round pick prior to his ACL tear in November of last year. Due to that injury, many thought that […]
full_text: Miami Dolphins wide receivers Kevin Coleman Jr. (21) and Chris Bell (18) talk during practice at Baptist Health Training Complex on Wednesday, Sept. 9, 2026, in Miami Gardens, Florida. (Alie Skowronski/Miami Herald/Tribune News Service via Getty Images) The Miami Dolphins may have struck gold when they nabbed wide receiver Chris Bell from Louisville in the third round of the 2026 NFL Draft. After all, the player was projected to be a late first round pick prior to his ACL tear in November of last year. Due to that injury, many thought that Bell would be eased back into action — possibly missing the first half of his rookie season. However, Bell’s recovery has been an expeditious one, and the receiver has been named a starter for the Dolphins ahead of their Week One clash in Las Vegas against the Raiders. And according to new head coach Jeff Hafley, Bell will be a full-go and will not be on a snap count when he takes the field on Sunday. Yesterday, while speaking with the South Florida media, Hafley confirmed that Bell will have no restrictions against Las Vegas. “We’re going to play him — see how he feels — but, there’s no pitch count on Chris.” Bell’s full availability is an extremely positive development for the Dolphins, especially this early in the season. Quarterback Malik Willis will have a full complement of weapons for his first start with Miami — including fellow rookies Caleb Douglas and Kevin Coleman Jr., as well as Malik Washington and tight end Greg Dulcich. Of course, Miami’s most explosive offensive player, De’Von Achane, will factor mightily into this tilt as well. Will that be enough to allow Miami to sneak past Las Vegas? We will all find out in just a few short days.
author: Marek Brave

title: What Will the 2026 Dolphins Passing Game Look Like? Let’s Ask the 2022–2023 Packers
summary: The Packers built a passing game without a WR1 — and the Dolphins might do the same. The Dolphins are heading into 2026 with one of the youngest receiver rooms in the league, with three rookies and a second‑year player expected to play real snaps – all catching passes from an unproven, first‑time starting quarterback. […]
full_text: LANDOVER, MD - AUGUST 14: Malik Willis #2 of the Miami Dolphins looks over the Washington Commanders defense during the first half of a preseason game at Northwest Stadium on August 14, 2026 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Packers built a passing game without a WR1 — and the Dolphins might do the same. The Dolphins are heading into 2026 with one of the youngest receiver rooms in the league, with three rookies and a second‑year player expected to play real snaps – all catching passes from an unproven, first‑time starting quarterback. That might sound terrifying in the short term, but we actually have a modern template for how this can work: The Packers from 2022–2023, who rebuilt their pass‑catcher group while transitioning to Jordan Love. The parallels are striking: A young quarterback stepping into a bigger role, a receiver room built almost entirely from scratch and a front office willing to bet on development. Jon‑Eric Sullivan helped architect Green Bay’s youth movement, drafting Christian Watson, Romeo Doubs, Jayden Reed, and Dontayvion Wicks in a two-year span, and now he’s trying to build the same long‑term payoff in Green Bay South. So How Did It Pan Out in Green Bay? Even early in the youth movement, Green Bay’s passing game was solid – which is perhaps to be expected when you have a first‑ballot Hall of Famer behind center. In 2022, Aaron Rodgers’ final season with the Packers, the team finished with 3,890 passing yards and 26 passing touchdowns. Fifteen different players caught passes, and eight of them topped 200 receiving yards. Among the rookies, Christian Watson finished second on the team with 611 yards and 7 touchdowns, while Romeo Doubs added 425 yards and 3 scores. In 2023, with Jordan Love taking over, the passing numbers improved. Love threw for 4,159 yards and 32 touchdowns, and once again the ball was spread widely: sixteen players caught passes, and nine of them reached 200+ receiving yards. Reed, Doubs, Wicks, and Watson combined for roughly 2,500 yards and 25 touchdowns, but none eclipsed 800 yards – a sign that the Packers built the room around depth. (Incidentally, the trend continued beyond these transitional years. Reed and Doubs led the team in 2024 and 2025 with 857 yards and 724 yards, respectively, and six touchdowns apiece.) What Might This Mean for Miami? This isn’t apples to apples – Miami’s offense will look different. For one, the attack will likely run through De’Von Achane, who Jeff Hafley joked would get the ball 40–45 times per game . And Malik Willis brings a running element that Jordan Love didn’t, which will change how defenses play Miami. But when Willis does throw, the distribution may look a lot like Green Bay’s. The Dolphins have six receivers on their 53‑man roster, plus Achane, pass‑catching tight end Greg Dulcich, and several other skill players who can handle targets. The Packers’ young receivers made an impact right away – Reed led the team in yards as a rookie – but at no point did they produce a traditional WR1 with 1,000 yards and double‑digit touchdowns. Miami’s passing game may follow the same pattern, with broad distribution, steady growth and no single player dominating the stat sheet. Keep Expectations in Check As much as we all might love a breakout 1,200‑yard receiver in Miami this season to replace the Cheetah and the Penguin, that might be setting us up for disappointment. But if you can live with a deep and versatile group that gets better as the year goes on – the Packers showed that’s absolutely possible. And with Jon‑Eric Sullivan now running Miami’s roster, it’s no coincidence the Dolphins are trying to build something similar.

title: 10 bold predictions for Dolphins 2026 season
summary: Every other city we go; every other video; no matter where I go, I see the same… NFL power rankings for the Miami Dolphins.  Pick a site… any site… and I guarantee you that you’ll see the Miami Dolphins ranked 32nd.  That negative 3-star restaurant that gave you expired sushi and cold pizza rolls?  They […]
full_text: Every other city we go; every other video; no matter where I go, I see the same… NFL power rankings for the Miami Dolphins. Pick a site… any site… and I guarantee you that you’ll see the Miami Dolphins ranked 32nd. That negative 3-star restaurant that gave you expired sushi and cold pizza rolls? They have a higher ranking than the Dolphins and they aren’t even an NFL team. Expectations are THAT low for the Dolphins. Everyone expects this team to be the Keystone Cops of the league, being a day off for any opponent to play them. Even the most optimistic media source out there predicts a high total of 5 wins. Five. One, two, three, four, FIIIIIFFFFTH! Well don’t let the eternal optimist within you listen to the negativity. The 2026 Miami Dolphins are here to spit in the wind face of all the doubters. Even if they don’t, they will be a tougher out than people are expecting and maybe even fun to watch. Ol’ Earl’s here with some bold predictions that will show you how. 1. MALIK WILLIS PROVES TO BE A FRANCHISE QUARTERBACK I was firmly on board the “Sign Malik Willis” train in March and was incredibly excited when I saw the news he was going to be a Dolphin. Losing receiver Jaylen Waddle put a dent into the expectations for the signal caller, but the rookie class has stepped up and may give some electricity to the pass catching units. But they are rookies and rookies have growing pains and lessons to learn and all the other 90s sitcoms tropes . But that won’t stop me from making this prediction. I highlighted what I think will be baseline expectations for Willis on Substack . Now, I’m predicting he will exceed them. I believe he will pass all the “eye test” criteria. I also think he will exceed the statistical baseline. I’m going to go with a 66% CP, 7.7 YPA, 5.7% TD%, and 1.8% INT%. Using my same dropbacks and attempts totals (595 dropbacks; 476 attempts), that gives him a stat line of 314-476, 3665 yards, 27 TDs, and 9 INTs. That would yield a passer rating of 100.17. Looking at 2025 stats, that would put 12th in yards (a grand total of 3 yards behind what Josh Allen threw for), 16th in completion percentage (just under, but in line with Burrow, Herbert, and Love), tied for 6th in TDs thrown, 7th in TD%, and 10th in passer rating. Those aren’t All-Pro numbers, MVP numbers, or numbers that necessarily stand out. But given the overall situation, these numbers mean that Miami has found their QB for now and the future. 2. TIGHT END GREG DULCICH ECLIPSES 1000 RECEIVING YARDS Dulcich was an afterthought to most fans during the 2025 offseason. The Dolphins added him to the practice squad in late August, then elevated him in late October. He played in 10 games, with 3 starts. He didn’t play until week 8. He didn’t receive a target until week 9. He managed to get 33 targets, 26 catches, 335 yards, and 1 TD. His 33 targets in those 9 games works out to 3.7 or so per game. In 2026, he does not have any target hogs in front of him. There is no more Tyreek Hill, Jaylen Waddle, or Darren Waller. The rookie class looks promising, but they need to prove it. While that loss of proven talent hurts overall, this gives Dulcich a big opportunity step into a prominent role. He has already developed some chemistry with Malik Willis and he was making plays in OTAs. He was quiet in preseason, but the starters didn’t get much playing time. Can he really get to 1000 yards though? Last season, his yards per reception average was 12.9. He had couple of games below 10, but he was mostly above 11. For the sake of argument, let’s say he averages 12 even. To get to 1000 yards, he would need 84 receptions. Based on his catch percentage, he’d need about 108 targets. On a per game basis, that’s 6.4 targets. Are you telling me that the Dolphins and all the questions regarding their pass catchers, can’t find 3 more targets per game to Dulcich? Yes, I know the Dolphins want to be more run oriented. But last season saw the Dolphins throw the least of any season under McDaniel. There were still targets to go around. It can be done. 3. THE OFFENSIVE LINE RANKS TOP 10 FOR THE SEASON Ah yes… the dreaded profootballfocus talk. They posted their 2026 OL rankings and surprisingly, the Dolphins were not ranked in the low 40s. They weren’t even last! They were in the bottom quartile, however. But do not fear folks… for I predict that the Miami Dolphins offensive line will have fans turning those thumbs the right way up and that the OL will be a top-10 unit in the league. In what you ask? Pressures allowed. Pressures allowed per game. Per dropback. Pass Block Win Rate. Run Block Win Rate. Best dressed. Iron Chef rankings. I care not for what metric is to be used. Miami’s offensive line will be top 10 in ALL of them. Outside of QB, I can’t think of a position or position group more polarizing to Dolphins fans. It doesn’t matter who they sign, how much they spend, who they draft, or how many players they draft. The offensive line remains a sore spot. In 2026, the OL will shut the fans up. Well… most of them. Patrick Paul continues to develop into one of the best LTs in the league and was named captain. Kadyn Proctor locks down the LG spot and strikes fear into the hearts of interior DL. Aaron Brewer continues his All-Pro run. Jonah Savaiinaea proves that his rookie season was an aberration and locks down the RG spot. Either Austin Jackson plays all season and plays well, or Caedan Wallace steps in and fills in seamlessly. In either case, the OL goes from constant weakness to a source of strength in 2026. And that’s the bottom line … 4. ALL THREE ROOKIE RECEIVERS HAVE A MINIMUM OF 500 YARDS EACH The Dolphins knew they needed help in the receiver room and the cheap vets they signed weren’t going to be the answer. They added 3 rookies in the draft. But at the time, there were serious questions. The “consensus” board had Caleb Douglas – the 75th overall pick – as a late day three player and was considered a reach. Chris Bell was coming off an injury that would force him to redshirt his rookie season. Kevin Coleman Jr. was a slot specialist only and would be stuck behind Malik Washington. All that “help” was just half-truths and gorilla dust. Fast forward to now… the “reach” earned his spot in the starting lineup. Bell hasn’t just returned from injury; he has played real football in a Dolphins uniform. It was real. I seent it. Oh… and guess who is the other outside starter at receiver ? Coleman? Making plays in preseason. One could very easily argue that the rookies would have shown out more in preseason if the QB play hadn’t been buns. Well… except for Douglas. He only played the limited reps with the starters and was stashed for the regular season. Of course, preseason doesn’t mean anything. We’ve all seen players show out, then disappear. But I don’t think this rookie group will. They will be used and used heavily. Receiver is a position that generally transitions quickly from college to the pros. Yeah, learning curve and growing pains and all that. But this trio is going to be a force. To the point they each get at least 500 yards. Is that too bold? Following the previous predictions, I have Willis at 3665 yards. Dulcich is getting at least 1000 of those. If the rookie trio ( assignment for the class: create a nickname for the trio ) gets at least 1500 total, that leaves just over 1100 for everyone else. That’s Washington, Achane, and whomever else. So no, I don’t think it’s too bold. I would argue I’m underselling it. 5. CHOP ROBINSON GETS DOUBLE DIGIT SACKS AND MAKES A PRO BOWL The Dolphins traded Jaelen Phillips last season and released Bradley Chubb this offseason. That left the edge room bereft of talent. They didn’t have the financial resources to go out and sign players. They didn’t really address it in the draft, with the first edge player being a 4th round pick and he is more of a hybrid player. That put the onus to lead the pass rush group firmly on the shoulders of the former 1st round pick.…

title: Vikings-Packers Wednesday Injury Report
summary: The Minnesota Vikings and Green Bay Packers released their first official injury reports of the season in advance of their Sunday afternoon matchup at US Bank stadium. Here they are. Minnesota Vikings Green Bay Packers Injury Report Terms and Glossary Injury designation definitions: Probable = the league defines a Probable injury designation as a 75% […]
full_text: The Minnesota Vikings and Green Bay Packers released their first official injury reports of the season in advance of their Sunday afternoon matchup at US Bank stadium. Here they are. Minnesota Vikings Player Name Position Injury Wednesday Thursday Friday Injury Designation Jakobe Thomas S Illness DNP Jacob Thomas S Ankle LP Caleb Tiernan T Ankle LP Green Bay Packers Player Name Position Injury Wednesday Thursday Friday Injury Designation Micah Parsons* Edge Knee DNP PUP – OUT Josh Jacobs* RB NIR DNP CE List- OUT Luke Musgrave TE Neck DNP PUP – OUT Jordan Riley DT Achilles DNP PUP – OUT Aaron Banks* LG Knee LP Zach Bako-Bewele* RT Knee LP Warren Brinson DT Calf DNP Ty’Ron Hopper LB Achilles DNP Javon Hargrave* DT Knee LP Jordan Morgan* LT Knee LP Devonte Wyatt* DT Ankle LP Barryn Sorrell EDGE Foot LP Injury Report Terms and Glossary FP = Full participant in practice. LP = Limited participant in practice. DNP = Did not participate in practice. NIR = Not injury related. PUP = Physically unable to participate list. IR = Injured reserve. Note: only starters on IR are listed. CE List = Commissioner’s exempt list. Player Name* = Starter. Injury designation definitions: Probable = the league defines a Probable injury designation as a 75% or greater chance of playing. Historically, 95% of players designated probable are active and played on game day. Questionable = the league defines a Questionable injury designation as being ‘uncertain’ of whether the player will play or not. This replaces the former definition of having a 50% chance of playing. Historically, 70-75% of players with a Questionable injury designation were active and played on game day. Doubtful = The league defines a Doubtful injury designation to mean the player is unlikely to participate in the game. In practical terms, teams use the designation when a player has less than a 50% chance to suit up, and active game appearances from this designation remain rare. Historically only around 6% of players with a Doubtful designation are active and played on game day. Out = will not play. Players with this designation are not active on game day and league rules prohibit them from playing. Notes on Injured Players For the Packers, Micah Parsons, Luke Musgrave, and Jordan Riley are all on the PUP list and will miss the first four games of the season. Josh Jacobs is on the Commissioner’s Exempt list following an offseason incident until further notice. The Packers also have three starting offensive linemen and two starting defensive linemen on their injury report, which isn’t ideal to start the season. Zach Bako-Bewele (formerly Tom) is recovering from offseason knee surgery to repair a partially torn patellar tendon. He said he plans to start on Sunday. Aaron Banks has been dealing with chronic tendinitis in his knee and has missed practice time because of it during training camp. It’s unclear if he’ll be able to go on Sunday or not, but Jager Burton, a rookie fifth-round pick, would be the likely starter at left guard if he can’t go. Starting left tackle Jordan Morgan was a surprise addition as a limited participant due to a knee injury. Unclear if this is a minor issue- which seems more likely- or if it more significant. Starting defensive tackles Javon Hargrave and Devonte Wyatt are both dealing with lingering injuries that aren’t likely to keep them out of Sunday’s game, but they could be limiting during the game. Defensive tackle Warren Brinson, who rotates as a backup, seems less likely to be active on Sunday. For the Vikings, no starters on their injury report and the issues with the two Thomas’ are unlikely to keep them out of Sunday’s game. Caleb Tiernan may or may not be active for the game based on his status on the depth chart as much as the ankle injury he has been dealing with for a couple weeks now. That’s all for today. I’ll have an update again tomorrow and Friday with final injury designations. Follow me on X/Bluesky @wludford

Minnesota Vikings News and Links Week 1 NFL picks, predictions for Kalshi, Polymarket, Underdog: Seahawks-Patriots, Packers-Vikings market s https://www.cbssports.com/prediction/news/week-1-nfl-picks-predictions-kalshi-polymarket-underdog-seahawks-patriots-packers-vikings-markets/ Vikings vs. Packers preview Two bitter rivals will collide when the Minnesota Vikings host the Green Bay Packers for an NFC North clash at 4:25 p.m. ET. Minnesota has had the upper hand over its rivals in recent years, winning three of the past four meetings with Green Bay. The Vikings are coming off a disappointing 9-8 campaign, which included a 4-4 record. Minnesota’s offense averaged just 275 yards per game last season, which is why the Vikings signed former No. 1 overall pick Kyler Murray this offseason. The Packers finished the 2025 campaign with a 9-7-1 record, losing to the Bears in the NFL Wild Card round. Head coach Matt LaFleur will look to lean on running back Josh Jacobs, who racked up 13 rushing touchdowns in 2025. Jacobs has now scored 12 or more rushing touchdowns in three of his past four seasons, but SportsLine’s model is projecting Minnesota’s defense to hold Jacobs to just 3.4 yards per carry on Sunday. The SportsLine Projection Model is calling for the Vikings to walk away with a 22-20 victory at home over Green Bay. Minnesota to win is trading at $0.54 per share, while the Packers are trading at $0.47 per share to beat the Vikings. Vikings Have Advantages Over Packers in 3 Key Areas Ahead of Week 1 https://www.si.com/nfl/vikings/onsi/vikings-have-advantages-over-packers-in-3-key-areas-ahead-of-week-1-01m1t666gw17 Wide receivers and running backs The Packers have a lot of good players at their skill positions, but they don’t have a wide receiver like Justin Jefferson. As it currently stands, it looks like Jefferson will be matched up against rookie Brandon Cisse, who is an insanely difficult player to face in your first NFL game. Then you have Keisean Nixon, who will likely go against Jordan Addison after a season allowing a passer rating of 105.2 when targeted. Pass rush Packers star edge rusher Micah Parsons is starting this season on injured reserve and will not be available in Week 1. That means it will be up to Lukas Van Ness and Barryn Sorrell to generate pressure on the edges. Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores is known for being aggressive when getting after quarterbacks. Edge rushers Andrew Van Ginkel and Dallas Turner should be able to feast on a Green Bay offensive line that has its own issues. Offensive line Zach Bako-Bewele is expected to start at right tackle for the Green Bay offense, but he is still struggling during his recovery from a partial patellar tendon tear he sustained in Week 15 of the 2026 NFL season. Bako-Bewele didn’t play at all during the preseason. When asked whether he’d be ready for the regular season opener against Minnesota on August 26, he said he would, but his answer didn’t sound confident. Meanwhile, Packers starting left guard Aaron Banks is dealing with a lingering knee issue caused by tendonitis. There is no telling whether the injury will hold him out of the game against Minnesota or if he will be able to play on a play-by-play basis in the season opener. Having two question marks on the offensive line is not a good thing for Green Bay. The biggest issue for the Vikings on the offensive line is that Blake Brandel is entering his first year as Minnesota’s starting center and has struggled to deliver the ball to the quarterback accurately out of shotgun formation. He has worked on that part of his game during training camp and at practices, so hopefully that will be ironed out by the time he is on the field in Week 1. Former Vikings Player Has Clear Week 1 Advice for Kyler Murray https://heavy.com/sports/nfl/minnesota-vikings/former-player-clear-advice-kyler-murray/ “Taking care of the football,” Sirles said on the Sept. 8 edition of the “Purple Insider” about what Murray needs to do against the Packers. “That’s the number one thing I’m looking for with Kyler Murray. Can we make sure we make good decisions with the football, get the ball out on time, and don’t hold on to it and take a bad sack because everyone’s covered? “Those are such elementary quarterback plays that you think are pretty average. But you’re talking about a guy who hasn’t played football in a while. [He] got benched the last half of that year. The game, preseason, everything, the game speeds up exponentially. Crazy amounts between preseason and Week 1. Watching him get through his reads, put the ball not in harm’s way, and then take care of it and operationally move the offense up and down.” “I don’t need the crazy Sam Darnold 80 yards on a rope that we saw,” Sirles added. “I don’t need the hundred-yard scramble to make it look really cool; I just want to see you operationally in and out of the huddle, command the line of scrimmage, play on time and in rhythm in the passing game, and mostly just take care of the football for Week 1. “Show you can do all that stuff and, hey, we don’t have to worry about that going into Week 2, and then we can put more on your plate. I just don’t want to go in there with this huge expectation that he’s going to blow the doors off Week 1 and then be like, ‘Oh, he didn’t do it.’ Like, I think we need to let him walk a little before we run with the Kyler Murray experience at quarterback.” Meanwhile, Sirles isn’t the only one who wants to see the basics from Murray. Recently, NFL analyst Mark Schlereth wants to believe that will happen, but he has one key concern. “I have one concern: Will you be able to get Kyler Murray to play on schedule and to fall in love with the boring?” Schlereth said on the Sept. 7 edition of “The OG Football Show.” “Because Kyler Murray has told me in a one-on-one production meeting, calling a game, ‘Yeah, I just want to run more. I want to make more plays. I want to get outside the pocket more.’ “To be really good in this league, 70 percent of the time, and I just throw this number out there, you’ve got to be on schedule. You’ve got to do the boring. You’ve got to take what’s given, and then when things do break down, which they will, that’s when you go make plays. “But when you play kind of 50-50, off schedule, on schedule, more mistakes happen eventually, inevitably, than big plays, and that’s Kyler Murray’s biggest problem in my mind.” Vikings Bold Predictions: Kevin O’Connell’s offense in 2026 could be the best Minnesota’s had since 2009 https://atozsports.com/nfl/minnesota-vikings-news/vikings-bold-predictions-kevin-oconnell-offense-kyler-murray-jordan-addison-pro-bowl/ Murray has never worked with anybody as talented as wide receiver Justin Jefferson on the…

title: Patriots express confidence in Drake Maye after Seahawks loss
summary: The New England Patriots see Drake Maye as the face of their franchise. On Wednesday night, he was relegated to being the face of their defeat. Going up against the same Seattle Seahawks team that beat him and his team in Super Bowl LX seven months earlier, the third-year quarterback played one of the worst […]
full_text: The New England Patriots see Drake Maye as the face of their franchise. On Wednesday night, he was relegated to being the face of their defeat. Going up against the same Seattle Seahawks team that beat him and his team in Super Bowl LX seven months earlier, the third-year quarterback played one of the worst games of his career. Maye threw interceptions on each of the Patriots’ final three possessions, playing a critical part in a 10-0 lead turning into a 13-10 defeat . Maye himself was critical of his performance, calling the three picks “unacceptable” during his postgame press conference. The rest of his team, meanwhile, was not that harsh on the 24-year-old. “We have nothing but the utmost confidence in him and everybody on this football team,” said head coach Mike Vrabel. “He’s going to make a lot of plays for us.” Maye did just that on Sunday, even after his interception woes began. Following his first two picks, which allowed Seattle to take a lead for the first time all day, he marched the Patriots into the red zone on what very well could have been the game-winning drive. Along the way, he showed his trademark playmaking ability as both a passer and a runner. However, that series, like the two previous ones, ended with a costly mistake by the former third overall draft pick. And yet, his teammates made sure not to pin the defeat on Maye. “It’s not on one person at all,” said running back Rhamondre Stevenson. “This is a team game. We win together and we lose together. I wouldn’t pinpoint on one single person in that room. We all have to get better. Back to the drawing board and figure it out.” “I have the utmost confidence in him,” added wide receiver Romeo Doubs, the target on the first of Maye’s three INTs. “I know what he can do. I’ve watched him and what he’s done in this league a long time, and, like I said, this doesn’t define him. It’s just this league, it’s always a pendulum in this league.” The message of support did not only come out of the offense. The Patriots defense echoed those remarks as well. “We have all the confidence in the world in Drake,” said cornerback Carlton Davis. “He’s our guy. We are going to stick together right now, and we’ll move forward.”
author: Bernd Buchmasser

title: 10 things we learned from Patriots vs. Seahawks
summary: The New England Patriots lost their season opener in Seattle on Wednesday night, and the defeat was somehow worse than anyone could have predicted. The Patriots jumped to a 10-0 lead in the third quarter, but gave up 13 straight points down the stretch — in large part due to three straight interceptions from quarterback Drake […]
full_text: The New England Patriots lost their season opener in Seattle on Wednesday night, and the defeat was somehow worse than anyone could have predicted. The Patriots jumped to a 10-0 lead in the third quarter, but gave up 13 straight points down the stretch — in large part due to three straight interceptions from quarterback Drake Maye — to lose 13-10. Here is what the defeat taught us. It’s simple: Drake Maye just collapsed When talking about this game, we have to start with Drake Maye. The Patriots’ quarterback was playing smart for three quarters, taking what the defense gave him and not putting the ball in harm’s way. In the fourth quarter, he completely collapsed. Yes, he was let down by his receivers at times, but all three of his picks, which were exclusively thrown in the fourth period, were clearly on him. This is, by his own admission, unacceptable and cannot continue to happen for a third-year player considered to be one of the best quarterbacks in the NFL. The concerning part is that this is not the first time this has happened in his career either. Losing to Drew Lock is embarrassing I know that Sam Darnold is not an elite quarterback. I know that the Seahawks don’t run around him. It still hurts to see Drew Lock be the quarterback to not just beat you, but also outplay your own MVP runner-up quarterback along the way. Regardless of what else happens in the game, that simply cannot happen. And yet, it did. It’s a big reason why the Patriots left Seattle as losers. The Seahawks coached circles around the Patriots Mike Macdonald is one of the best defensive coaches in football, and he showed that again on Wednesday night. The Patriots were never comfortable pushing the ball down the field, Maye looked rattled, and, once the Seahawks adjusted to the swing pass to beat the blitz, the Patriots had almost no consistent offense to speak of. To make things worse, the Seahawks offensive was led by a rookie coordinator who found a way to move the ball consistently in the second half with a backup QB . The Patriots’ lack of adjustments was obvious, and the home team flat out smashed them in the coaching matchup. Mike Vrabel, Josh McDaniels and Zak Kuhr are all very good coaches, but they were far from good enough on Wednesday night. The Patriots have had the coaching advantage in a lot of games since Vrabel took over as their head coach, but in the last two games they have played, they have simply been outcoached. The Patriots were dominated on the line of scrimmage The Patriots spent a lot of money and resources in the offseason trying to make their running game more effective, and, for Wednesday night at least, they did not seem to be successful. They were unable to get almost any consistent push on the offensive line, or open up real holes for their backs until the last drive of the game. If their identity is going to be a physical, smash-mouth football team, this is going to have to vastly improve moving forward. Averaging 2.6 yards per carry between Rhamondre Stevenson and Corey Kiner is just nowhere near good enough. On the defensive side of the ball, Seattle was able to run the ball effectively, though they didn’t do it a ton. The Patriots did end up with a pair of sacks, but the pressure was far from consistent, and too often Drew Lock had a clean pocket to make an easy throw. There is no sugar-coating it either. The Patriots need to be much better on both sides of the line to give themselves a chance to win more games, because what they got on Wednesday was simply not good enough. That said, I do think that the pass blocking overall was much improved outside of a miscommunication or two, so at least that was a positive to take away from what was mostly a rough game from the trenches. The A.J. Brown injury is a serious concern A.J. Brown went down with an ankle injury and left the stadium in a walking boot, and I don’t think it’s a coincidence that the Patriots offense went off the rails after that happened. The concern is this potentially being an injury that sidelines Brown for an extended period of time. If that’s the case, they are going to need a whole heck of a lot more out of every receiver not named Mack Hollins. The Patriots gave up a 2028 first-round pick to get Brown, and they were hoping to make him the focal point of the offense. Losing him would be a massive blow. I would also like to mention that I advocated for the Patriots to include conditions to the pick they sent to the Eagles that revolved around playing time and performance. Hindsight is 20/20, but they might end up kicking themselves for not doing that if this injury ends up being of the serious variety. Romeo Doubs has a rough debut The Patriots shipped Kayshon Boutte out of town because, besides trading for A.J. Brown, they also went out and signed Romeo Doubs away from the Packers in free agency. In his first game with his new team, he was targeted three times, with one target being an interception, one being a bad drop that led to an interception on the next play, and the third falling incomplete on a third down. Doubs looked slow, showed off bad hands, and couldn’t get open all night. Other than that, how was the play Mrs. Lincoln? In case Brown is going to miss time due to his ankle injury, the Patriots are going to need Doubs to step up in a big way. Mack Hollins looked roughly better than Doubs on Wednesday, and that simply cannot happen given the investment made in the latter. Gabe Jacas plays well Gabe Jacas basically looked like he didn’t belong on an NFL field for most of training camp and preseason. In his first regular season game, however, he finished with a sack and two tackles for loss. He did have a bad penalty on special teams, but he showed some promise along the edge, and that is exactly what the Patriots are going to need from him moving forward. Of all the negatives in this game, Jacas wasn’t one of them, and that’s a good thing. Will Campbell plays well Speaking of positives, Campbell was much-maligned in the playoffs and Super Bowl, and people like me told you that it was because he was injured and that he would be better. I’m happy to report that, at least for one game, the glass-half-full outlook appears to be the correct one. Campbell received a questionable holding call and had a correct block in the back call, so it wasn’t perfect. Unlike the Super Bowl, however, he held his own against a very good Seahawks defense. It was a definitive step in the right direction. Maybe the Patriots should have played their starters in preseason Of all the criticisms, the most obvious one is that New England simply should have played its guys in the preseason. And there is an argument for that, just ask ex-Patriot Jason McCourty: You can tell starters didn’t play in the preseason!!! — Jason McCourty (@JasonMcCourty) September 10, 2026 The Patriots looked rusty and uncomfortable at times out there. The offensive operation was clunky, and Drake Maye certainly needs more time to develop chemistry with his new receivers. Now, did they lose this game because they didn’t play their starters in the preseason? Absolutely not, but I am always an advocate for giving players at least a series or two to get them back to full-speed and full-contact football. Joint practices are fine, but they are not tackling, and they can’t hit the quarterback. It’s a different feeling when you have 11 guys bearing down on you trying to knock you out, and it seems that Maye could have used those reps. Mini-bye awaits The Patriots are going to have 10 days to let this one settle, as they don’t play again until September 20 when they host the Steelers for their home opener. As poorly as the Patriots played, it’s important to remember that it was against a fantastic football team. The Steelers, on the other hand, are a good bounce-back opportunity. If Drake Maye plays like he did in the fourth quarter, then the Patriots could lose to any team in the NFL. However, they have plenty of time…

title: 6 winners and losers from Patriots’ loss to the Seahawks
summary: The New England Patriots dropped their season opener Wednesday night with a 13-10 loss to the Seattle Seahawks. Here is who caught our eye for better or worse upon live-viewing the Patriots’ Week 1 contest. Winners ED Dre’Mont Jones: New England entered the regular season with question marks along the edge, but free agent addition […]
full_text: Sep 9, 2026; Seattle, Washington, USA; New England Patriots defensive end Dre'Mont Jones (5) reacts after sacking Seattle Seahawks quarterback Sam Darnold (14) during the first quarter at Lumen Field. Mandatory Credit: Joe Nicholson-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New England Patriots dropped their season opener Wednesday night with a 13-10 loss to the Seattle Seahawks . Here is who caught our eye for better or worse upon live-viewing the Patriots’ Week 1 contest. Winners ED Dre’Mont Jones: New England entered the regular season with question marks along the edge, but free agent addition Dre’Mont Jones started his Patriots tenure strongly. Jones ended the Seahawks opening drive of the game with a third-down sack and went on to log a team-high six other pressures the rest of the night. The sturdy edge defender also flashed against the run. CB Christian Gonzalez: After inking his record-breaking contract extension roughly 48 hours ago, Gonzalez looked in mid-season form Wednesday night. The Patriots top corner allowed just two catches on five targets, including just one reception for five yards and a pass breakup while in coverage on Jaxon Smith-Njigba (16 routes). WR Mack Hollins: Even before A.J. Brown’s injury, Hollins played the second-most amount of snaps in the wide receiver room as he continued to hold a large offensive role. Hollins’ made several key plays over the middle of the field and finished with a team-high 51 receiving yards on four catches, his biggest being a 4th-and-9 conversion late in the fourth quarter. Losers QB Drake Maye: Unacceptable. That was the word Drake Maye used to describe his performance post game , which sums things up. Maye used his legs and the underneath passing attack to move the football early in the game while they built a 10-0 lead. Averaging just 2.4 air yards per pass, Maye was 17-of-22 for 127 yards and a touchdown playing an efficient style of offense. Then, the quarterback admitted he lost patience in the fourth quarter. Maye threw three bad fourth quarter interceptions as he hunted big plays — seeing his average air yards per attempt jump to 8.0 in the final frame. Seattle played nearly 90 percent of their defense in zone to limit explosives, and Maye’s aggressiveness and poor decisions late cost the Patriots on Wednesday. WR Romeo Doubs: New England’s free agent pass catcher failed to haul in any of his three targets in his Patriots debut Wednesday night. Doubs had a bad drop downfield before Maye’s next pass was intercepted, and was earlier the target on Maye’s first interception of the night. “I just wasn’t locked in enough. That’s all,” Doubs said post game. “Like I said, I’ll be better.” LG Alijah Vera-Tucker: The Patriots did a better job of blocking things in front of Drake Maye than they did in the Super Bowl, as the quarterback was under pressure on 12 of his 42 drop backs (28.6%). It wasn’t perfect, however, as Maye was sacked three times and still faced some free rushers. Free agent addition Alijah Vera-Tucker allowed a team-high four pressures and was on scene for one of the sacks allowed as he failed to pick up a stunt off the left side. The 27-year old hopefully just had some rust to shake off on a new offensive line after missing all of last season. Honorable mentions Rhamondre Stevenson handled a heavy workload (85% of snaps) in the backfield and totaled 95 scrimmage yards on 23 touches. The Patriots run game as a whole struggled with a 22% success rate as Stevenson averaged 2.8 YPC and saw 50 of his 51 rushing yards come after contact. Eli Raridon caught his first career touchdown on his first career catch on a play-action delayed release. Will Campbell had a clean sheet in pass protection. He was on the left side on the aforementioned stunt and was called for holding in the run game. Elsewhere on the edge, rookie Gabe Jacas had some strong moments after a shaky preseason. Jacas logged his first career sack on a hustle play and flashed his athleticism to record a TFL. As a whole, the Patriots run defense remained inconsistent vs. Seattle. With some Super Bowl flashbacks, rookie Jadarian Price found running room outside the tackles. Christian Barmore had three pressures on 18 pass rush snaps. In addition to Gonzalez, cornerback Carlton Davis didn’t allow a catch on two receptions while also recording two run stuffs. Andy Borregales knocked through a 50-yard field goal and his lone extra point. Punter Mitch Wishnowsky had an impressive Patriots debut with three i20s while helping limit electric returner Rashid Shaheed to just one return for nine yards. New England’s coverage teams deserve credit as well, such as rookie Namdi Obiazor who recorded three special teams tackles.
author: Brian Hines

title: ‘Unacceptable’ Drake Maye’s interceptions prove costly in Patriots’ season-opening loss
summary: As the New England Patriots fell 13-10 in their season opener against the Seattle Seahawks Wednesday night at Lumen Field, quarterback Drake Maye watched a 10-point halftime lead slip away in the second half. Three interceptions following halftime contributed to the collapse. Maye’s decision-making placed his team in difficult situations to maintain that advantage and […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - SEPTEMBER 09: Drake Maye #10 of the New England Patriots flicks the ball against the Seattle Seahawks during the fourth quarter in the game at Lumen Field on September 09, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images As the New England Patriots fell 13-10 in their season opener against the Seattle Seahawks Wednesday night at Lumen Field, quarterback Drake Maye watched a 10-point halftime lead slip away in the second half. Three interceptions following halftime contributed to the collapse. Maye’s decision-making placed his team in difficult situations to maintain that advantage and close out the contest with an early-season victory. “We had the game under control. I thought we had a good plan to try to start chipping away and be patient; I lost patience, and it cost us,” Maye said after the defeat. “[They were] decisions that cost us the game on my part. I’ve asked myself to be better and realize it’s a long season, but at the same time (you) can’t have those [plays]. “It was unacceptable … That wasn’t how I play football or how I want to represent my game and playing quarterback for the Patriots.” With 26 seconds remaining in the fourth quarter from Seattle’s 16-yard line, Maye lobbed a soft pass to wide receiver Mack Hollins toward the sideline in the end zone; however, the attempt fell short and landed in the hands of Seahawks cornerback Josh Jobe, who secured the game-sealing turnover. Trailing by just three points at the time, Patriots kicker Andy Borregales warmed up on the sideline to attempt a manageable field goal to send the game to overtime at 13 apiece. Maye’s ensuing decision prevented that opportunity. “I was trying to get rid of [the ball], realized Mack [Hollins] was back there, and I didn’t put enough on it to get it out,” Maye said. “It was unacceptable. We had a chance to send [the game] to overtime at the worst.” During New England’s prior drive, Maye’s second interception set Seattle up in Patriots territory. Its following drive concluded with the matchup’s go-ahead field goal. The third-year quarterback, targeting DeMario Douglas over the middle of the field, attempted a late throw that allowed opposing safety Julian Love to jump Douglas’ route just past midfield. Maye’s first interception came after a lofty throw deep to Romeo Doubs in heavy coverage. Early in the second quarter, Maye also had an opportunity to connect with A.J. Brown for a 34-yard touchdown connection. Yet Maye, despite the resulting defensive pass interference call, drastically underthrew his new receiver. “The one to A.J. [Brown], I didn’t want to try to overthrow it on the flea-flicker,” Maye added about the play. “Ball placement is key in this league. I’m trying to make sure that I put [the ball] in the right spot, and I didn’t.” Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel, when asked about Maye’s final turnover, explained that the signal-caller can’t throw three interceptions, which he says Maye “knows.” He also noted that New England “wants to be aggressive, but not reckless.” Still, Vrabel trusts his quarterback, who was the NFL’s MVP runner-up just one season ago, saying the team has “nothing but the utmost confidence” in Maye. “We have to stick together, and that starts with me getting back to work and having the right intention in practice,” Maye said. “These guys are here for me. They’ve done a great job supporting me and have had my back. I know I have their trust, but I need to keep on putting better football out there. “It’s Week 1, but at the same time, we have to get this going early. We have to start off on the right foot, and I know what we had last year, but we have a new season and a new team. We need to build that.”
author: Andrew Guindon

title: Instant analysis from Patriots’ 13-10 loss to Seahawks
summary: Seven months removed from Super Bowl LX, the end result remained the same. The New England Patriots fell to the Seattle Seahawks in Wednesday night’s season opener at Lumen Field, where a 10-0 lead became a 13-10 loss. Here’s a glance back on the 8:20 p.m. ET kickoff as head coach Mike Vrabel’s side returns […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - SEPTEMBER 09: Drake Maye #10 of the New England Patriots runs with the ball against the Seattle Seahawks during the first quarter in the game at Lumen Field on September 09, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Jane Gershovich/Getty Images) | Getty Images Seven months removed from Super Bowl LX, the end result remained the same. The New England Patriots fell to the Seattle Seahawks in Wednesday night’s season opener at Lumen Field, where a 10-0 lead became a 13-10 loss. Here’s a glance back on the 8:20 p.m. ET kickoff as head coach Mike Vrabel’s side returns home at 0-1. After early TD, Maye finds three picks in as many drives The Patriots were prepared to go silent in Seattle . There was still a chance to make some noise while there. Drake Maye completed 23-of-33 passes for 178 yards against Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald’s defense. He added 47 rushing yards across seven scrambles, beginning with a gain of 10 and soon continuing with unnecessary roughness out of bounds. But the 24-year-old reigning All-Pro ultimately delivered one touchdown and three interceptions by the end of Wednesday night. Starting in “21” personnel with Reggie Gilliam at fullback and captain Hunter Henry at tight end, the Patriots’ first drive netted a pair of first downs before ending in a punt. The second series brought the same outcome after being halted in the backfield on third-and-1 handoff. The third series, though, spanned 10 plays, 77 yards and trickery on the way to tight end Eli Raridon’s first career touchdown catch at the goal line. Peeling to the back corner of the end zone, the rookie out of Notre Dame gave New England a 7-0 lead with 9:11 to go before halftime. By intermission, the visiting offense stood with no sacks, no turnovers, no penalties and a conversion rate of 43 percent on third down. Coming out of it, what was once a punt became a penalty on the Seahawks for roughing the kicker. Yet a 10-0 advantage was put to the test by field position before long. It was also put to the test a jump ball intended for wide receiver Romeo Doubs that bobbled into the hands of cornerback Nehemiah Pritchett for a pick in the fourth quarter. A subsequent drop by the March signing set the stage for the second turnover by New England’s quarterback. Safety Julian Love read it in the middle of the field. Trailing 13-10, Maye kept the Patriots’ hopes alive on fourth-and-2 with his legs and on fourth-and-9 with his arm. But while in range for a field goal on third-and-5 with 25 seconds to go, a dangerous decision was paid for in the right corner of end zone. Cornerback Josh Jobe toe-tapped the third interception in as many drives to seal the Seattle comeback. New-look receiver room finishes without No. 1 There’d be no Nick Emmanwori or Ty Okada at safety for the Seahawks. There would be A.J. Brown at wide receiver for the Patriots. That was until an ankle injury saw him downgraded from questionable to out in the second half after visits to the blue medical tent and locker room. The June acquisition caught three passes for 26 yards in his brief 2026 debut, with his initial look coming at the 3:24 mark in the first quarter. The three-time Pro Bowler and All-Pro also drew defensive pass interference on a flea-flicker to set up September’s first touchdown. Elder statesman Mack Hollins started alongside No. 1 and finished with four receptions worth a team-high 51 yards. Slot receiver DeMario Douglas, kickoff returner Kyle Williams and the aforementioned Doubs stepped in behind them. As New England went big with four active tight ends, Efton Chism III became a healthy scratch 90 minutes prior to kickoff. Down Henderson, Stevenson tallies 95 yards from scrimmage An ankle injury sustained late in training camp kept TreVeyon Henderson out of practice for the past two weeks. It also kept the 2025 PFWA All-Rookie running back out for Wednesday night in the Pacific Northwest. New England still had a ground commitment. It was led by Rhamondre Stevenson. The established starter turned 18 carries into 51 yards versus the teeth of Seattle’ defense. He added a handful of catches out of the backfield to the tune of 44 yards, including a play-action swing pass for 17. Corey Kiner, who landed in Foxborough via trade ahead of the NFL’s 53-man roster deadline, made his Patriots debut with 11 rushing yards. And UC Davis alum Lan Larison, a standard elevation from the practice squad, rounded out the depth chart with nine receiving yards after spending his rookie year on injured reserve. Patriots offensive line’s shot at redemption The Seahawks hit home for six sacks against the Patriots in February. By and large, that stayed at bay to begin September. The offensive line broke the huddle with Will Campbell at left tackle, Alijah Vera-Tucker at left guard, Jared Wilson at center, Mike Onwenu at right guard and 35-year-old team captain Morgan Moses at right tackle. The reshaped starting five hadn’t taken a snap during the preseason. Yet as the decibels rained down at Lumen Field, so did a familiar front. Defensive lineman Leonard Williams cleaned up B-gap pressure for Seattle’s first sack with 5:22 to go in the fourth quarter. Outside linebacker Derick Hall got the second in the closing seconds. By the end of Wednesday night, one false start, one illegal block in the back and one holding penalty had been charged to the tackles on New England’s line. August addition Greg Van Roten reported as an eligible for the defending AFC champions. The backup blockers in uniform also included No. 28 overall pick Caleb Lomu and draft classmate Dametrious Crownover after Ben Brown was ruled out with a knee injury earlier in the week. Recent trade acquisition Walter Rouse went to the inactives list. Darnold completes one pass before exit Sam Darnold had been held without a turnover when his side last crossed paths with the Patriots. He had been sacked just once, too. But the season opener ended just as it began for him. The Super Bowl LX champion under center limped to the locker room at the 7:29 mark in the first quarter after the evening got underway with a takedown and a punt. Downgraded from questionable to out due to a hip injury, the Seahawks quarterback finished 1-of-2 passing for 13 yards. Backup Drew Lock stepped in to go 16-of-22 for 185 yards with one touchdown, no interceptions and a late scramble to move the chains. Seattle’s offense left the field by way of four consecutive punts before time expired in the first half. Another punt by Michael Dickson was how the second half got going, too. Yet a two-score game trimmed to a one-score game. And then a deadlock gave way to a 13-10 Seahawks advantage that couldn’t be outlasted. New England’s starting defensive front included Milton Williams and Cory Durden on the interior. Elijah Ponder aligned off one edge and Dre’Mont Jones, who made a previous stop in Seattle, aligned off the other for the first sack of the evening. A sack courtesy of rookie outside linebacker Gabe Jacas followed as Seattle’s pass protection was flagged for multiple false starts. From record-setting extension to Smith-Njigba With a four-year, $135 million contract extension in hand, Christian Gonzalez set his sights on the 2025 NFL Offensive Player of the Year once again. The record-setting Patriots cornerback had been integral in limiting Jaxon Smith-Njigba to 27 receiving yards on 10 targets last time around. The Seahawks wideout, capable of making every route in the tree look the same, would have a hand in a team-high 122 receiving yards and one touchdown on 11 targets this time around against the New England secondary. A short pass on fourth-and-1 unraveled into a 45-yard sprint through traffic. No. 0 had a hand in a pair of deflections, including a near interception, while starting across from Carlton Davis III. The cornerbacks were joined in the three-safety nickel by captain Kevin Byard III, Dell Pettus and Craig Woodson, who missed a tackle on the way…

title: 5 moments that defined the Patriots’ loss to the Seahawks
summary: Seven months after getting beaten by the Seattle Seahawks in the Super Bowl, the New England Patriots had a chance at some payback. While they did find themselves in a more competitive position in their season opener on Wednesday, the end result was equally disappointing: a 13-10 defeat at the hand of the world champions. […]
full_text: SEATTLE, WASHINGTON - SEPTEMBER 09: Jaxon Smith-Njigba #11 of the Seattle Seahawks runs the ball to score a 45 yard touchdown against Kevin Byard #31 of the New England Patriots during the fourth quarter in the game at Lumen Field on September 09, 2026 in Seattle, Washington. (Photo by Steph Chambers/Getty Images) | Getty Images Seven months after getting beaten by the Seattle Seahawks in the Super Bowl, the New England Patriots had a chance at some payback. While they did find themselves in a more competitive position in their season opener on Wednesday, the end result was equally disappointing: a 13-10 defeat at the hand of the world champions. Here is a Patriots-centric view at some of the key moments of the game. Moment No. 1: Game-changing sack GET IT @TheOfficial_80 💪 📺 NBC pic.twitter.com/u5lpIR788U — New England Patriots (@Patriots) September 10, 2026 At first glance, Dre’Mont Jones’ 5-yard sack of Sam Darnold to end Seattle’s first drive was nothing remarkable. The offseason addition showcased some good hustle getting the quarterback down, but the play looked like your standard clean-up takedown. However, in the process of being brought to the ground, Darnold hurt his hip and later left for the medical tent and locker room. He never emerged, leaving the Seahawks offense in the hands of backup Drew Lock. Moment No. 2: Rookie touchdown First NFL catch, first NFL TD @EliRaridon !! 📺 NBC pic.twitter.com/M9ZmApdGAt — New England Patriots (@Patriots) September 10, 2026 The first half was mostly a defensive battle, but the Patriots were able to break the stalemate midway through the second quarter. Moving the chains three times on third down, Drake Maye and company marched 77 yards in 10 plays to score the game’s first touchdown. That TD came courtesy of the team’s third-round draft pick earlier this year, tight end Eli Raridon: the rookie got wide open behind Seattle’s defense to haul in a 2-yard catch for the score. As a consequence, Raridon became the first Patriots rookie to catch a touchdown in his NFL debut in 13 years. The last one was wide receiver Aaron Dobson back in 2013. Moment No. 3: Complementary bad football Tipped and intercepted by Nehemiah Pritchett! NEvsSEA on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/MbMdmJBzfE — NFL (@NFL) September 10, 2026 One of the Patriots’ biggest issues in their Super Bowl loss to the Seahawks in February was losing the turnover battle, and Wednesday saw more of the same. The first negative play in that regard happened in the early fourth quarter, when Drake Maye made a bad decision to target Romeo Doubs in double coverage. The pass was broken up with the ball popping into the air and eventually getting intercepted. THERE GOES JSN NEvsSEA on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/SIt21pDRO8 — NFL (@NFL) September 10, 2026 The Patriots defense followed suit after the Maye pick. While the unit did force Seattle into a 4th-and-1 situation on the very next drive, it did not do a good job defending it. Selling out to stop the run, New England allowed Jaxon Smith-Njigba to get wide open. A missed tackle later and the NFL Offensive Player of the Year found himself in open space on his way to a. 45-yard game-tying touchdown. Moment No. 4: Pick No. 2 JULIAN LOVE WITH ANOTHER SEAHAWKS INT NEvsSEA on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/gj5YJDH3hT — NFL (@NFL) September 10, 2026 The Patriots’ string of bad football continued on the next drive, when Drake Maye threw a second straight interception. That pick in particular was a tough one because it came right after what should have been an easy first down to Romeo Doubs. However, the big-ticket free agency signing dropped an easy catch to set up that eventually doomed 3rd-and-14 play — one that allowed Seattle to take possession in New England territory and score a field goal. Moment No. 5: Game-ender JOSH JOBE TOE TAP INT NEvsSEA on NBC/Peacock Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/MrmQx0a3fo — NFL (@NFL) September 10, 2026 Down 13-10, the Patriots were still in a position to win the game. It did take two fourth-down conversions, but with under 30 seconds to go they found themselves at the Seattle 16-yard line. A game-tying field goal was a gimme from that distance and the winning touchdown still a possibility. Instead, however, Drake Maye threw his third pick in as many possessions to end the game.
author: Bernd Buchmasser

Original story 9/9/2026: A.J. Brown leaving Seahawks game with ankle injury New England Patriots wide receiver A.J. Brown left the team’s season opener after injuring his right ankle. He is officially questionable to return. The injury came on 3rd-and-4 on the Patriots opening drive of the second half, as Maye looked to Brown on a slant route. The low pass was broken up with a Seahawks defender seeming to land on the wide receiver’s ankle in the process. After acquiring medical attention on the field, Brown slowly walked off with trainers. As the Patriots drive continued, Brown stayed on the sideline and went into the blue medical tent. He eventually departed to the locker room. The 29-year old receiver was off the a good start in his Patriots debut, recording three catches (two first downs) for 26 yards in the first-half.
