title: Patriots vs. Seahawks final score, highlights, game recap from NFL Week 1
summary: The New England Patriots did not get their revenge. Facing the Seattle Seahawks in a rematch of Super Bowl LX, the team of head coach Mike Vrabel was defeated 13-10. The Patriots got off to a good start, jumping to a 10-0 lead by the third quarter. From that point on, however, things went downhill. […]
full_text: The New England Patriots did not get their revenge. Facing the Seattle Seahawks in a rematch of Super Bowl LX, the team of head coach Mike Vrabel was defeated 13-10. The Patriots got off to a good start, jumping to a 10-0 lead by the third quarter. From that point on, however, things went downhill. One player in particular was at the center of that meltdown: quarterback Drake Maye, whose three costly interceptions allowed the reigning champions to overcome their deficit and eventually win the game — all despite having lost their own starting QB to an injury in the first quarter. Final score: Patriots 10 : 13 Seahawks Wednesday, Sept. 9, 8:20 p.m. ET | Lumen Field, Seattle, WA | Broadcast information | Inactives | Game day roster First Quarter Starting the game on defense after winning the coin toss, the Patriots surrendered back-to-back first downs to open the game. However, aided by a subsequent false start penalty against the Seahawks, the unit eventually got off the field thanks to a Dre’Mont Jones sack on third down — a play that forced Seattle quarterback Sam Darnold to take a trip to the blue medical tent. The Patriots offense opened deep in its own territory, but a 10-yard Drake Maye scramble gave the unit some breathing room and moved the chains for a first time. It would have remained New England’s only first down of the series if not for a late hit on Maye following another rushing attempt on a 3rd-and-5. The team was unable to capitalize on the Seattle error, however, and was forced to punt after Maye was pressured into throwing incomplete on the next third down. The next drive saw a change at quarterback for the Seahawks. With Darnold heading to the locker room due to a hip injury he sustained on the opening series, backup Drew Lock entered the contest. Seattle’s offense did manage one first down on Lock’s first possession, but stalled when Christian Elliss met running back George Holani in the hole and short of the line to gain on a 3rd-and-2 rushing attempt. New England’s second offensive series saw Drake Maye’s first pass completions of the night to Mack Hollins and A.J. Brown, respectively. However, the momentum built by those plays was not sustained and the Patriots eventually had to punt after Rhamondre Stevenson was tackled for a loss on a 3rd-and-1 carry. Second quarter The defensive battle continued into the second quarter. Seattle gained one first down on its third drive, but had to punt the ball away after a Drew Lock throw on third down came close to being picked off by Christian Gonzalez. Their third drive was one of multiple firsts for the Patriots. They converted their first third downs of the game on throws to DeMario Douglas and A.J. Brown, and they moved into Seattle territory for the first time on the day. Most importantly, they scored their first points: after a pass interference penalty drawn by Brown on a flea-flicker, Maye hit a wide-open Eli Raridon for a touchdown. | Patriots 7, Seahawks 0 First NFL catch, first NFL TD @EliRaridon !! 📺 NBC pic.twitter.com/M9ZmApdGAt — New England Patriots (@Patriots) September 10, 2026 The Patriots’ rookies began leaving their mark in the second quarter. After the Eli Raridon touchdown on the previous drive, fellow draft pick Gabe Jacas registered his first career sack the next series: he took down Drew Lock on a second-effort play for a loss of 7 yards. Seattle nearly dug itself out of a 3rd-and-22 hole thanks to a 21-yard pass to Jaxon Smith-Njigba, but an offsides penalty on the ensuing 4th-and-1 prompted yet another. Seahawks punt. The Patriots continued to find some offensive success on their first drive after the Raridon touchdown, but they were unable to sustain it. Despite returning into Seahawks territory thanks to a third-down conversion to A.J. Brown and another Drake Maye scramble, the series eventually ended in Mitch Wishnowsky’s third punt of the night. Seattle didn’t do anything with the ensuing possession to close out the first half. Third quarter The Patriots’ first drive of the second half was halted after an incompletion on third down intended for A.J. Brown. That was not the biggest problem, though: the offseason trade acquisition remained on the ground after hurting his ankle while trying to make the catch ; he limped off the field and into the blue medical tent; he later left for the locker room and was ruled out. In the meantime, New England was gifted a fresh set of downs after Seattle made contact with Mitch Wishnowsky on a punting attempt. The team took advantage, adding three points to its total on a 50-yard Andy Borregales field goal. | Patriots 10, Seahawks 0 Now defending a 10-point lead, the Patriots defense continued to put the straps on Seattle’s Drew Lock-led offense. Gabe Jacas added a tackle for loss, while Dre’Mont Jones pressured Lock into a short throw on third down. The Michael Dickson punt that followed was a good one, however, and pinned New England at its own 6-yard line. Backed up deep in their own territory, the Patriots opened their next drive with a 2-yard loss on a Rhamondre Stevenson carry. A pair of short completions did not salvage the possession, and New England was forced to punt. The 46-yard kick was accompanied by a 9-yard return, allowing the Seahawks to take over on the Patriots’ 43-yard line. Starting out from a favorable field position, the Seahawks marched deep into the Patriots red zone in part due to an impressive Cooper Kupp grab over tight coverage from Marcus Jones. It appeared that they scored their first touchdown shortly thereafter, but an illegal motion penalty negated the score and ultimately prompted Mike Macdonald to send his field goal crew onto the field for a 30-yard kick. | Patriots 10, Seahawks 3 The Patriots started their next drive behind the chains due to a Morgan Moses false start, but managed to make up the lost yardage and more on a 17-yard swing pass to Rhamondre Stevenson. Another big play — a screen to DeMario Douglas to convert a 3rd-and-8 — closed out the third quarter with New England in possession of the ball at the Seattle 46-yard line. Fourth quarter The fourth quarter started in unfortunate fashion for the Patriots. Attempting a deep shot intended for a double-covered Romeo Doubs, Drake Maye’s pass popped into the air only to be intercepted by Seattle’s Nehemiah Pritchett. The pick and subsequent return allowed the home team to take over at its own 33-yard line. The Seahawks moved the chains to start their next drive, but New England’s defense set up a 4th-and-1 after a Milton Williams run stuff. However, the Patriots defense fell hard for a run fake on that play, allowing Jaxon Smith-Njigba to get wide open behind. The reigning NFL Offensive Player of the Year caught Drew Lock’s pass uncontested, and quickly turned up field to tie the game on a 45-yard catch-and-run. | Patriots 10, Seahawks 10 New England responded to the Seahawks touchdown with two good runs by Rhamondre Stevenson, but followed those up with three bad plays. First, a Stevenson run for a loss of 4 yards. Next, a bad drop by a wide open Romeo Doubs that would have turned a 2nd-and-14 into a fresh set of downs. Finally, Drake Maye getting picked off again while trying to hit DeMario Douglas over the middle. Instead of the Patriots putting the pressure back on, Seattle took over at the Patriots 47-yard line with a chance to take its first lead of the night. Just like they did after the first interception, the Seahawks were able to get some points out of the second Drake Maye pick. Chunk passes to Jaxon Smith-Njigba and Cooper Kupp quickly allowed the team to drive into the New England red zone. The Patriots started showing some resistance at that point, particularly in the form of their best player, Christian Gonzalez, breaking up a slant intended for JSN. However, a 26-yard field goal still allowed Seattle to take the lead with 5:50 left in the game. | Patriots 10, Seahawks 13 The Patriots offense moved backwards to…

full_text: The New England Patriots are going big against the Seattle Seahawks. As a look at their game day roster for the Week 1 contest shows, the team of head coach Mike Vrabel opted to make all four of its tight ends plus fullback Reggie Gilliam active for the Wednesday night showdown. There could be a variety of reasons for that. One is the team’s desire to establish a consistent presence on the ground, something the Patriots failed to do in their Super Bowl loss to the Seahawks back in February. In addition, Tanner Arkin and Cameron Latu in particular could help shore up the protection in front of Drake Maye — a crucial area for New England going against one of the most disruptive defensive lines in football. The Patriots’ full game day roster for the conference title game looks as follows. Brown (1), Romeo Doubs (87), DeMario Douglas (3), Mack Hollins (13), Kyle Williams (18) Tight end (4): Hunter Henry (85), Eli Raridon (82), Tanner Arkin (84), Cameron Latu (36) Offensive tackle (4): Will Campbell (66 | LT), Morgan Moses (76 | RT), Caleb Lomu (74), Dametrious Crownover (68) Interior offensive line (4): Alijah Vera-Tucker (75 | LG), Jared Wilson (55 | C), Mike Onwenu (71 | RG), Greg Van Roten (70) Interior defensive line (5): Milton Williams (97), Christian Barmore (90), Cory Durden (94), Joshua Farmer (92), Leonard Taylor III (93) Defensive edge (4): Dre’Mont Jones (5), Elijah Ponder (91), Gabe Jacas (50), Quintayvious Hutchins (45) Linebacker (4): Robert Spillane (14), Christian Elliss (53), Namdi Obiazor (48), Darius Muasau (54) Cornerback (5): Christian Gonzalez (0), Carlton Davis III (7), Marcus Jones (25 | PR), Charles Woods (22), Channing Canada (29) Safety (4): Kevin Byard (31), Craig Woodson (4), Jaylen Reed (23), Dell Pettus (24) Specialists (3): Andy Borregales (8 | K), Mitch Wishnowsky (19 | P | PS elevation), Julian Ashby (47 | LS) The aforementioned Tanner Arkin is one of nine players on the Patriots’ game day roster to make their NFL debuts on Wednesday. The others are fellow rookies TE Eli Raridon, OT Caleb Lomu, OT Dametrious Crownover, ED Gabe Jacas, ED Quintayvious Hutchins, LB Namdi Obiazor and CB Channing Canada. Sophomore running back Lan Larison, who was promoted from the practice squad, has also never played in an NFL game. As for Canada, he gets the nod over fellow rookie Karon Prunty as the fifth cornerback. Special teams might have played a role in that: the UDFA spent time as a gunner in preseason and with Brenden Schooler on the NFI list looks like the potential next man up. Britt (35), LB Riley Wilson (51), CB Kindle Vildor (28), S Mike Brown (33), S Elliott Davison (27) Injured reserve (6): TE Julian Hill (80), WR Jeremiah Webb (29), RB Myles Montgomery (39), OT Marcus Bryant (52 | short-term), LB Khalil Jacobs (59 | short-term), P Bryce Baringer (17 | short-term) NFI/reserve (1): S Brenden Schooler (41) PUP/reserve (1): ED Harold Landry (2) The Patriots already ruled out running back TreVeyon Henderson on Tuesday, who together with offensive lineman Ben Brown is the only non-healthy scratch among the inactives. The Patriots’ Week 1 game in Seattle will be kicked off at 8:20 p.m. ET.

title: Patriots inactives for NFL Week 1 vs. Seahawks
summary: The New England Patriots will not be using their entire wide receiver depth to kick off their 2026 season. Efton Chism has been deemed a healthy scratch for the Wednesday night opener against the Seattle Seahawks. The second-year man spent the summer as the last option among New England’s roster-caliber wideouts. While he still saw […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MASSACHUSETTS - NOVEMBER 2: Efton Chism III #86 of the New England Patriots looks on during the national anthem prior to an NFL football game against the Atlanta Falcons at Gillette Stadium on November 02, 2025 in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Michael Owens/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New England Patriots will not be using their entire wide receiver depth to kick off their 2026 season. Efton Chism has been deemed a healthy scratch for the Wednesday night opener against the Seattle Seahawks. The second-year man spent the summer as the last option among New England’s roster-caliber wideouts. While he still saw regular action with the starting offense around quarterback Drake Maye, especially as a do-it-all injury replacement, his role was that of a backup. With the rest of the group all healthy for Week 1, the game plan simply did not call for him to be used. Chism therefore starts his sophomore campaigned as one of seven inactives. Patriots inactives QB3 Behren Morton RB TreVeyon Henderson WR Efton Chism III OL Ben Brown OL Walter Rouse LB Erick Hunter CB Karon Prunty The Patriots entered Wednesday with two players already ruled out for the game. Running back TreVeyon Henderson, who hurt his ankle in practice on Aug. 24, remained sidelined throughout the preparation for the contest and was eventually deemed unable to go despite making the trip to Seattle. Backup interior offensive lineman Ben Brown, who is nursing a knee injury, remained in Foxborough to begin with. The other inactives, meanwhile, are all healthy scratches just like Efton Chism. Behren Morton serves as the emergency quarterback, while late pickups Walter Rouse and Erick Hunter as well as rookie cornerback Karon Prunty are not yet at a point where they can contribute at their respective positions. Seahawks inactives QB Jalen Milroe WR Tory Horton TE Nick Kallerup OL Beau Stephens ED Mike Morris S Nick Emmanwori S Ty Okada The most notable name on the Seahawks’ list of inactives is safety Nick Emmanwori, the team’s starting nickel and a crucial piece of their secondary. Emmanwori was listed as questionable because of an ankle injury and his absence, together with that of fellow safety Ty Okada, will put pressure on Seattle’s safety depth on Wednesday night. Kickoff between the Patriots and Seahawks at Seattle’s Lumen Field is scheduled for 8:20 p.m. ET .

title: Our offense vs. their defense: Detroit Lions
summary: Tyler Shough and the New Orleans Saints are finally set to begin their 2026 campaign on the road against the Detroit Lions this Sunday. After a relatively disappointing season that finished with a positive swing in momentum last year, expectations and vibes surrounding the team are now higher than they’ve been in over five years. […]
full_text: ARLINGTON, TEXAS - AUGUST 28: Noah Fant #87 of the New Orleans Saints runs on the field during the first half of the 2026 NFL preseason game against the Dallas Cowboys at AT&T Stadium on August 28, 2026 in Arlington, Texas. (Photo by Sam Hodde/Getty Images) | Getty Images Tyler Shough and the New Orleans Saints are finally set to begin their 2026 campaign on the road against the Detroit Lions this Sunday. After a relatively disappointing season that finished with a positive swing in momentum last year, expectations and vibes surrounding the team are now higher than they’ve been in over five years. Ahead of this weekend’s kickoff, let’s take a look at the offensive matchup for the Saints. Detroit’s defense will be down a couple of key players in its secondary as CB Kerby Joseph and SS Brian Branch both landed on the injured reserve list, meaning each will be out at least the first four weeks of the season. The Lions’ defense had a down year in 2025 after giving up an average of over 330 yards per game. Luckily for the Lions, DE Aidan Hutchinson is still an elite edge rusher and with Dan Campbell’s defensive background, the Michigan product should be able to make an impact in the backfield even if just hurrying the processing time of the offense. Although the Saints will have limited options at the WR position available on Sunday due to injuries and roster cuts, Shough’s ability to build chemistry with his pass catchers early on could become a critical factor in New Orleans’ chances to steal a win in the Motor City. New Orleans’ initial depth chart for this weekend showed just three options at wideout to go along with the typical three tight ends. New Orleans struggled to put points on the board last season, averaging just 18 per contest, a mark that ranked 28th in the league. Now, with a full offseason under their belts in the Big Easy, head coach Kellen Moore and Shough will seek to improve the team’s efficiency when in possession of the football, especially when inside of the redzone. With new additions to the Saints such as RB Travis Etienne Jr., OL David Edwards, TE Noah Fant, and more, it is seemingly likely that New Orleans will find more success for their offensive production between the tackles. This, in turn, should allow other areas such as the play action passing game to open up further.

title: NFL Picks Week 1: Fresh Off The Assembly Line

Thanks to a draft that has added some high-quality parts to this rebuilt chassis, these Saints find […]
full_text: The kickoff of the 2026 Saints season begins with fresh optimism in New Orleans. This Saints team enters the season with second-year head coach Kellen Moore and second-year quarterback Tyler Shough for their first full season behind the wheel together. Thanks to a draft that has added some high-quality parts to this rebuilt chassis, these Saints find themselves poised to turn some heads this season. The expectations have greatly increased for the Saints this season, with the team expected to be a front-runner for the division title, following a last-place finish a season ago. These Saints might not quite yet have what it takes yet to compete for the Lombardi Trophy in Super Bowl LXI in Los Angeles, California next February, but they will certainly attempt to shock the league. Their chance to open the throttle and kick into the next gear begins here in Week 1. All season and postseason, we will be presenting you with each and every game on the NFL schedule along with my picks for each game. It’s been a long wait for this season to begin, so let’s get started. WEEK 1 Wednesday, September 9th – NFL Kickoff 2026 Patriots at Seahawks This rematch of February’s Super Bowl LX will hopefully turn out much better than that game. Seattle’s rivals in Los Angeles are getting the spotlight this season, but the reigning Super Bowl Champions will remind everyone that they are still the team to beat. New England has had an interesting offseason to say the least, but this team is every bit as good as the one that reached the Super Bowl last season. The problem for the Pats is that Seattle is still just as talented and well coached as they were that Super Bowl Sunday. Seattle wins 26-17. Pick: Seahawks *** Thursday, September 10th – NFL International Game 49ers at* Rams – East Melbourne, Victoria, Australia Few teams enter an NFL season with the level of expectations that the Rams face this season. They boast arguably the most intimidating defensive line we have seen in many years, and soon we will see if this team is more than just the hype that precedes them. On the other side, their rivals from San Francisco have faced an offseason full of turmoil and injuries. Despite it all, the Niners have an annoying ability to play better than they have any right to, under Kyle Shanahan. Without Aaron Donald, and with great familiarity between these bitter rivals, this showdown Down Under will be a pretty close one. Los Angeles wins 33-26. Pick: Rams *** Sunday, September 13th – Early Games Bears at Panthers Chicago found themselves so very close to the NFC Championship Game last season, and now look to take that next step under second-year coach Ben Johnson. The reigning NFC South Champs hope their triumph from last season wasn’t just a fluke. Tough break for the Panthers, facing these Bears right from the jump. Chicago wins 26-14. Pick: Bears *** Buccaneers at Bengals Tampa saw their unimpressively long reign atop the NFC South come to an unceremonious end last season, and this season may very well prove the Bucs’ glory days are in the past. Cincy, on the other hand, looks to regain their place among the AFC’s contending elite. While Cincy’s reworked defense looks to get its footing, their offense will take care of business. Cincinnati wins 37-23. Pick: Bengals *** Bills at Texans – Game of the Week If not for some bad bounces on both sides, it could’ve been these two teams that played each other in last season’s AFC Championship Game. Now they face off in a game that starts the season, but may have long-term ramifications come the end of the season. Buffalo is hoping that a change at head coach is just what they need to finally reach their elusive goal, but this elite Houston defense will win this game for the home team. Houston wins 23-20. Pick: Texans *** Ravens at Colts Both of these teams hade the making of AFC contenders to start last season, but both ultimately missed the playoffs in the end. Now, a season of redemption arrives for both teams. Indy, with a returning Daniel Jones at QB, and Baltimore, with a new head coach leading the franchise. This will be a close one, but Baltimore wins this one in the closing moments. Baltimore wins 25-24. Pick: Ravens *** Browns at Jaguars Jacksonville started the Liam Coen era by winning the AFC South Championship last season, and look to fend off a division that improved across the board during the offseason. The offseason for Cleveland has left Browns fans wanting for more, a sentiment they will certainly feel throughout this season. Jacksonville wins 25-20. Pick: Jaguars *** Falcons at Steelers Pittsburgh finds themselves in unfamiliar territory, no longer being led by longtime head coach Mike Tomlin, but Mike McCarthy instead. It feels like an timeline in flux in the City of Steel, but they are being gifted an opening matchup with Atlanta, who features a head coach they are very familiar with in Kevin Stefanski and a quarterback they should have no problems with. This could easily be the start of a very long season for the Falcons. Pittsburgh wins 17-13. Pick: Steelers *** Jets at Titans This matchup of two of last season’s worst teams certainly won’t spark much interest to start the season, but Tennessee’s investments in their young offense should pay dividends this week. Tennessee wins 27-17. Pick: Titans *** Saints at Lions The Saints open the season with a notably brutal one-two punch at Detroit and Baltimore. The 2026 Saints should be a dramatic improvement over last year’s version, but they face quite an uphill battle right at the starting line on the road this week. Tyler Shough has been given more weapons to work with, as well as an upgrade in protection, and that should do wonders for the sophomore signal caller. If the defense can play up to their levels from a season ago, the Saints should certainly see themselves fighting for control of the NFC South this season. Can the Saints win this game? Certainly. Will the Saints win this game? It just doesn’t feel like it. Detroit may not have been a playoff team last year, but like the Saints, they are a team primed for a rebound. Dan Campbell still has quite a talented roster at his disposal, and Detroit’s division will forge his team in fire this year. Injuries to the Lions’ secondary will keep this one close throughout, but unfortunately, the task will be a little too tall for the Saints to open the season. Detroit wins 26-21. Pick: Lions *** Sunday, September 13th – Late Games Cardinals at Chargers The Chargers are looking to keep pace with a very difficult fight for the top of the AFC West. They have the coach, they have the quarterback, they have the overall roster to reach the next level, but something always seems to be missing. Thankfully for the Bolts, they face an Arizona team still searching for their identity going forward, and they will win a game that is much closer than is has any business being. Los Angeles wins 21-20. Pick: Chargers *** Dolphins at Raiders The Fernando Mendoza era will be here soon enough, but until then Kirk Cousins will lead the Silver and Black under new head coach Klint Kubiak. Miami also enters this season with a new head coach and quarterback, but it will be the home team that starts off their new era with a win. Las Vegas wins 27-16. Pick: Raiders *** Packers at Vikings These fierce NFC North rivals look not only to fend off each other but the reigning champion Bears and the likely resurgent Lions. Every divisional game in the NFC North will be crucial, and this one will come down to Green Bay’s advantage at quarterback, in the end. Green Bay wins 26-22. Pick: Packers *** Commanders at Eagles After facing each other in the NFC Championship Game two seasons ago, these NFC East rivals suffered through disappointing campaigns last season, with Philly unceremoniously failing in the playoffs, while Washington missed the playoffs entirely. Now, both look to rebound, but Philly will take this one at home. Philadelphia wins 23-21. Pick:…

title: A look back at the history between the Saints and Lions
summary: The New Orleans Saints will open the 2026 season on the road Sunday afternoon against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field. The Saints and Lions first met on Nov. 24, 1968, at Tiger Stadium in Detroit, with the game ending in a 20-20 tie. Since then, the teams have met just 28 times, with New […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LOUISIANA - DECEMBER 03: Alvin Kamara #41 of the New Orleans Saints runs with the ball in the fourth quarter against the Detroit Lions at the Caesars Superdome on December 03, 2023 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Chris Graythen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints will open the 2026 season on the road Sunday afternoon against the Detroit Lions at Ford Field. The Saints and Lions first met on Nov. 24, 1968, at Tiger Stadium in Detroit, with the game ending in a 20-20 tie. Since then, the teams have met just 28 times, with New Orleans holding a 14-13-1 advantage in the all-time series. The last time these teams faced one another, Detroit came away with a 33-28 victory in New Orleans in 2023, giving the Lions the edge in the most recent chapter of the series. The Saints enter the 2026 season looking to improve on their 6-11 record from a year ago. Following another losing season, New Orleans made several changes during the offseason in an effort to turn things around and return to playoff contention. With a new season comes renewed optimism, but that optimism will ultimately have to translate into wins. The Saints believe they have added enough talent to compete in the NFC South, and Sunday’s opener against Detroit provides their first opportunity to show they are ready to take the next step. The Lions enter the season with a similar goal after a disappointing 2025 campaign. Detroit finished 9-8 and missed the playoffs, a significant step backward after going 15-2 and earning the NFC’s No. 1 seed in 2024. Despite that disappointing finish, Detroit remained one of the NFL’s most productive offensive teams, averaging 28.3 points per game, which ranked fourth in the league. The Lions will look to carry that offensive firepower into 2026 while putting last season’s struggles behind them. For both teams, Sunday’s matchup represents a fresh start and an early opportunity to set the tone for the season. Kickoff is at 12:00 pm and the game will be broadcast on FOX with Kenny Albert (play-by-play), Jonathan Vilma (color analyst) and Megan Olivi (sideline)

title: NY Giants’ C.J. Okoye says landing in New York ‘a really good outcome’
summary: EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J — NFL players don’t usually admit to reading the tea leaves and trying to figure out whether or not they fit on a roster as cutdowns to 53 players approach. New York Giants defensive tackle C.J. Okoye, though, is an unusual NFL player. During an exclusive interview with Big Blue View on […]
full_text: C.J. Okoye with the Ravens during the preseason. | Getty Images EAST RUTHERFORD, N.J — NFL players don’t usually admit to reading the tea leaves and trying to figure out whether or not they fit on a roster as cutdowns to 53 players approach. New York Giants defensive tackle C.J. Okoye , though, is an unusual NFL player. During an exclusive interview with Big Blue View on Wednesday, Okoye admitted he had been looking at the Baltimore Ravens depth chart this summer and trying to figure out if the Ravens — a team he played 13 games for last season — had a spot for him. “My [defensive line] room back in Baltimore was a deep room, but I had a great camp coming out,” Okoye said. “I was like, if they’re gonna cut me, I know I’m gonna have to go somewhere else.” Being traded to the Giants right before roster cuts was a best-case scenario for the Nigerian-born 6-foot-6, 265-pound 24-year-old. “That morning, it was like a shock to me, but it wasn’t a shock,” Okoye said. “I was kind of happy, like it was a trade, you know what I mean? So, it was, it was a good, it was a good outcome. “It was a really good outcome.” Giants head coach John Harbaugh and defensive line coach Dennis Johnson were familiar with Okoye from last season in Baltimore. In need of defensive line depth, they turned to the Ravens to find it. After the trade, Harbaugh said this about Okoye : He’s a guy that we got to know recently last year, came in, was with the Chargers actually with my brother [Jim] for a couple years in the international program,” Harbaugh said. “So a guy who had been a developmental-type guy, learning the game and tremendous physical skills, hard worker, has really dedicated himself over the last few years to learning the game really because he didn’t play it growing up and made great strides, made great strides with Dennis Johnson, our defensive line coach last year. That’s where he kind of broke through and had a really good season. “We see him as an inside defender, a defensive tackle, A gap, B gap player, run stopper, pocket pusher in terms of the past game and just a really big physical player,” Harbaugh said. “So kind of a type of guy we’ve been looking for and we’re really excited to get him up here.” Okoye is thrilled to be back under Johnson’s tutelage. “Coach Dennis, he’s my guy; he’s the one that, like, he’s one of the people that brought, like, that brought CJ out, you know what I mean?,” Okoye said. “So, yeah, so, I was really happy that I’m coming to a system I knew already.” No matter where it is on the defensive line that the Giants ask him to play, Okoye just wants to play. “Right now, I don’t know [how he will be used] and I don’t care,” Okoye said. “Just line me up, mano a mano. Just line me up. So far as I know the play, if you want me to play anything, anything the team wants, I’m here.” Okoye’s journey Okoye’s journey to the NFL began when he attended an International Pathway Program camp in Africa run by former Giants great Osi Umenyiora. Until then, Okoye had been a basketball player. “I learned about football through a movie,” Okoye said. The movie? ‘The Game Plan’ starring Dwayne ‘The Rock’ Johnson. “That’s when I learned about football,” Okoye said. “I was playing basketball before then, the whole thing, then the camp came, and I didn’t even know, I thought it was like a, that [it] was one of those charity events or something like that, but I went through, made the camp, saw it was real, the rest is history, but I had never played football. My first snap of football was in the league.” Okoye was impressive enough that he ended up being allocated to the Los Angeles Chargers for the 2023 season. He spent two seasons learning the game on the Chargers’ practice squad. Okoye recorded a sack in his first-ever NFL game, a 2023 preseason contest against the Los Angeles Rams. It is a story he has recounted many times, but Okoye did not know what he had done. “I thought it was a tackle for loss. I didn’t even know it was a sack because I didn’t know, like I was playing the game,” Okoye said. “I didn’t even know what I was doing.” If you have ever watched little kids play basketball and get thoroughly confused when the teams switch ends of the court after halftime, you will empathize with the other “welcome to the NFL” story Okoye told about that game. “After the first quarter, they were switching,” Okoye said. “I’m like, why are you guys switching? I didn’t even know why they were switching. I’m like, okay, we’re switching now. They said, yeah, we switch every quarter. I’m like, okay.” Okoye learned something else important that day. He learned he could play football at the highest level despite his inexperience. “I knew I can play this game because as someone that had never played, if I can still whoop ass like that, imagine when I have like five, seven years of this,” Okoye said. Okoye switched quickly from offensive to defensive line after joining the Chargers. “I like it better,” Okoye said. “I’d rather be the aggressor than sit and absorb. “I’d rather just go and knock somebody back than try to absorb somebody knocking me back, you know what I mean?” ‘I’m never going to be satisfied’ Okoye played 214 defensive snaps and 41 special teams snaps for the Ravens last year, the first regular-season action of his career. Entering his fourth season, where does Okoye think he is in terms of his development and understanding? “I’ll say I’m still behind,” Okoye said. “I look at myself like that because I’m playing catch-up. I’m never going to be satisfied, you know what I’m saying? Because I always feel like the person I’m going against went to college, and he’s more prepared than me. “So it makes me want to work more. It makes me want to go out there and prove myself, you know what I’m saying? So just because of him going to college, I feel like he, he thinks he got the edge over me.” Okoye praised veteran defensive tackles D.J. Reader and Shelby Harris for sharing their knowledge. He said Reader and Harris are “no doubt” more forthcoming with information than his veteran Ravens teammates were. “They’re both amazing guys,” Okoye said. “I feel like I’m going to learn here more. I’m going to add to my play here more than Baltimore because they’re ready to like give you everything, like as much as you can, as much as you can like learn, they are willing to teach.” The Giants, of course, are hoping that Okoye’s ascension continues and that he becomes a true force on their defensive line.

title: NY Giants-Cowboys matchup: New York to unveil new-look, physical offense
summary: The New York Giants are looking to start the John Harbaugh era off with a bang, and come away from their season-opening Sunday Night Football game with a win over the Dallas Cowboys. The matchup between the Giants’ offense and Cowboys’ defense is one of the most intriguing of the weekend. The Giants’ offense will […]
full_text: Malik Nabers catches a touchdown against the Dallas Cowboys. | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New York Giants are looking to start the John Harbaugh era off with a bang, and come away from their season-opening Sunday Night Football game with a win over the Dallas Cowboys. The matchup between the Giants’ offense and Cowboys’ defense is one of the most intriguing of the weekend. The Giants’ offense will look significantly different from a year ago, with Jaxson Dart at quarterback, Darnell Mooney , Odell Beckham Jr. , and Malachi Fields at receiver, Isaiah Likely at tight end, Patrick Ricard at fullback, and a new coaching staff. The Cowboys, meanwhile have a reshuffled roster of their own and a completely new scheme under Christian Parker. As things stand now, we simply don’t quite know what either unit will look like or how they’ll play. So what can we expect when Jaxson Dart and the Giants’ offense takes the field against the Cowboys’ defense? Let’s start with what we do know and then make some educated guesses. What will the Giants’ offense look like? This has been, perhaps, the most beguiling question hanging over the Giants’ offseason — at least for me. The Giants having four former offensive coordinators on their staff (OC Matt Nagy, QB coach/passing game coordinator Brian Callahan, senior assistant Greg Roman, and tight ends coach Tim Kelly) may not be unprecedented, but it is unorthodox. We won’t really know how it will work until the game is well under way. However my personal speculation has been that Nagy will serve as the master distiller who blends various aspects of Roman, Callahan, and Kelly’s philosophies into a single product. It could blow up in the Giants’ faces, or the various twists on existing schemes could present defenses with unexpected looks or combinations of concepts. That said, we might be able to use context clues to define the negative space and get a rough outline of what the Giants want to do on offense. Power running game – This one became blatantly obvious when the Giants hired John Harbaugh and painfully obvious when they hired Greg Roman as “Senior Offensive Assistant”. Harbaugh has always favored a run-heavy offense, while Roman loves a down-hill rushing attack and is among the best in the NFL at scheming one up. The Giants will likely attempt to displace the defense vertically and force them to crowd the box. We’ll also likely see Jaxson Dart used as a runner more than those fearing the Blue Tent would likely prefer. After all, John Harbaugh was once called the “Prince Of Analytics” by ESPN, and forcing defenses to play true 11-on-11 football is typically confers an analytic advantage for the offense. Heavy sets – Again, this one is pretty obvious based on John Harbaugh’s past preferences. It was only reinfoced when the Giants released Darius Slayton and left themselves with just four receivers. That doesn’t mean the Giants will forego the passing attack, but rather they’ll be getting their tight ends and backs heavily involved as pass catchers. Isaiah Likely was Jaxson Dart’s most common target in training camp, while Theo Johnson flashed brilliance (in addition to frustrating drops) in his second season. Likewise, each of the Giants’ four running backs are dangerous pass catchers. Former receiver Tyrone Tracy is the obvious standout, however Cam Skattebo, Najee Harris, and Devin Singletary all have upside as pass catchers. Precision passing game – Teams often like contrast between their running and passing game. So if the Giants want a downhill rushing attack, we could see that paired with a passing attack that uses precise route running to set receivers up for yards after the catch. This is where Brian Callahan’s influence (may) come in. Where Matt Nagy is a traditional West Coast Offense guy, having learned under Andy Reid, Callahan comes from the “New West Coast” tree. In other words, we could see influences from the “Kubiak-Shanahan-McVay” school of offense. In that vein, it’s notable that the Giants’ four remaining receivers are all talented route runners. Even 6-foot-4, 220-pound rookie Malachi Fields is far more nimble than his frame would suggest. The release of Slayton may also suggest that Malik Nabers is trending toward being ready to play Week 1. There will certainly be a vertical aspect to the offense, Lamar Jackson was tied for the fourth-highest intended air yardage in the NFL last year (9.1 yards downfield), while Matt Stafford was third with 9.2 intended air yards. So while much of the passing attack may be to set Malik Nabers and Darnell Mooney up with YAC opportunities, we should also expect to see the Giants attempt to generate chunk plays. Condensed sets – Modern NFL offenses like to weaponize every aspect of play design, including formation width. While spread formations can be conducive to running the ball (by forcing defenses to spread out an lighten the box), condensed sets are coming into vogue. The Giants featuring tight ends and a fullback suggests that they’ll go with that trend, though perhaps not for the reason fans expect. Condensed sets certainly make it easier to insert receivers or detached tight ends into gaps as blockers for inside runs. But they also allow offenses to create traffic for their passing concepts. That, in turn, makes play-action passes to the intermediate area even more effective and can force teams to pay for playing a base defense. The Fangio factor In addition to not knowing quite what to expect from the Giants’ offensive scheme to start the season, we also don’t know quite what to expect from the Dallas defense either. The Cowboys fired their previous defensive coordinator after fielding a historically bad defense for much of the 2025 season, and hired former Philadelphia Eagles Passing Game Coordinator and defensive backs coach Christian Parker. Parker spent 2024 and 2025 with the Cowboys after spending 2022 and 2023 as the Denver Broncos’ defensive backs coach. Parker is considered one of the bright young minds on the defensive side of the ball and is a disciple of Eagles’ DC Vic Fangio. In other words, we should expect the new-look Cowboys’ defense to be similar in structure to what the Eagles run. The Fangio scheme is based on quarters coverages, man-match coverage rules, nickel sets, and post-snap rotations. Coverage rotations are a signature aspect of Fangio’s scheme, usually starting out in quarters coverages and rotating to a Cover 3 look, or to Cover 6 and Cover 8 looks. Cover 6 and Cover 8 are hybrid coverages that mix Cover 2 and Cover 4 principles. The primary difference is that Cover 6 plays the “quarters” side to the passing strength, while Cover 8 plays the “quarters” away from the passing strength. The purpose of the rotations is to disguise rotations, help simulate pressure, and allow nickel sets to play heavier than they appear on paper. Speaking of nickel sets, while the “Fangio” defense is based in the 3-4, his primary alignments are 4-2-5 Nickel and 3-3-5 Penny sets. In either case, STAR Caleb Downs will be a key piece for the Dallas defense as the third DB. He’ll be playing a similar role as Cooper DeJean does in Philly, and be Dallas’ primary “Pivot” player who changes the look between Quarters, Cover 6, and Cover 8, as well as changing how Dallas defends gaps up front. The Giants will likely want to go back and study last year’s Week 8 loss to the Philadelphia Eagles in preparation for this game. The Giants trounced the Eagles just two weeks prior, however that game featured Fangio abandoning his usual tendencies to attack the rookie QB with blitzes. Jaxson Dart comported himself well in that game, but struggled once Fangio returned to his usual defense in Week 8. full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know as the Giants get ready to battle the Dallas Cowboys this Sunday night. Bill Barnwell’s 2026 NFL playoff field, plus Super Bowl pick | ESPN.com My pick for 2026: In the playoffs (NFC wild card). The Giants? Yes, the same Giants who finished 4-13 in 2025. Do I think they’re better than the Packers? No. But acknowledging that history tells us three teams from this bucket at the bottom of the 2025 standings will make it to the playoffs in 2026, the Giants look a lot like the Bears and Jaguars did a year ago — better than they seemed the year before and in position to make a leap. Can New York overcome a difficult schedule? The Giants rank eighth in projected strength of schedule, per the FPI, with a slightly easier slate than the Cowboys and Commanders, whom they might compete with for a playoff spot. Of course, a year ago, the Bears were projected to face the league’s fourth-toughest schedule heading into the season, but with improved coaching and a step forward from their second-year quarterback, they jumped from worst to first in the NFC North. I don’t think the Giants make that sort of push and win the division, but I do think they’re capable of being the league’s most surprising wild-card team. Jaxson Dart strives for greatness "I want to do something special" pic.twitter.com/BNaqhPXfNx — New York Giants (@Giants) September 9, 2026 Inside Jaxson Dart’s quest to turn NY Giants’ faith into victories | The Record Jaxson Dart has the spectacular mastered. He reminded us that again this summer with a remarkable touchdown pass to rookie Malachi Fields in the preseason opener against the Minnesota Vikings, one that only a handful of NFL quarterbacks can make. John Harbaugh gets testy as Giants’ Malik Nabers questions pile up | New York Post “We can put a stop to all these questions,” Harbaugh said after Wednesday’s practice. “Because I’m not going to tell you who is playing in the game. I’m not going to tell you who is starting. I’m not going to tell you what package we have in. I’m not going to tell you what plays we are running. I’m not going to tell you any of that. So we can have a great press conference, or we can make it uncomfortable.” “But I’m not going to tell you because when you know, the Cowboys know — or every other team we play knows. And that’s not in the competitive interest of our football team. Does that make sense? So, I think you can respect that.” Presser Points: Coach John Harbaugh previews season opener | Giants.com On releasing veteran wide receiver Darius Slayton: “We always make all of our personnel decisions about what’s best for the team immediately and in the long-term future. What gives us the best chance to be the best team we can be and that’s the choice that we made.” A lot of factors went into the timing. “Maybe you can get a trade,” Harbaugh said. “Maybe you try to wait as long as you can to see if you work out a contract change, right? There’s a lot of reasons to it.” Intel on all 32 NFL teams | The Athletic Coach John Harbaugh is expected to ride the ground game to help quarterback Jaxson Dart as much as possible. And like their counterparts in New Jersey, the Giants can be scary if they can build early leads. Outside linebackers Brian Burns, Abdul Carter and Kayvon Thibodeaux, as well as inside linebacker Arvell Reese, are as athletic as any collection of rushers in the league. Keys to beating Dallas What the Giants MUST do to BEAT the Cowboys? @CarlBanksGIII @BobPapa_NFL https://t.co/dWaxsgg47Z pic.twitter.com/fjkgln7a21 — Bleav (@BleavNetwork) September 9, 2026 Bold predictions for 2026 NFL season, including for Jets and Giants | SNY.tv The Giants win eight games. The Giants didn’t just hire a new coach. They hired one who had only three losing seasons in 18 years with Baltimore. Malik Nabers looks primed to play in the opener. That’s huge. The offensive line is as talented as it’s been in more than a decade. The defense is loaded with pass rushers. Tennessee, Arizona, Washington twice, Indianapolis, and Cleveland are all winnable games. Win those six, and the Giants need to steal two others. I like their chances of doing that with Harbaugh. I do have reservations about Jaxson Dart. The quarterback wasn’t good this summer, struggling to pick up offensive coordinator Matt Nagy’s pro-style scheme. But if it clicks and he plays like a top-15 passer, there’s no reason the Giants can’t get to nine wins and sneak in as a Wild Card team. That is a big if. Shocking stat shows New York Giants are due for home opener win | USAToday.com Since the opening of the $1.6 billion stadium, the Giants have hosted seven regular-season opening games in East Rutherford. As has been the case for Big Blue in general over the last decade plus, they haven’t fared too well in Week 1 home games. In fact, the Giants haven’t won a Week 1 home game since they beat the Carolina Panthers, 31-18, to begin the 2010 season. That was also the very first game played at MetLife Stadium, which was known as New Meadowlands Stadium at the time. title: Malik Nabers looks ready as NY Giants open practice for Week 1 game vs. Dallas Cowboys

Neither the Giants nor Nabers have committed to the 2024 first-round pick playing on Sunday. The signs, though, point toward that […]
full_text: Wide receiver Malik Nabers was on the field Wednesday with teammates from the beginning of practice and moving well as the New York Giants began practice for Sunday’s season-opening game against the Dallas Cowboys. Neither the Giants nor Nabers have committed to the 2024 first-round pick playing on Sunday. The signs, though, point toward that happening. Nabers practiced all summer with no real hiccups as he worked his way back from two surgeries to repair a torn ACL suffered in Week 4 of the 2025 season. Nabers was listed as a full practice participant while the Giants practiced in full pads. “I think he’s ready to go, man,” head coach John Harbaugh said. “We’ll see, though, there’s still four days, five days until we play. “If he’s ready to go, and he feels like he’s ready to go, he’ll play. If he’s not ready, he won’t play.” The release by the Giants on Monday of veteran wide receiver Darius Slayton could also be taken as a sign that the team expects Nabers to play. Tight end Theo Johnson (shoulder) and running back Tyrone Tracy (stinger) were practicing without the red non-contact jerseys they wore last week. Every player on the active roster was a full practice participant. title: Can John Harbaugh succeed with the Giants where others have failed?
summary: No NFL head coach has ever won a Super Bowl with two different teams. That’s the history John Harbaugh will be trying to buck over the next few years as he starts his tenure as Giants’ head coach this Sunday. Seven head coaches have tried, though, including some of the NFL’s most illustrious names. What […]
full_text: Andy Reid and John Harbaugh | Getty Images No NFL head coach has ever won a Super Bowl with two different teams. That’s the history John Harbaugh will be trying to buck over the next few years as he starts his tenure as Giants’ head coach this Sunday. Seven head coaches have tried, though, including some of the NFL’s most illustrious names. What can we learn from their experiences, other than that it’s really hard to do? Don Shula Hall of Famer Don Shula took over for Weeb Ewbank, whose great Baltimore Colts teams of the late 1950s had drifted toward mediocrity in the 1960s. Shula won the NFL Championship in his fourth season, 1968, by throttling Cleveland 34-0. Unfortunately for Shula, by then the NFL and AFL champions were playing each other in what was now being called the Super Bowl, and we know what the New York Jets did to the Colts in that game. HOFer Johnny Unitas was injured much of that season and ex-Giant Earl Morrall, a good quarterback who carved out a 21-year NFL career, started but could do nothing against the Jets’ ferocious defense. Shula brought Unitas in with the Colts trailing in the second half, but to no avail. Shula left the Colts voluntarily after one more season, lured by Miami Dolphins owner Joe Robbie to try to right the ship for the woeful expansion team. Shula immediately led them to a 10-4 season and the Divisional Round of the playoffs behind quarterback Bob Griese, the dual running attack of Larry Csonka and Jim Kiick, and wide receiver Paul Warfield. A year later that team was in the Super Bowl, and they won it all the two following seasons, when they had possibly the best defense in the NFL. Griese, Csonka, and Warfield are all Hall of Famers. Dick Vermeil Vermeil was head coach at UCLA when I was a grad student there, his two-year stint capped by a remarkable upset of No. 1, undefeated Ohio State in the Rose Bowl. The Philadelphia Eagles immediately lured him to the NFL. It took three seasons for him to turn the Eagles into a winning, playoff team. The Eagles made the playoffs four consecutive times and reached the Super Bowl once, in 1980, with Ron Jaworski, a solid but not great quarterback, at the helm. They were defeated soundly by the Oakland Raiders and Jim Plunkett. After the 1982 strike-shortened season, Vermeil stepped down, citing burnout. After being out of the NFL for 14 years, the St. Louis Rams hired Vermeil as their head coach in 1997. After two losing seasons, Vermeil finally won a Super Bowl. The difference? That team had The Greatest Show on Turf, led by Hall of Fame quarterback Kurt Warner and featuring wide receivers Isaac Bruce and Torry Holt and running back Marshall Faulk, all of whom are also HOFs except Holt, a. perennial HOF finalist. Bill Parcells You all know about Parcells’ tenure with the Giants. He never had a Hall of Fame-caliber QB, but Phil Simms was a plus player who might have been considered in the second tier of quarterbacks below the HOFers had he stayed healthy for more of his career. Those Giants teams had that suffocating defense, especially at the first two levels, with HOFers in Harry Carson and Lawrence Taylor. They also had a more than capable Jeff Hostetler to hold the fort after Simms went down in 1990. Really, that Giants team might have gotten another ring, in either 1988 or 1989, but the defense wasn’t quite as good as it needed to be in crunch time, and no thanks to @#!% Al Toon and Flipper Anderson. Parcells stepped down after the 1990 season but came back to coach New England in 1993. He got the Patriots to the Super Bowl in the 1996 season but lost to the Green Bay Packers. Those Patriot teams were quarterbacked by Drew Bledsoe, a good, even prolific at times passer, but not a Super Bowl-caliber QB. Parcells made other coaching stops. He almost got to another Super Bowl with the Vinny Testaverde-led Jets, but his team blew a 10-0 third quarter lead with 6 turnovers and lost to the Denver Broncos and HOFers John Elway and Terrell Davis. Mike Holmgren Holmgren coached the Green Bay Packers for seven years in the 1990s, had a winning record every season, and got them to the playoffs in every season but his first. Holmgren won the Super Bowl with HOFer Brett Favre as his QB in the 1996 season, beating the Parcells-led Patriots. He was right back in the Super Bowl the following year but lost to the Denver Broncos and their two HOFers. Holmgren later coached the Seattle Seahawks and got them to the Super Bowl as well. This time he lost to the Pittsburgh Steelers due to a long rushing touchdown and a trick play for a passing touchdown. Likely future HOFer Ben Roethlisberger quarterbacked the Steelers, but he had a poor game, contributing mainly via a controversial TD on a keeper. Holmgren’s quarterback Matt Hasselback, a solid but not elite QB, had a better game in defeat. Holmgren was a little unlucky not to walk away with a second ring. Andy Reid Reid coached the Philadelphia Eagles for 14 seasons before becoming head coach of the Kansas City Chiefs. During most of his time in Philadelphia his QB was Donovan McNabb, who was replaced by Michael Vick for his final three seasons there. McNabb led the Eagles to the playoffs 8 times and to the Super Bowl once. It was his misfortune for that one time to be against the emerging Patriots dynasty, a game he lost 24-21, putting up 357 yards, 3 TDs and 3 INTs. Reid was fired by the Eagles after the 2012 season and was hired by the Kansas City Chiefs. He immediately turned the perennially losing Chiefs into a winner, going from 2-14 the year before to 11-5 in Reid’s first year there. This past 6-11 season was Reid’s first sub-.500 season since he got there. Still, under the good but not great Alex Smith Reid’s teams never reached the Super Bowl. Then the Chiefs drafted Patrick Mahomes, sat him for a year, and started him in 2018. The rest is history. Honorable mention Dan Reeves and John Fox both lost Super Bowls with two different teams but never won one. Reeves actually coached in four Super Bowls, three with Denver and one with Atlanta, winning none. Of course Reeves’ first loss was to the 1986 Giants. Elway was his quarterback in each of those losses. Chris Chandler, a solid but not elite player, was his QB for the Atlanta Super Bowl loss. Reeves coached the Giants in between his Denver and Atlanta stints but only got them to the playoffs once. Fox coached the Carolina Panthers to the Super Bowl in 2003, where QB Jake Delhomme played heroically in a close loss to the emerging Patriots dynasty. He later coached the Denver Broncos to the Super Bowl in 2013, where an aged Peyton Manning had the misfortune of facing Seattle’s Legion of Boom at their peak at Met Life. What does this mean for John Harbaugh? Harbaugh has an opportunity to become the first head coach in NFL history to win a ring with two different teams. In addition to that being unprecedented, it would be more a of a feather in his cap to do it with the Giants than when he did it with the Ravens. In Baltimore, Harbaugh took over a Baltimore franchise that had produced 9, 10, 10, 12 and 13 win seasons under his predecessor, Brian Billick – including a Super Bowl win (no need to remind Giants fans of that). Although the Ravens had dropped to 5-11 in Billick’s last season, they had been 13-3 just the year before. This is a franchise that has had expectations of winning ever since they moved to Baltimore from Cleveland. Furthermore, although Harbaugh got a ring in 2012 with a very good but not elite Joe Flacco at QB, he did it against a 49ers team that somewhat mirrored his own – coached by his brother, both of them coming off heartbreaking losses in the the conference championship the year before (the 49ers’ loss being to the Giants, the Ravens’ to the Patriots). That Ravens team had HOFers Ray Lewis and Ed Reed, though both were nearing the ends of their careers. This is definitely not the situation Harbaugh walks into with the downtrodden Giants. To elevate this…

title: NFL power rankings: Nick’s picks for how teams stack up before Week 1
summary: The New York Giants are eager to open a new chapter for their illustrious franchise. The Brian Daboll era is over, and John Harbaugh has assumed the head coaching responsibilities. The Giants were one of 10 teams that changed head coaches after the 2025 season, so new identities — in new locations — will look […]
full_text: John Harbaugh watches Monday’s practice. | Getty Images The New York Giants are eager to open a new chapter for their illustrious franchise. The Brian Daboll era is over, and John Harbaugh has assumed the head coaching responsibilities. The Giants were one of 10 teams that changed head coaches after the 2025 season, so new identities — in new locations — will look to be established across the league. I’ll be writing a new column this year: an NFL Power Rankings piece ahead of each Thursday Night Football game. In this case, that means Wednesday’s season opener—a Super Bowl rematch between the Seattle Seahawks and New England Patriots. The piece will include the power rankings, plus a short blurb on each team’s status. So, without further ado, here are the final preseason power rankings before the start of the 2026 NFL season. No. 1 — Seattle Seahawks Seattle receives the number one honors after defeating the Patriots in Super Bowl LX, 29-13. However, Seattle still has a lot to prove, and credible cases could be made for the second and third teams to be ranked number one. Seattle lost offensive coordinator Klint Kubiak to the Raiders’ coaching gig, and Super Bowl MVP Kenneth Walker took his talents to Kansas City, leaving the Seahawks with a rushing attack led by first-round pick Jadarian Price, as Zach Charbonnett recovers from his torn ACL. Still, Seattle has arguably the best defense in the league, and they’re an insanely deep and well-coached team. Interestingly enough, though, the second team in the power rankings resides in their division. No. 2 — Los Angeles Rams The Rams traded for Myles Garrett and have Aaron Donald coming out of retirement to play in Chris Shula’s vaunted defense. Les Snead also traded for cornerback Trent McDuffie. The improved defense should assist reigning MVP Matt Stafford. I expect the offense to continue its heavier personnel usage, while names like Terrance Ferguson will become better known as the third pass-catcher behind Puka Nucau and Devonte Adams. No. 3 — Denver Broncos The loss of Bo Nix at the end of the Divisional Round stifled the momentum of Denver, who was forced to play Jarrett Stidham in a sloppy 10-7 loss in the AFC Championship game last year. Sean Payton identified a few problems and traded for wide receiver Jaylen Waddle, which gives Nix the star number one receiver Denver desperately needed to pair with Courtland Sutton. It will be on new OC Davis Webb to ensure the engine of the offense is well-oiled within Payton’s identity. The Broncos led the league in sacks last season, and Vance Joseph coordinates the defense; I expect Denver’s defense to remain a top-five unit. No. 4 — New England Patriots Off-season scandals aside, the Patriots did well improving the offensive infrastructure around star quarterback Drake Maye. The trade for AJ Brown and the signing of Romeo Doubs gave Maye two legitimate wide receivers, with the former being an ideal fit for Maye’s skill set. New England also locked up Christian Gonzalez. The schedule is MUCH more difficult than in 2025, but I am a Drake Maye believer. Mike Vrabel has built a STRONG, well-coached defense, and the defending AFC representative edged out their divisional rival, the Buffalo Bills, by a hair here. No. 5 — Buffalo Bills Sean McDermott is out, and Joe Brady is in, as well as DJ Moore. Josh Allen is arguably the best quarterback in the NFL, but the Bills have consistently failed to get over the hump. Buffalo lost 33-30 to the Broncos in overtime last year, but former Broncos assistant head coach Jim Leonhard is now the defensive coordinator for Buffalo. The Leonhard hire may prove to be one of the more impactful coordinator hirings in recent NFL history. The Bills and Patriots are an AFC East heavyweight matchup in a division with two other strawweights. No. 6 — Philadelphia Eagles Offenive coordinator Sean Mannion has to be an upgrade over the dismal Kevin Patullo offense of 2025. Jalen Hurts still has his limitations, and the departure of A.J. Brown will undoubtedly hurt, but heavier personnel behind a quality offensive line should lend itself to a more run-oriented attack. If Philadelphia can get Saquon Barkley going with more 12-personnel looks, the Eagles could remain a force to be reckoned with. Howie Roseman has built a deep roster, and the team still boasts one of the league’s best defenses under Vic Fangio. No. 7 — Houston Texans DeMeco Ryans is one of the best coaches in the NFL, with one of the most physical defenses that only allowed 17.4 points per game last season, which was second in the NFL. They were first in yards allowed per game, with a 277.2 average. Reed Blankenship and Jadeveon Clowney were added in the offseason, but the offense added several playmakers to help CJ Stroud and star receiver Nico Collins. Drafting Keylan Rutledge in the first round should help the newly-acquired David Montgomery establish the run, while Kayshon Boutte will operate as a solid number two behind Collins now that Jayden Higgins tore his ACL. The big question is Stroud, who enters a massive year for his reputation and future contract — his fifth-year option was exercised for 2027. No. 8 — Baltimore Ravens John Harbaugh’s squad had a step-back year in 2025 due to a variety of issues, including injuries to Lamar Jackson. Baltimore finished 8-9, fired Harbaugh after the Week 18 missed Tyler Loop field goal that propelled the Steelers into the playoffs, and then went on to hire Chargers’ defensive coordinator Jesse Minter to be head coach, with Declan Doyle coordinating the offense. Doyle is an extension of the Sean Payton and Ben Johnson trees. Baltimore lost some pieces on offense, but the talent of Lamar Jackson — with a fresh approach — is still dangerous. No. 9 — Dallas Cowboys Dallas made upgrades across their defense, but none more important than defensive coordinator Christian Parker, who takes over for Matt Eberflus. With the additions of Caleb Downs, Rashan Gary, Jalen Thompson, and Cobie Durant, along with the retention of Quinnen Williams and Kenny Clark, Parker gives the team a much higher floor. The offense still has two of the league’s best receivers and a strong offensive line, though the loss of guard Tyler Smith is devastating. Prescott is one of the quickest-processing quarterbacks in the league, and Dallas — unfortunately — should be a much better than their 2025 7-9-1 record. No. 10 — Cincinnati Bengals The Bengals have traditionally been a slow-starting team, but any offense with Joe Burrow, Ja’Marr Chase, and Tee Higgins is a threat that deserves respect. The trenches were beefed up on defense; the presence of Dexter Lawrence and Jonathan Allen should give Al Golden the type of unit that can shut down opposing rushing attacks. The roster isn’t elite, but the Bengals are always a threat because of their signal caller. No. 11 — Chicago Bears Ben Johnson is one of the most exciting coaches in the NFL — one who is striving to beat the NFL scoring record. The offense is poised to take a massive step despite the loss of DJ Moore. Johnson drafted Luther Burden III and Colston Loveland — both of whom should have monster seasons alongside Rome Odunze and a solid rushing attack led by D’Andre Swift. The defense, however, could be a problem, especially after the trade of Gervon Dexter. Dennis Allen is one of the best defensive minds in the sport; the personnel is solid, but the unit was opportunistic last year. They were +22 in turnover differential with 33 turnovers forced — will that carry over? No. 12 — Los Angeles Chargers The Chargers brought in Mike McDaniel to coordinate a Justin Herbert offense; McDaniel had Tua Tagovailoa looking like an MVP, and a rushing attack that was efficient and effective. McDaniel could take this offense into the top-five, with Justin Herbert as a true MVP candidate. There were upgrades on the offensive line with the signing of Cole Strange, while both Rashawn Slater and Joe Alt return healthy. The defense,…

title: Giants-Cowboys, Week 1: 5 storylines for the season opener
summary: The long wait for regular-season New York Giants football is nearly over. Here are five storylines to watch for Sunday’s season-opening game against the Dallas Cowboys. Will Malik Nabers play? The release of Darius Slayton has to be a sign that the Giants believe Nabers, their most explosive offensive player, will be ready to take […]
full_text: Malik Nabers | Getty Images The long wait for regular-season New York Giants football is nearly over. Here are five storylines to watch for Sunday’s season-opening game against the Dallas Cowboys. Will Malik Nabers play? The release of Darius Slayton has to be a sign that the Giants believe Nabers, their most explosive offensive player, will be ready to take the field Sunday night. That is not guaranteed, though, as Nabers works back from a torn ACL. If he plays, how much will he play? How well will he play? How will he react to getting hit for the first time? Right now, these are all questions without answers. How will the Giants replace Slayton? After releasing Slayton on Monday, the Giants did not fill their open roster spot on Tuesday. Will they do so on Wednesday? Whenever they do it, who will get the 53rd roster spot? The most obvious thing to do is replace a wide receiver with a wide receiver. That would likely mean adding either Braxton Berrios or Dalen Cambre to the 53-man roster. If the Giants go that way, my guess would be Cambre. As a vested veteran, Berrios’ salary would be fully guaranteed for the season if he were to sign to the 53-man roster before Week 1. The Giants might want to have both on the gameday roster, and as a second-year player Cambre would cost less. Linebacker Malik Harrison and edge defender Trace Ford could also be possibilities Caleb Downs revenge game Early in Harbaugh’s tenure as head coach, podcast host Mike Francesa asked him about Ohio State Caleb Downs. What Harbaugh said made just about everyone who follows the draft begin connecting Downs and the Giants. “Big fan, big fan,” Harbaugh said of Downs. “We favor Hall of Fame safeties, so if we have a chance to draft a potential future Hall of Fame safety in Caleb Downs, that would be just fine with me. “We’ll take the best player. You know, when you draft that high, you take the best player. It’s not a need pick. It’s the best player pick because you’re going for the guy that’s going to be that kind of a player. You’re talking about a guy that you would like to see someday wearing a gold jacket if possible. That’s what the goal is with that pick. … That guy would be just fine with me. I’d take him in a second.” Then, the Giants passed twice on chances to select Downs. They took linebacker Arvell Reese No. 5, and guard Sisi Mauigoa No. 10. The Giants are quite happy with both players, with each having given indications they will live up to their draft positions. Still, the Cowboys took Downs No. 11, meaning the Giants will have to see Downs twice a year for the foreseeable future. Will Downs make them play. Will Tae Banks really start? The Giants’ unofficial depth chart shows Banks as a starter instead of Paulson Adebo. Considering the way the pst two seasons went for Banks — poor play, poor tackling, poor attitude — and thew fact that Adebo is the highest-paid cornerback on the roster, Banks as a starter and Adebo as a bench player would be a stunning outcome. That, though, appears to be what we will see on Sunday night. Change in fortunes? The Giants’ struggles at the beginnings of seasons have been well-documented. I wrote this a few days ago : The Giants have begun seasons 0-2 or worse in 10 of the last 13 years. It seems appropriate that the Giants will begin the John Harbaugh era in a nationally-televised game against the Cowboys. The Giants and Cowboys have played seven times in season-opening games since 2012. The Giants are 1-6 in those games, with their only victory coming in 2016. Primetime games at any time of the year have not been kind to the Giants, either. Since 2014, the Giants are 11-36, a .234 winning percentage, in primetime. Sunday, they get the trifecta. The Giants get the Cowboys in a primetime season-opening game. Will things be any different this season?

title: New York Jets Flight Connections 09/10/26
summary: When you go to your state fair, most people enjoy going on the rides. However, New York Jets fans have been playing a cruel version of musical chairs all offseason. It seemed like the music had stopped last week when the Jets claimed Blake Grupe off waivers from the Indianapolis Colts. Hey coach, we have […]
full_text: Indianapolis Colts kicker Blake Grupe (10) prepares to kick the ball Monday, Aug. 3, 2026, during practice at Colts Camp at Grand Park in Westfield. | USA TODAY Network via Reuters Co When you go to your state fair, most people enjoy going on the rides. However, New York Jets fans have been playing a cruel version of musical chairs all offseason. It seemed like the music had stopped last week when the Jets claimed Blake Grupe off waivers from the Indianapolis Colts. Hey coach, we have our starting kicker for the Tennessee Titans game, right? “Well, we still have Jason (Sanders), that’s on the practice squad, and I’m going to let that play out, right. Those guys are going to continue to kick, continue to compete. And again, we’ll make the right decision when that decision needs to be done,” head coach Aaron Glenn responded.
